=== NOTES 2:34 | Budget in Parliament – Stages, Cut Motions, Appropriation and Finance Bills, Funds
## SUB 0 | Annual Financial Statement (Art. 112) – Budget Basics, Presentation and Firsts
[34:0:0] # Article 112 – the "Budget"
[34:0:1] - **Constitutional name:** the Budget = **Annual Financial Statement (AFS)**, **Article 112** – a statement of the **estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year** (not the Economic Survey, not last year's surplus).
[34:0:2] - **"Budget" not in the Constitution:** the word **Budget** nowhere appears; Annual Financial Statement, Appropriation Bill and Consolidated Fund of India do. (Budget ← French **"bougette"** = little bag.)
[34:0:3] - **Laid by:** the **President** "causes" the AFS to be laid before **both Houses** every financial year; the **Finance Minister** presents it in the **Lok Sabha** (Union Budget 2023-24: **Nirmala Sitharaman**).
[34:0:4] - **Financial year:** **1 April – 31 March**; Budget shown as **Revenue Budget + Capital Budget**; it must show **charged** and **voted** expenditure separately (Art. 112(2)).
[34:0:5] - **Prepared by:** the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs (DEA)**, Ministry of Finance – not Revenue, Expenditure or Financial Services; process starts with the **Budget Circular** (usually **September**).
[34:0:6] - **Halwa ceremony** (North Block) marks the start of the secrecy/printing of Budget documents.
[34:0:7] - **Economic Survey:** prepared by the Finance Ministry (DEA), presented **before** the Budget (a day or a few days earlier).
[34:0:8] # Budget articles in order
[34:0:9] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [34:0:9.0] 112 | Annual Financial Statement; 112(3) charged items
  [34:0:9.1] 113 | Estimates as Demands for Grants; only LS votes; Art. 113(3) President's recommendation
  [34:0:9.2] 114 | Appropriation Bill; 114(3) no withdrawal except under appropriation by law
  [34:0:9.3] 115 | Supplementary, additional, excess grants
  [34:0:9.4] 116 | Vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional grants
  [34:0:9.5] 117 | Financial Bills (President's recommendation)
  [34:0:9.6] 265 | No tax except by authority of law
  [34:0:9.7] 266 / 267 | Consolidated Fund & Public Account / Contingency Fund
[34:0:10] # Firsts and changes in practice
[34:0:11] TABLE head: Fact | Detail
  [34:0:11.0] First Budget of independent India | 26 Nov 1947, R.K. Shanmukham Chetty – the first Finance Minister (John Mathai 2nd, C.D. Deshmukh 3rd)
  [34:0:11.1] Time of presentation | 5 p.m. (colonial) → 11 a.m. from 2001 (Yashwant Sinha)
  [34:0:11.2] Railway Budget | Separated 1924 (Acworth Committee, 1921); merged in 2017; first combined Budget by Arun Jaitley, 1 Feb 2017
  [34:0:11.3] Budget date | 1 February from 2017 (earlier last working day of February)
  [34:0:11.4] Outcome Budget / Gender Budget Statement | First in 2005-06
  [34:0:11.5] Union Budget 2012-13 | Presented 16 March 2012 (Pranab Mukherjee)
[34:0:12] # Latest budgets (as of 2026)
[34:0:13] - **Union Budget 2026-27:** presented **1 Feb 2026**; proposed an **Economic Stabilisation Fund** of **Rs 1 lakh crore**.
[34:0:14] - **AP Budget 2026-27:** **14 Feb 2026**, FM **Payyavula Keshav**; separate **agriculture budget** by **K. Atchannaidu** – AP is one of the few States with a separate **Agriculture Budget**.
[34:0:15] - **Interim Budget 2019-20:** **Piyush Goyal**, 1 Feb 2019 – **'Vision 2030'** with **ten dimensions**, the first: infrastructure for a **USD 10 trillion** economy.
[34:0:16] > Exam angle: "Article for AFS" (asked ×7) → 112; "term not in the Constitution" → Budget; "who prepares" → DEA; "first FM / first Budget" → Shanmukham Chetty.

## SUB 1 | Consolidated Fund, Public Account and Contingency Fund (Arts. 266-267)
[34:1:0] TABLE head: Basis | Consolidated Fund of India | Public Account of India | Contingency Fund of India
  [34:1:0.0] Article (Union / States) | 266(1) / 266(1) | 266(2) / 266(2) | 267(1) / 267(2)
  [34:1:0.1] Receipts | All revenues (taxes and other receipts), all loans (Treasury Bills, ways and means advances), loan repayments | Money held in trust: provident funds, small savings, judicial deposits, savings bank deposits, remittances | Imprest for unforeseen expenditure
  [34:1:0.2] Withdrawal | Only under appropriation made by law – Parliament's authorisation (Art. 266(3), 114) | Executive action, no vote of Parliament (banking transactions) | Advance by the President, before Parliament's approval
  [34:1:0.3] Controlled by | Parliament | Executive | President; held by the Finance Secretary, DEA (not Expenditure)
[34:1:1] - **All revenues** of the Union by taxes and other receipts → **Consolidated Fund of India** (not Public Account or Contingency Fund).
[34:1:2] - **Withdrawal from the CFI:** authorisation must come from **Parliament** (an Appropriation Act) – not the President, PM, Finance Minister or CAG. In India the CAG has **no "comptroller" power** over issue of money; the Ministries draw under the Appropriation Act.
[34:1:3] - **Article for "no money withdrawn from the CFI without Parliament's sanction":** **Art. 266(3)** (appropriation "in accordance with law") read with **Art. 114(3)**.
[34:1:4] - **Contingency Fund of India:** created by **Parliament by law** – **Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950**; at the **President's disposal**, who **advances** money for **unforeseen** expenditure (also additional/excess needs) **pending authorisation** by Parliament – spent **before** Parliament's approval. Corpus **Rs 30,000 crore** from **2021-22** (Rs 500 crore from 2005; Rs 50 crore earlier).
[34:1:5] - **State Contingency Fund:** established by the **State Legislature** by law (**Art. 267(2)**); placed at the disposal of the **Governor**, who operates it (not the CM or State FM).
[34:1:6] - **CAG** audits all three funds of the Union and the States.
[34:1:7] > Exam angle: "Contingency Fund – Article?" → 267; "State Contingency Fund – who operates?" → Governor (asked ×4); "authorisation for CFI withdrawal" → Parliament (×3).
[34:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.364-365 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.370 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Constitution Arts. 266, 267
## SUB 2 | Charged Expenditure on the Consolidated Fund (Art. 112(3))
[34:2:0] - **Charged expenditure** = expenditure from the CFI that the Constitution makes **non-votable** – **not submitted to the vote** of Parliament but **can be discussed** in either House (Art. 113(1)); it still needs an Appropriation Act (Art. 114).
[34:2:1] # Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India – Art. 112(3)
[34:2:2] - **President** – emoluments, allowances, office expenses (Art. 59(3)).
[34:2:3] - **Chairman and Deputy Chairman** of the RS; **Speaker and Deputy Speaker** of the LS – salaries and allowances (Art. 97).
[34:2:4] - **Supreme Court judges** – salaries, allowances, **pensions** (Art. 125); SC administrative expenses.
[34:2:5] - **High Court judges** – **only pensions** (Art. 112(3)(d)(iii)); their **salaries** are charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State** (Art. 202(3)(d); salaries fixed under Art. 221).
[34:2:6] - **CAG** – salary, allowances, pension and office expenses (Art. 148).
[34:2:7] - **UPSC** chairman and members – salaries, allowances, pensions (Art. 322); a **State PSC's expenses** are charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State** (Art. 322).
[34:2:8] - **Debt charges** of the Government of India; sums to satisfy a **judgment, decree or arbitral award**; anything Parliament declares charged.
[34:2:9] # Not charged (voted)
[34:2:10] - **Prime Minister and Ministers** – salaries fixed by Parliament (Art. 75(6)); **voted**, not charged.
[34:2:11] - **Election Commission** – salaries and expenses are **voted**, not charged.
[34:2:12] - **Vice-President:** no salary **as VP**; he draws it **as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** – that salary is **charged on the CFI** (not paid from the Public Account).
[34:2:13] - **Governor:** emoluments charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State** (Art. 158(3)), not the CFI; one Governor for two or more States → shared in the proportion the **President** fixes by order (**Art. 158(3A)**). Governors' pensions are not in Art. 112(3).
[34:2:14] - **Second Schedule** – emoluments, allowances and privileges; **Third Schedule** – forms of oaths.
[34:2:15] > Exam angle: "NOT charged on the CFI" → PM / Ministers, Election Commission, (VP as such); "HC judges' salaries" → State Consolidated Fund, pensions → CFI.
[34:2:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.365 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.365 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Constitution Arts. 112(3), 158, 202, 322
## SUB 3 | Stages of the Budget, Demands for Grants, Guillotine and Cut Motions
[34:3:0] # Six stages (Laxmikanth)
[34:3:1] - **1. Presentation** of the Budget (no discussion that day).
[34:3:2] - **2. General discussion** – both Houses, 3-4 days; no cut motion, no vote.
[34:3:3] - **3. Scrutiny by the Departmentally Related Standing Committees** (House adjourned 3-4 weeks).
[34:3:4] - **4. Voting on Demands for Grants** (Art. 113) – **Lok Sabha only**; estimates of expenditure are submitted as **Demands for Grants**; it may pass, reject or **reduce**, never increase; a **demand becomes a grant after it is voted**.
[34:3:5] - **5. Passing of the Appropriation Bill** (Art. 114).
[34:3:6] - **6. Passing of the Finance Bill** – last stage; gives effect to the tax proposals.
[34:3:7] - **Sequence:** Presentation → DRSC scrutiny → **Appropriation Bill → Finance Bill**. The **vote on account** is passed **after the general discussion** (before the demands are voted).
[34:3:8] - **Not stages** of normal financial legislation: vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional grants.
[34:3:9] - **Guillotine:** on the last allotted day the **Speaker** puts **all remaining demands** to vote – those **not discussed for want of time** – at once.
[34:3:10] # Cut motions – motions to reduce a demand
[34:3:11] TABLE head: Cut motion | Reduces the demand | Purpose
  [34:3:11.0] Policy cut | To Re 1 | Disapproval of the policy behind the demand
  [34:3:11.1] Economy cut | By a specified amount | Economy in expenditure
  [34:3:11.2] Token cut | By Rs 100 | Air a specific grievance within the Government's responsibility
[34:3:12] - **Object:** to **move a proposal to reduce expenditure** in the Budget (a demand for grant) and draw the House's attention to a matter.
[34:3:13] - Moved **only in the Lok Sabha**, at the **voting on Demands for Grants**; **admitted at the discretion of the Speaker**; cannot relate to charged expenditure.
[34:3:14] - **Passage** = loss of confidence → the Government is expected to **resign**.
[34:3:15] > Exam angle: guillotine = undiscussed demands; cut motion admitted by the Speaker; order "I, II, IV, III" (Appropriation before Finance).
[34:3:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.362 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.366-369 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 4 | Vote on Account and Other Special Grants (Arts. 115-116)
[34:4:0] TABLE head: Grant | Article | Meaning
  [34:4:0.0] Supplementary | 115 | Sanctioned amount insufficient for the year
  [34:4:0.1] Additional | 115 | New service not in the Budget
  [34:4:0.2] Excess | 115 | Spent more than granted; voted after the year, PAC approval first
  [34:4:0.3] Vote on account | 116 | Advance grant for part of the year pending passage of the Budget (≈2 months, one-sixth; 3-5 months in election years)
  [34:4:0.4] Vote of credit | 116 | Blank cheque for an unexpected/indefinite demand
  [34:4:0.5] Exceptional | 116 | Not part of the current service of any year
  [34:4:0.6] Token grant | – | New service met by re-appropriation; token sum voted by the LS
[34:4:1] - **Vote on account:** needed **when the regular Budget will not be passed in time** (e.g. an election year); it lets the Government **withdraw money from the CFI** before the Appropriation Act.
[34:4:2] - **Since the 1 February Budget (2017)** a vote on account is normally needed only in **election years** (with an Interim Budget) – it has not become ineffectual.
[34:4:3] - **AP angle:** the **February 2019 AP Budget** (election year) was a **vote-on-account budget**.
[34:4:4] - **Latest:** the LS approved the **second batch of Supplementary Demands for Grants 2025-26** (Art. 115).
[34:4:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.368-370 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.360 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Constitution Arts. 115, 116
## SUB 5 | Appropriation Bill, Finance Bill and Parliamentary Control over Finance
[34:5:0] - **Appropriation Bill:** authorises withdrawal from the CFI for **voted grants + charged expenditure**; must be **passed by both Houses** (as a Money Bill) and assented to; **Art. 114(3)**: no withdrawal except under it – even charged expenditure needs it.
[34:5:1] - **No amendment** may vary the amount or alter the destination of a voted grant, or vary charged expenditure.
[34:5:2] - **Automatic repeal clause:** since the **Appropriation Act, 2016** (after the Appropriation Acts (Repeal) Act, 2016 repealed 758 old Acts) Appropriation Acts carry an **automatic repeal (sunset) clause**.
[34:5:3] - **Finance Bill:** gives effect to the tax proposals; amendments to **reduce or abolish** a tax **can** be moved, **not** to increase it; must be enacted within **75 days** (Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931). Changes in existing tax rates also need law (Art. 265) – usually via the Finance Bill.
[34:5:4] - **Parliament's control over public finance:** placing the AFS; withdrawal only after the Appropriation Act; supplementary grants and vote on account; the Finance Bill. India has **no Parliamentary Budget Office** (so UPSC 2012 answer = 1, 2, 3 and 5).
[34:5:5] - **Department of Economic Affairs** (not Revenue) prepares the Budget; **Public Account** disbursements need **no** Parliament authorisation (UPSC 2015 → only "no withdrawal from the CFI without Parliament").
[34:5:6] - **Money Bill (Art. 110(1)):** covers custody of the CFI/Contingency Fund and appropriation out of the **CFI** – not "appropriation out of the Contingency Fund".
[34:5:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.364-369 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.362 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Appropriation Acts (Repeal) Act, 2016 (Deccan Herald, deccanherald.com; PRS India)

=== NOTES 2:35 | Parliamentary Committees – Pac, Estimates, Public Undertakings, DRSCs, Ad Hoc
## SUB 0 | Financial Committees – Composition (Estimates, PAC, COPU)
[35:0:0] TABLE head: Committee | Strength | Rajya Sabha members | Chairman
  [35:0:0.0] Estimates | 30 (largest) | None – all 30 from the Lok Sabha | Appointed by the Speaker; invariably from the ruling party
  [35:0:0.1] Public Accounts (PAC) | 22 = 15 LS + 7 RS | Yes – 7 | Appointed by the Speaker; Opposition member since 1967 (convention)
  [35:0:0.2] Public Undertakings (COPU) | 22 = 15 LS + 7 RS | Yes – 7 | Appointed by the Speaker from its LS members
[35:0:1] - **The three financial committees:** **PAC, Estimates, COPU** – the Business Advisory Committee, Petitions, Government Assurances and Library committees are **not** financial committees.
[35:0:2] - **Only committee with no RS member:** the **Estimates Committee** (PAC, COPU, Government Assurances, Petitions all have RS members/counterparts). Committee on Empowerment of Women is joint (20 LS + 10 RS).
[35:0:3] - **Election:** members elected **every year** by **proportional representation – single transferable vote**; **term one year**; **Ministers ineligible**.
[35:0:4] - **PAC** is a **joint committee** of both Houses (LS members elected by the LS, 7 RS members associated) – not a select committee of the LS alone.
[35:0:5] - **⚠ Trap:** "Estimates = 20 LS + 10 RS" is **false** (that is the SC/ST Welfare or Women's Empowerment committee).
[35:0:6] - **Budget** = control **before** spending; financial committees = scrutiny **after** – they support, not replace, the budgetary process.
[35:0:7] > Exam angle: "no RS member" (asked ×9) → Estimates; "largest" → Estimates; "not a financial committee" → Business Advisory.
[35:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.365-367 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.394-399 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 1 | Public Accounts Committee – Functions, Chairman, Reports
[35:1:0] - **Oldest parliamentary committee:** PAC, first set up in **1921** under the **Government of India Act, 1919**.
[35:1:1] - **Function:** examines the **Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts** and the **CAG's audit reports** – the financial accounts of the Government; checks that money was spent "**within the scope of the demand**"; looks at waste, loss and nugatory expenditure.
[35:1:2] - **"Watchdog"** on departmental expenditure and irregularities; the **CAG** is its "guide, friend and philosopher" and assists it.
[35:1:3] - **Limits:** a **post-mortem** check; not concerned with **policy**; recommendations **advisory**; cannot appoint officials or issue orders.
[35:1:4] - **Chairman:** **appointed (nominated) by the Speaker** from its members; since **1967** an **Opposition** member by **convention** – not a rule of procedure, law or Presidential order.
[35:1:5] - **Reports:** submitted to the **Speaker / Lok Sabha** (i.e. to Parliament; a copy laid in the RS) – not the President, PM, FM or CAG.
[35:1:6] # Chairmen asked
[35:1:7] TABLE head: Period | PAC chairman
  [35:1:7.0] 2009-14 (incl. 2010-11) | Murli Manohar Joshi (BJP, Opposition)
  [35:1:7.1] 2024-27 (as of 2026) | K.C. Venugopal (Congress, Opposition)
[35:1:8] > Exam angle: "who nominates PAC chairman" (asked ×6) → Speaker; "PAC submits report to" → Speaker/Lok Sabha; "Opposition chair – why?" → convention.
[35:1:9] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.396-398 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.366-367 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Lok Sabha – Committee on Public Accounts (loksabha.nic.in)
## SUB 2 | Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings
[35:2:0] # Estimates Committee
[35:2:1] - **Origin:** traces to the Standing Financial Committee (1921); first post-independence Estimates Committee **1950** on the recommendation of **John Mathai** (then FM); 25 members, raised to **30 in 1956**.
[35:2:2] - **Function (Rule 310):** report what **economies, improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform** consistent with the policy underlying the estimates may be effected; suggest **alternative policies** for efficiency and economy in administration; suggest the form of the estimates → a **"continuous economy committee"**.
[35:2:3] - **⚠ Key:** "Estimates Committee – which reform to ensure efficiency?" → **administrative reform** (the words of the rule), not new legislation, defence, electoral or judicial reform.
[35:2:4] - **Limits:** examines estimates only after they are voted; cannot question policy laid down by Parliament; no CAG assistance; advisory.
[35:2:5] - **Chairmen asked:** **Ummareddy Venkateswarlu** (1999-2004, 13th LS); **Sanjay Jaiswal** (18th LS, as of 2026).
[35:2:6] # Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU)
[35:2:7] - Created **1964** on the recommendation of the **Krishna Menon Committee**; 15 (10 LS + 5 RS) raised to **22 (15 + 7) in 1974**.
[35:2:8] - Examines reports and accounts of public undertakings and the CAG's reports on them; whether they run on sound business principles; not major policy or day-to-day administration.
[35:2:9] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.398-400 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.366 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure Rule 310; Wikipedia, Estimates Committee (list of chairpersons, citing loksabha.nic.in)
## SUB 3 | Other Standing Committees – Petitions, Subordinate Legislation, Assurances, Offices of Profit
[35:3:0] # Six groups of standing committees (Laxmikanth)
[35:3:1] - **Financial** (PAC, Estimates, COPU); **24 DRSCs**; **to inquire** (Petitions, Privileges, Ethics); **to scrutinise and control** (Government Assurances, Subordinate Legislation, Papers Laid, **Welfare of SCs and STs**, Empowerment of Women, Offices of Profit); **day-to-day business** (Business Advisory, Private Members' Bills, Rules, Absence of Members); **house-keeping** (General Purposes, House, Library, Salaries of MPs).
[35:3:2] - **Welfare of SCs and STs** is itself a standing committee (30 = 20 LS + 10 RS; **Ministers cannot serve**; examines the reports of the **National Commissions for SCs and STs** and welfare programmes) – it is the **only one of PAC / Estimates / COPU / SC-ST that is not a financial committee**.
[35:3:3] - **No parliamentary committee on Welfare of Minorities** (there are committees on Public Undertakings, Government Assurances, Estimates; OBC welfare is an LS committee).
[35:3:4] TABLE head: Committee | Function | Strength / note
  [35:3:4.0] Petitions | Petitions on Bills and public-interest matters; representations of citizens – the "Ombudsman" of Parliament | LS 15, RS 10
  [35:3:4.1] Subordinate Legislation | Whether rules, regulations, sub-rules, bye-laws made under powers delegated by Parliament or conferred by the Constitution are properly exercised by the Executive | 15 each House (1953)
  [35:3:4.2] Government Assurances | Tracks ministers' assurances till implemented | LS 15, RS 10 (1953)
  [35:3:4.3] Joint Committee on Offices of Profit | Which offices should disqualify MPs | 15 = 10 LS + 5 RS
  [35:3:4.4] Privileges | Breach of privilege | LS 15, RS 10
  [35:3:4.5] Ethics | Members' conduct | RS 4 Mar 1997, LS 16 May 2000
  [35:3:4.6] Business Advisory | Allots time for Government and other business | LS 15, Speaker chairs
[35:3:5] - **Delegated legislation** = rule-making power **delegated by the legislature to the executive**; watched by the Committee on Subordinate Legislation.
[35:3:6] - **Lok Sabha-only:** Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions; Committee on Absence of Members.
[35:3:7] - **Watchdog group** (NextGen): Subordinate Legislation, Government Assurances, Estimates, PAC, COPU, DRSCs – **not** the Business Advisory Committee.
[35:3:8] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.394-395, 405-407 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.365-366 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Lok Sabha – Committee on Petitions (loksabha.nic.in)
## SUB 4 | Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs)
[35:4:0] - **Set up 1993** (17) on the recommendation of the **Rules Committee** of the Lok Sabha; **24 since 2004** = **16 under the Lok Sabha + 8 under the Rajya Sabha**.
[35:4:1] - **Each: 31 members = 21 LS + 10 RS** → standing committees draw LS and RS members in the ratio **2 : 1**; **quorum 11**; **Ministers ineligible**; term one year.
[35:4:2] - **Functions:** examine **Demands for Grants** (between general discussion and voting), **Bills referred**, **annual reports** and long-term policy documents of their ministries; no cut-motion-type suggestions.
[35:4:3] - **Regulators:** the **DRSCs** and **ad hoc committees** (e.g. the 2G JPC) may review independent regulators (telecom, insurance, electricity) – not the Finance Commission, FSLRC or NITI Aayog (UPSC 2019 → 1 and 2).
[35:4:4] - **Chairs asked (APPSC G1 2004):** Railways – **Basudeb Acharia**, Defence – **Balasaheb Vikhe Patil** (14th LS) and External Affairs – Laxminarayan Pandey are given as correct; the Committee on **Food – A. Narendra** pairing is the **wrong** one (printed key; chair lists not independently verified).
[35:4:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.400-405 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); PRS India, UPSC 2019 answer explanation
## SUB 5 | Ad Hoc Committees, JPCs and the Role of Committees
[35:5:0] - **Role:** Parliament exercises control over the **administration** mainly **through parliamentary committees** – detailed scrutiny the whole House has no time for (not via ministries' advisory committees or writs).
[35:5:1] - **Ad hoc committees:** temporary, end with the report – (i) **Inquiry committees** (e.g. on the conduct of members during the President's address, Railway Convention Committee, MPLADS); (ii) **Advisory committees** – **Select / Joint Committees on Bills**, Committee on the **Draft Five Year Plan** → "all the above".
[35:5:2] - A Bill goes to a Select Committee (one House) or Joint Committee (both Houses) by a **motion adopted in the House**.
[35:5:3] TABLE head: JPC on | Year | Chairman
  [35:5:3.0] Bofors | 1987 | B. Shankaranand
  [35:5:3.1] Harshad Mehta securities scam | 1992 | Ram Niwas Mirdha
  [35:5:3.2] Ketan Parekh scam | 2001 | Lt Gen Prakash Mani Tripathi (retd)
  [35:5:3.3] Soft-drink pesticides | 2003 | Sharad Pawar
  [35:5:3.4] 2G spectrum | 2011 | P.C. Chacko (report to Speaker Meira Kumar)

=== NOTES 2:36 | Parliamentary Privileges; Anti-defection Law (tenth Schedule) and the Speaker
## SUB 0 | Tenth Schedule – 52nd and 91st Amendments, Dates and Firsts
[36:0:0] # The 52nd Amendment, 1985
[36:0:1] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [36:0:1.0] Law | 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 – added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law); amended Arts 101, 102, 190 and 191
  [36:0:1.1] Bill | Passed by Parliament 30-31 January 1985; Presidential assent 15 February 1985 (the date most keys give as "Bill passed")
  [36:0:1.2] In force | 1 March 1985
  [36:0:1.3] Aim | Curb defections "induced by the lure of office", ensure party discipline and stable governments; ban floor crossing by members elected on a party ticket
  [36:0:1.4] First | First constitutional recognition of political parties (1985) – the term "political party" appears in the Tenth Schedule
[36:0:2] - **Asked as:** "52nd Amendment relates to" → **Defection**; "Tenth Schedule deals with" → **anti-defection / defections** (not official languages = Part XVII/8th Sch., not land reforms = 9th, not Panchayati Raj = 11th); "anti-defection enacted in" → **1985**; "which amendment first introduced anti-defection" → **52nd** (not 44th, 54th, 61st, 86th, 92nd, nor the Representation of the People Act).
[36:0:3] - **Applies to:** members of **both Houses of Parliament and the State Legislatures** (MPs and MLAs, incl. **MLCs**) – party, **independent** and **nominated** members.
[36:0:4] - **Not applicable to the presidential election:** the Schedule covers voting **in the House**; no binding whip operates in the electoral college.
[36:0:5] # Before 1985
[36:0:6] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [36:0:6.0] 1967 | "Aaya Ram Gaya Ram" (Gaya Lal, Haryana); Y.B. Chavan Committee on defections (1967-69)
  [36:0:6.1] 1973, 1978 | Anti-defection Bills lapsed
  [36:0:6.2] 1979 | Jammu and Kashmir – first State with its own anti-defection law
  [36:0:6.3] 1984 | AP: Nadendla Bhaskara Rao toppled N.T. Rama Rao's government; NTR restored after a month
[36:0:7] - **⚠ Trap:** the **old Tenth Schedule** (Sikkim's association with India) was added by the **35th Amendment (1974)** and omitted by the **36th (1975)** – not the anti-defection schedule.
[36:0:8] # 91st Amendment, 2003
[36:0:9] TABLE head: Change | Provision
  [36:0:9.0] One-third split exception deleted | Para 3 omitted
  [36:0:9.1] Union ministry ≤ 15% of Lok Sabha strength | Art. 75(1A)
  [36:0:9.2] State ministry ≤ 15% of Assembly, minimum 12 | Art. 164(1A)
  [36:0:9.3] Disqualified defector barred from Minister / remunerative political post until re-elected | Arts 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B (361B = remunerative political post)
[36:0:10] - 91st Amendment statement test: capped the Union and State Councils of Ministers ✓, deleted the split ✓; it did **not** touch Art. 105 privileges.
[36:0:11] > Exam angle: "52nd / 1985 / Tenth Schedule / J&K 1979 / 15 Feb (assent) / 1 March 1985 (in force)" – one cluster asked ~16 times.
[36:0:12] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Sheets #77 p.91-92 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Anti-defection Law p.843-846 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt); app notes 2:36 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 1 | Grounds of Disqualification, Merger and Split
[36:1:0] TABLE head: Member | Disqualified if | Exception / allowed
  [36:1:0.0] Party member | Voluntarily gives up party membership (inferred from conduct); votes or abstains against the whip without prior permission (Para 2(1)(b)) | Prior permission, or the party condones within 15 days
  [36:1:0.1] Independent | Joins any political party after election | May become a Minister without joining a party
  [36:1:0.2] Nominated | Joins a party after six months of taking his seat | May join within six months; not joining is no ground
  [36:1:0.3] Presiding officer | Joins another party (Para 5) | May give up party membership on election to the Chair and rejoin after demitting office – both are exceptions
[36:1:1] - **Giving up membership ≠ resigning:** conduct such as campaigning for a rival party is enough (Ravi S. Naik 1994).
[36:1:2] - **Expelled member:** does **not lose his seat**; he still belongs to the party for Tenth Schedule purposes (G. Viswanathan 1996) and sits as unattached; joining another party then = giving up membership.
[36:1:3] - **Merger (Para 4, in force):** no disqualification when the **original party merges** with another and **not less than two-thirds** of its legislature party agree.
[36:1:4] - **Split (Para 3, one-third):** **deleted by the 91st Amendment (2003)** – a one-third group that breaks away is now disqualified.
[36:1:5]   - Number test: party of **100** MLAs – no break-away faction is protected now; a merger needs **67**. **34** (one-third) was the pre-2003 answer.
[36:1:6] - **Statements commonly marked wrong:** "one-third split protects" ✗; "disqualified defector can become a Minister" ✗; "nominated member who fails to join a party in six months is disqualified" ✗; "expelled member loses his seat" ✗; "Speaker not disqualified if he joins another party" ✗.
[36:1:7] - **Criticism – en-bloc defections:** it "banned only **retail** defections and legalised **wholesale** defections" – **en-bloc (bulk) defection** via merger is not covered; individual defection, defections in spells and votes against the whip are.
[36:1:8] - **Main criticism:** it stifles intra-party **dissent** and members' free expression, yet has not stopped mass defections (the two-thirds merger route can **defend mass defection**).
[36:1:9] > Exam angle: "merger fraction" = **two-thirds** (asked ×3); "not covered by the law" = **en-bloc defections**; UPSC 2022 – nominated member six-month statement ✗, no time-frame ✓.
[36:1:10] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Sheets #77 p.91-92, #54 p.25 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Anti-defection Law p.844-846 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt); app notes 2:36 (sub 3, 4)
## SUB 2 | Parliamentary Privileges – Articles 105, 194 and 122
[36:2:0] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [36:2:0.0] 105 / 194 | Powers, privileges and immunities of each House, its members and committees – Parliament / State Legislatures; free speech (105(1)) and immunity for anything said or voted (105(2))
  [36:2:0.1] 122 / 212 | Courts cannot inquire into proceedings for irregularity of procedure
[36:2:1] - **Not codified** in a single statute; rest on the Constitution, conventions (originally the House of Commons), rules, statutes and court rulings.
[36:2:2] - **Notice:** Lok Sabha **Rule 222** / Rajya Sabha **Rule 187** – a member raises breach of privilege or contempt by a minister, member or outsider.
[36:2:3] - **Procedure:** Presiding Officer consents → House or **Privileges Committee** examines → the **House decides**. Committee: LS **15** members nominated by the Speaker; RS **10**, usually chaired by the **Deputy Chairman**.
[36:2:4] TABLE head: Collective (of each House) | Individual (of members)
  [36:2:4.0] Publish its debates and proceedings; restrain others from publishing | Freedom of speech in the House and committees
  [36:2:4.1] Exclude strangers; hold secret sittings | Freedom from arrest in civil cases – during a session and 40 days before and after; not in criminal or preventive detention cases
  [36:2:4.2] Make its own rules; regulate internal affairs | Exemption from jury service; may refuse to attend as a witness while the House sits
  [36:2:4.3] Receive immediate information of a member's arrest, detention, conviction or release | 
  [36:2:4.4] Punish members and outsiders for breach or contempt | 
  [36:2:4.5] No arrest or legal process within the precincts without the presiding officer's permission | 
[36:2:5] - **Punishments:** **reprimand, admonition, imprisonment** (only till the session ends), and for members **suspension or expulsion** (seat declared vacant). **No fine**; "six months' imprisonment" ✗.
[36:2:6] - **Contempt is wider** than breach: every breach is contempt, but not every contempt (e.g. disobeying a House order) is a breach of a specific privilege.
[36:2:7] - "Privileges are only collective" ✗ / "only individual" ✗ – they are **both**.
[36:2:8] TABLE head: Case | Holding
  [36:2:8.0] Raja Ram Pal (2007) | Expulsion valid; privilege decisions reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality
  [36:2:8.1] Sita Soren (2024) | 7 judges: no immunity for bribery to speak or vote; overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)
[36:2:9] > Exam angle: "courts barred from inquiring" = **Art. 122**; privileges article = **105**; "wrong statement" = arrest immunity "whether in session or not" ✗; punishment = **expulsion**, not fine.
[36:2:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.378 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity APPSC 21 p.9 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-21.txt); app notes 2:36 (sub 0)
## SUB 3 | Speaker as Deciding Authority and Key Cases
[36:3:0] TABLE head: Basis | Defection | General disqualification
  [36:3:0.0] Provisions | Tenth Schedule; Arts 102(2), 191(2) | Arts 102(1), 103 / 191(1), 192
  [36:3:0.1] Decided by | Speaker / Chairman acting as a tribunal (Para 6) | President / Governor
  [36:3:0.2] ECI | Not consulted | Opinion binding (for MPs and State legislators alike)
[36:3:1] - **Final decision** on a Lok Sabha member's defection: the **Speaker** – not the President, Vice-President or ECI. "President decides on the Council of Ministers' advice" ✗ (UPSC 2025).
[36:3:2] - **Speaker's own disqualification:** decided by **such member of the House as the House may elect** (Para 6(1)).
[36:3:3] - **Petition needed:** the presiding officer acts on a petition by a member – **no suo motu** case (Defection Rules 1985).
[36:3:4] - **No time limit** in the Schedule; Speakers stay members of their parties – hence delays.
[36:3:5] - **Para 7** (bar on courts) **struck down** in Kihoto: it needed State **ratification under Art. 368(2)**. **Judicial review only after** the decision, on limited grounds – mala fides, perversity, natural justice, constitutional mandate.
[36:3:6] TABLE head: Case | Holding
  [36:3:6.0] Kihoto Hollohan (1992) | Tenth Schedule valid (no violation of free speech or basic structure); Para 7 struck down; 3:2
  [36:3:6.1] Ravi S. Naik (1994) | Giving up membership ≠ resigning; inferred from conduct
  [36:3:6.2] G. Viswanathan (1996) | Expelled member still belongs to the party
  [36:3:6.3] Karnataka (2019) | Upheld disqualification of 17 rebel MLAs; Speaker cannot bar them from contesting
  [36:3:6.4] Keisham Meghachandra (Jan 2020) | Decide petitions ordinarily within three months; Parliament to consider a permanent independent tribunal
  [36:3:6.5] Subhash Desai (May 2023) | The political party (not the legislature party) appoints the whip and leader; legislators alone cannot bring a "deemed merger"
[36:3:7] - **Telangana (BRS) matter:** SC gave the Speaker a final **three weeks** for the last **2 of 10** BRS petitions (Feb 2026, app notes).
[36:3:8] - **Jul 2026 (app notes):** Bench of **P.S. Narasimha** and **Alok Aradhe** said gaps in Para 4 are "**matters for Parliament**".
[36:3:9] > Exam angle: "who decides" (×3) = **Speaker**; Speaker's own case = **member elected by the House**; Kihoto = validity + review; Keisham = 3 months; Desai = party appoints whip.
[36:3:10] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Sheets #77 p.92 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Anti-defection Law (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt); Tenth Schedule para 6-7; app notes 2:36 (sub 5, 6)
## SUB 4 | Working of the Law, AP Angle and Reform Proposals
[36:4:0] - **Record:** the law has not stopped defections; its main effect has been to make **presiding officers** the deciders of defection cases (often criticised for partisan delay) – APPSC ASO 2017 key.
[36:4:1] - **Resort politics:** legislators sequestered before a floor test to prevent poaching.
[36:4:2] - **Resignation route:** MLAs **resign**, lowering the majority mark, and re-contest on the new party's ticket (**Karnataka 2019, MP 2020**).
[36:4:3] - **AP 2014-19:** **23 YSRCP MLAs** moved to the TDP; the petitions were **never decided**.
[36:4:4] - **June 2019:** **4 of 6 TDP** Rajya Sabha MPs "merged" with the BJP under **Para 4**; the RS Chairman accepted it.
[36:4:5] - **Apr 2026 (app notes):** **7 of 10 AAP** Rajya Sabha MPs claimed a merger with the BJP – cited as misuse of the merger exception.
[36:4:6] TABLE head: Body | Recommendation
  [36:4:6.0] Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) | Disqualify only for voluntarily giving up membership or defying the whip on a confidence motion; decision by President/Governor on EC advice
  [36:4:6.1] Law Commission 170th Report (1999) | Delete both split and merger exceptions; treat pre-poll alliances as parties
  [36:4:6.2] NCRWC (2002) | Defectors barred from office; defector's vote invalid
  [36:4:6.3] Election Commission | President/Governor to decide on the EC's binding advice
  [36:4:6.4] Manish Tewari Bill (2010) | Limit the law to confidence and money votes
[36:4:7] - Chronology of proposals: **Goswami (1990) → Law Commission 170th (1999) → NCRWC (2002) → Tewari Bill (2010)**.
[36:4:8] - Limiting the whip to votes that threaten the government lets members **dissent freely** on other matters.
[36:4:9] - **Newer:** **fixed timelines** for Speakers and an **independent tribunal** (SC, Keisham 2020).
[36:4:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Anti-defection Law p.845-846 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt); app notes 2:36 (sub 7, 8)

=== NOTES 2:37 | Productivity and Decline of Parliament – Debate Quality, Disruptions and Reforms
## SUB 0 | Leader of the Opposition
[37:0:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [37:0:0.0] First recognised | Ram Subhag Singh (Congress-O), 1969 – the first official LoP in the Lok Sabha
  [37:0:0.1] First under the statute | Y.B. Chavan (1977) – the answer most keys give for "first LoP" when Ram Subhag Singh is not offered
  [37:0:0.2] Statute | Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977 – the office is statutory (not in the Constitution)
  [37:0:0.3] Status | Salary, allowances and facilities equal to a Cabinet Minister
  [37:0:0.4] Threshold | Largest opposition party with at least one-tenth (10%) of the House's total strength – about 55 Lok Sabha seats (Speaker's direction)
[37:0:1] - **⚠ Traps:** "**Morarji Desai** (1969-71) was the first LoP" ✗; **A.K. Gopalan** led the largest opposition group in the **first Lok Sabha** (CPI, 16 seats) but was **never recognised**; the largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha was the **CPI**, not the Swatantra Party (founded 1959); "**75 members**" ✗ (it is one-tenth); 12%, 15%, 20%, 1/5, 1/15 ✗.
[37:0:2] - **Roles:** constructive criticism and an **alternative government** (Jennings: "alternative Prime Minister"); in the USA the same functionary is the "minority leader".
[37:0:3] - **Tools:** Question Hour, motions, **PAC chaired by an Opposition member since 1967**.
[37:0:4] - **Monsoon 2026 (app notes):** united opposition pushed the **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** to a JPC.

=== NOTES 2:38 | Parliamentary Form of Government – Features, Merits, Demerits; Comparison with Presidential System
## SUB 0 | Features – Nominal Executive, Collective Responsibility, Double Membership
[38:0:0] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [38:0:0.0] Nominal and real executive | President = de jure head (Head of State), like the British Monarch; PM + Council of Ministers = real (de facto) executive
  [38:0:0.1] Aid and advice | Art. 74(1): advice binding on the President
  [38:0:0.2] Majority party rule | President appoints (Art. 75(1)) the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha, or of the alliance with a majority there, as PM – a convention
  [38:0:0.3] Collective responsibility | Art. 75(3): to the Lok Sabha only (not both Houses, not the President, not the ruling party); ministers hold office together while they command a majority – "swim and sink together"
  [38:0:0.4] Individual responsibility | Art. 75(2): ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President – individually responsible to the President (dismissed on the PM's advice)
  [38:0:0.5] Double membership | Ministers are MPs of either House; a non-member must enter Parliament within six months (Art. 75(5)), else ceases to be a minister
  [38:0:0.6] Leadership of the PM | Heads the Council of Ministers; Leader of the Lok Sabha (if a member) and chief spokesperson
  [38:0:0.7] Dissolution | Lok Sabha can be dissolved early on the PM's advice
[38:0:1] - **Not in the Constitution:** "PM is leader of the majority party" (convention); the **ranks** of ministers (Cabinet, State, Deputy).
[38:0:2] - **⚠ Traps:** collective responsibility to "Parliament" is accepted only when the Lok Sabha is not offered; "Council of Ministers responsible to both Houses" ✗ (UPSC 2007 A false, R true – members of both Houses can be ministers); "Cabinet headed by the Head of State" ✗ (UPSC 2013: 1 and 2 only); "President is the real head of the executive" ✗ (APPSC G2).
[38:0:3] - **Cabinet membership** is **not restricted** to Lok Sabha members.
[38:0:4] > Exam angle: "collectively responsible to" (×6) = **Lok Sabha**, **Art. 75(3)**; "individually responsible to" = **President**; non-member minister = **six months**.
[38:0:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-207 and ch. Central Council of Ministers (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Constitution Arts 74-75; app notes 2:38 (sub 1)
## SUB 1 | Parliamentary System – Meaning and Why India Is Parliamentary
[38:1:0] - **Names:** **cabinet government**, **responsible government**, Westminster model – the executive stays in power only while it has a **majority (confidence) in the popular House**.
[38:1:1] - **Defining test:** India is parliamentary because the **Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha** (Art. 75(3); States Art. 164(2)) – not because the Lok Sabha is directly elected, Parliament can amend the Constitution or the Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved (UPSC 2015).
[38:1:2] - **Parliamentary executive** = an executive **dependent on the support of a majority in Parliament** – not "elected by Parliament", not "Parliament acting as executive".
[38:1:3] - **Main principle:** **responsibility of the executive to the legislature**; the legislature controls the executive. "Legislature and Executive are independent" is the **presidential** feature.
[38:1:4] - **Removal:** the government is **responsible to Parliament and can be removed by it** (no-confidence) – not "all parties represented", not "elected by the people", not "fixed term" (UPSC 2020).
[38:1:5] - **Basis:** **fusion of powers** – co-operation of legislature and executive; presidential = separation of powers.
[38:1:6] - **Source of authority:** the Constitution sets up the parliamentary system at the **Centre and in the States**; both governments draw authority from the **Constitution**.
[38:1:7] - India = **secular, federal, parliamentary** – "presidential system" ✗; "government by experts" ✗ (ministers are amateurs). India is parliamentary, cabinet and responsible government.
[38:1:8] - **Statements:** "President **represents the nation but does not rule** it" ✓; "executive independent of and not accountable to the legislature" ✗.
[38:1:9] > Exam angle: "There is parliamentary government in India because…" = **CoM responsible to the Lok Sabha** (UPSC 2015 ×2); A-R UPPSC 2025: both true, R explains A.
[38:1:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); app notes 2:38 (sub 0)
## SUB 2 | Presidential System – Features and Contrast
[38:2:0] - President = **Head of State and Head of Government** – **single executive**; all executive power vested in him.
[38:2:1] - **Elected** for a **fixed term** (US: electoral college, 4 years); removable only by **impeachment**; **not accountable** to the legislature; **cannot dissolve** the legislature.
[38:2:2] - **Appoints his own Council of Ministers** (secretaries), who are not members of the legislature and are responsible only to him.
[38:2:3] - **Principle:** **separation of powers** with **checks and balances** – President and legislature check each other (veto, Senate confirmation, impeachment). "Fusion of powers" = parliamentary; "division of powers" = federalism.
[38:2:4] - **Origin:** first formed in the **USA** (oldest and purest form); USA has a presidential form – India, Canada and Britain are parliamentary.
[38:2:5] - APPSC G2 key: head of State ✓, head of Government ✓, directly elected ✓, "**accountable to the legislature**" ✗ → "i, ii and iii".
[38:2:6] TABLE head: Parliamentary | Presidential
  [38:2:6.0] Nominal head + real head (PM) – dual executive | One person is both heads – single executive
  [38:2:6.1] Collective executive (cabinet); ministers are legislators | Secretaries outside the legislature
  [38:2:6.2] Fusion of powers | Separation of powers
  [38:2:6.3] Removable by no-confidence | Fixed tenure; only impeachment; fixed term
  [38:2:6.4] Lower House can be dissolved early | No dissolution
[38:2:7] - **Semi-presidential:** directly elected President with real powers + **PM responsible to the legislature** – **France (Fifth Republic, 1958), Russia, Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution)**; **not India** (President indirectly elected, nominal).
[38:2:8] - **Parliamentary examples:** UK, Japan, Canada, India.
[38:2:9] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.207-208 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Rocket Polity Sheets p.3 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); app notes 2:38 (sub 2, 3)
## SUB 3 | India Compared with Britain and the USA
[38:3:0] TABLE head: Feature | India | Britain
  [38:3:0.0] Model | Westminster model, from Britain – the British Parliament is the "Mother of Parliaments" | Parliamentary form first introduced here
  [38:3:0.1] Head of State | Indirectly elected President, 5 years | Hereditary monarch
  [38:3:0.2] Supremacy | Constitutional supremacy (written Constitution) – not sovereignty of Parliament | Sovereignty of Parliament
  [38:3:0.3] Judicial review | Courts can strike down laws; Parliament subject to the basic structure | Courts cannot question Acts of Parliament
  [38:3:0.4] PM from | Either House | House of Commons
  [38:3:0.5] Ministers | Non-member allowed for six months | Must be MPs
  [38:3:0.6] Shadow cabinet; legal responsibility of ministers | No | Yes
[38:3:1] - **Key difference (UPSC 1998):** India has **judicial review**; a real and nominal executive, collective responsibility and bicameralism exist in both.
[38:3:2] - UK examples: ruling party can replace the PM (e.g. **Boris Johnson**, UK PM 2019-22, resigned as Conservative leader July 2022); in India removal needs loss of **Lok Sabha confidence**.
[38:3:3] TABLE head: Feature | India | USA
  [38:3:3.0] Executive | Parliamentary | Presidential
  [38:3:3.1] Residuary powers | Union (Parliament) | States
  [38:3:3.2] Pocket veto | President has it | President has it – common
  [38:3:3.3] Upper house | Nominated members (Rajya Sabha) | No nominated members in the Senate
  [38:3:3.4] Judicial review | Narrower – "procedure established by law" | Wider – "due process of law"; SC called a "third chamber"
  [38:3:3.5] Term limit | None for the PM | 22nd Amendment (1951)
[38:3:4] - **US facts:** Constitution in force **1789** (not 1810); **revenue bills originate in the House of Representatives**; **John Quincy Adams** and **George W. Bush** were both sons of Presidents.
[38:3:5] - **Common** to India and USA: written Constitution, federal structure, independent judiciary with judicial review, Fundamental Rights / Bill of Rights, pocket veto.
[38:3:6] - **Records (as of 2026):** longest-serving Chief Minister = **Pawan Kumar Chamling** (Sikkim, 1994-2019); on **22 March 2026** **Narendra Modi** (8,931 days as head of an elected government, CM + PM) passed Chamling's **8,930** (app notes).
[38:3:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); US Constitution Art. I s.7 (archives.gov); app notes 2:38 (sub 4, 5)
## SUB 4 | Merits, Demerits and the Constituent Assembly's Choice
[38:4:0] TABLE head: System | Merits | Demerits
  [38:4:0.0] Parliamentary | Responsible government – executive continuously accountable; harmony of legislature and executive; prevents despotism; ready alternative government | Unstable government; no continuity of policy; cabinet dictatorship with a large majority; "government by amateurs"; against separation of powers
  [38:4:0.1] Presidential | Stable, fixed-term executive; continuity of policy; experts as secretaries | Executive-legislature deadlock; personality cult; irresponsible executive
[38:4:1] - **Main advantage** of the parliamentary form: the **executive remains responsible to the legislature** (UPSC 2017) – "continuity of policy" is the presidential merit.
[38:4:2] - **Why the Constituent Assembly chose it:** **familiarity** from the **1919 and 1935 Acts**; vast size and diversity; avoid US-style deadlock.
[38:4:3] - **Dr B.R. Ambedkar:** a democratic executive must satisfy **stability and responsibility**, which cannot both be maximised; the Draft preferred **more responsibility** to more stability. The parliamentary system gives a "**daily as well as a periodic assessment**" of the Government (CAD, 4 Nov 1948).
[38:4:4] TABLE head: Person / body | Contribution
  [38:4:4.0] Vasant Sathe | Proposed a presidential form, 1970s-80s
  [38:4:4.1] NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02) | Advised keeping the parliamentary system
[38:4:5] - **One Nation, One Election:** amendments to Arts **83, 172, 327**; critics say fixed tenures graft presidential mechanics onto the system.
[38:4:6] - **Shamsher Singh (1974):** a Governor publicly criticising Cabinet policy runs "**counter to the parliamentary system**".
[38:4:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.208-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Constituent Assembly Debates vol. 7, 4 Nov 1948; app notes 2:38 (sub 6, 7, 8)

=== NOTES 2:39 | Governor – Appointment, Powers, Discretion, Article 200/201 and Article 356
## SUB 0 | Office of the Governor – Articles 153-161, Term, Removal, Immunity
[39:0:0] # Articles on the office
[39:0:1] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [39:0:1.0] 153 | A Governor for each State; proviso added by the 7th Amendment, 1956 – the same person may be Governor of two or more States
  [39:0:1.1] 154 | Executive power of the State vested in the Governor, exercised directly or through subordinate officers
  [39:0:1.2] 155 | Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal – neither directly nor indirectly elected
  [39:0:1.3] 156 | Term – holds office during the pleasure of the President; resigns to the President; normal term 5 years (156(3))
  [39:0:1.4] 157 | Qualifications – citizen of India (not necessarily by birth) and completed 35 years
  [39:0:1.5] 158 | Conditions – not a member of Parliament or a State Legislature (seat vacated on appointment), no office of profit; emoluments fixed by Parliament by law, not reduced during the term
  [39:0:1.6] 159 | Oath before the Chief Justice of the High Court (in his absence, the senior-most judge)
  [39:0:1.7] 160 | President provides for the Governor's functions in an unforeseen contingency
  [39:0:1.8] 161 | Pardoning power (offences against State laws)
[39:0:2] - **Nominal / constitutional head** of the State and its **executive head**; the **Chief Minister and Council of Ministers** are the **real executive**.
[39:0:3] - **Article 168**: the Governor is an **integral part of the State Legislature**, though not a member.
[39:0:4] - Emoluments **charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State** (Art. 202(3)); a Governor of two or more States has them shared in the **proportion the President fixes** (Art. 158(3A)).
[39:0:5] - **Conventions:** usually an **outsider** to the State; the State **CM is consulted** (not compulsory).
[39:0:6] # Term and removal
[39:0:7] - Normal term **5 years**, but he **continues until his successor enters office** (Art. 156(3)) – "quits immediately after his term expires" is **wrong**.
[39:0:8] - The five years are **not secure**: he serves at the President's pleasure (= Union Council of Ministers) and can be **removed or transferred at any time**, and reappointed.
[39:0:9] - **No procedure or grounds for removal** are laid down in the Constitution; he is **not impeached** and **the State Legislature cannot remove** him (President, Election Commissioner and HC judges are removed by Parliament; the Governor is not).
[39:0:10] - He is **responsible to the President**; **not answerable** to either House of Parliament, either House of the State Legislature or the State Council of Ministers.
[39:0:11] - **B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010)**: the pleasure doctrine is **not unfettered** – removal must not be **arbitrary** or merely because the **Government at the Centre changed**; limited judicial review.
[39:0:12] # Immunity – Article 361
[39:0:13] - **361(1)**: not answerable to **any court** for acts done in the exercise of his powers and duties.
[39:0:14] - **361(2)**: **no criminal proceedings** instituted or continued during the term – not even with a court's permission; **361(3)**: no arrest or imprisonment.
[39:0:15] - **361(4)**: **civil proceedings** for **personal acts** only after **two months' written notice** – so "a Governor cannot be sued for any act" is **false**.
[39:0:16] - Members of a State Legislature are separately immune for anything said or any vote in the House (**Art. 194(2)**).
[39:0:17] > UPSC 2013: "No procedure has been laid down in the Constitution for the removal of a Governor" = correct. UPSC 2025: Art. 361(1), 361(2) and 194(2) all correct.
[39:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.295-296; NextGen Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.29-31; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt p.452, -02.txt p.1-6)
## SUB 1 | Powers of the Governor – Executive, Legislative, Financial, Judicial
[39:1:0] # Executive powers
[39:1:1] TABLE head: Power | Article
  [39:1:1.0] All executive action of the State expressed in the Governor's name | 166
  [39:1:1.1] Appoints the CM (not the President) and other Ministers on the CM's advice | 164(1)
  [39:1:1.2] Appoints the Advocate-General, fixes his pay | 165
  [39:1:1.3] Appoints Chairman and members of the SPSC – only the President removes them | 316/317
  [39:1:1.4] Appoints the State Election Commissioner | 243K
  [39:1:1.5] Constitutes the State Finance Commission (Panchayat/municipal finances) every 5 years | 243I / 243Y
  [39:1:1.6] Appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court | 233
  [39:1:1.7] Report recommending President's Rule (not Art. 360) | 356
  [39:1:1.8] Seeks information from the CM | 167
[39:1:2] - **Executive head** of the State; represents the Centre in the State and by convention sends **fortnightly reports to the President** on the State's affairs.
[39:1:3] - **Chancellor** of State universities under the State university laws (not Central or private ones); appoints their VCs.
[39:1:4] - Does **not** appoint **High Court judges** (the President does; the Governor is consulted).
[39:1:5] - Places the **CAG** report on the State, the **SPSC** report and the **State Finance Commission** report before the Legislature.
[39:1:6] # Legislative powers
[39:1:7] TABLE head: Power | Article
  [39:1:7.0] Summons, prorogues (174(2)(a)) the Houses and dissolves the Assembly; gap between sessions ≤ 6 months | 174
  [39:1:7.1] Optional address / messages at any time | 175
  [39:1:7.2] Mandatory special address – first session after each general election and first session of each year | 176
  [39:1:7.3] Nominates one-sixth of the Legislative Council | 171
  [39:1:7.4] Decides disqualification of MLAs (not anti-defection) on the Election Commission's opinion | 192
  [39:1:7.5] Ordinance during recess | 213
[39:1:8] - Dissolves the Assembly on the CM / Council of Ministers' advice (Speaker, CM or Chief Justice cannot).
[39:1:9] - Under **Nabam Rebia (2016)** the Art. 174 and Art. 176 functions are on aid and advice; the address must reflect **Cabinet policy**. **January 2026**: Governors in Opposition-ruled States walked out of / skipped the Art. 176 address.
[39:1:10] # Financial powers
[39:1:11] - **Money Bill** introduced in the Assembly only on the **Governor's recommendation** (Art. 207); no demand for grants except on his recommendation.
[39:1:12] - Causes the **annual financial statement (budget)** to be laid (Art. 202).
[39:1:13] - **Contingency Fund of the State** is placed **at the disposal of the Governor** (Art. 267(2)).
[39:1:14] # Ordinance and pardon – Governor vs President
[39:1:15] TABLE head: Basis | President | Governor
  [39:1:15.0] Ordinance | Art. 123; Union + Concurrent List; co-extensive with Parliament | Art. 213; State + Concurrent List
  [39:1:15.1] Approval | Parliament | State Legislature (not the President)
  [39:1:15.2] Prior Presidential instructions | Not applicable | Needed when a Bill with the same provisions would need prior sanction or reservation
  [39:1:15.3] Lapse | 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles | 6 weeks after the Legislature reassembles
  [39:1:15.4] Withdrawal | Any time – 123(2)(b) | Any time – 213(2)(b)
  [39:1:15.5] Pardon | Art. 72 – all cases, incl. court-martial and death sentence | Art. 161 – offences against State laws only; cannot pardon a death sentence (can suspend, remit, commute)
  [39:1:15.6] Discretion | Very limited | Comparatively wider
[39:1:16] - A Governor's ordinance has the **same force as an Act** of the State Legislature.
[39:1:17] - **Perarivalan (2022)**: the Governor is **bound by Cabinet advice** on remission under Art. 161.
[39:1:18] - **Art. 333** nomination of an Anglo-Indian to the Assembly **ended on 25 January 2020** (104th Amendment).

## SUB 3 | Discretionary Powers – Article 163
[39:3:0] # Article 163
[39:3:1] - **163(1)**: a Council of Ministers headed by the CM **aids and advises** the Governor **except where he is required to act in his discretion** – the Constitution **explicitly mentions** the Governor's discretion (it gives the President none).
[39:3:2] - **163(2)**: the Governor's decision on **whether a matter is within his discretion is final** – his discretionary acts cannot be called in question (not complete immunity after case law).
[39:3:3] - **163(3)**: courts **cannot inquire** into the advice tendered by Ministers to the Governor.
[39:3:4] - So the Governor is **not bound by advice in all matters**; he can **reserve a Bill even against ministerial advice**. His discretion is **wider than the President's**.
[39:3:5] - Of four categories of the Governor's orders (executive action, orders on aid and advice, pardon, discretion), the one **not subject to judicial review** is where he **acts in his own discretion** without aid and advice.
[39:3:6] - The President cannot **suo motu** reserve a State Bill; only the Governor reserves it.
[39:3:7] # Constitutional vs situational discretion
[39:3:8] TABLE head: Constitutional (express) | Situational
  [39:3:8.0] Reserving a Bill for the President (Art. 200) | Appointing a CM in a hung Assembly
  [39:3:8.1] Report recommending President's Rule (Art. 356) | Dismissing a ministry that lost majority (Art. 164 pleasure clause)
  [39:3:8.2] Seeking information from the CM (Art. 167) | Dissolving the Assembly when the ministry lost majority
  [39:3:8.3] Administrator of an adjoining UT (Art. 239(2)) | Asking the Government to prove majority
  [39:3:8.4] Sixth Schedule royalty share; special responsibilities under Arts. 371-371J | –
[39:3:9] - **Not discretion**: **appointing Ministers** (on the CM's advice) and **making rules of business** (Art. 166(3)); consulting the High Court is not a Governor's power at all.
[39:3:10] - **Art. 239(2)**: as administrator of an adjoining UT the Governor acts **independently of his State Council of Ministers**.
[39:3:11] - Special responsibility for law and order: **371A Nagaland**, **371H Arunachal Pradesh**.
[39:3:12] - **Fifth Schedule**: Governor **reports to the President** on Scheduled Areas; makes regulations for **peace and good government** after consulting the **Tribes Advisory Council** (not more than **20** members, about three-fourths ST MLAs). **Sixth Schedule**: Autonomous District Councils.
[39:3:13] - A CM who loses majority **must resign or may be dismissed** – e.g. **West Bengal, May 2026**: Mamata Banerjee refused to resign; the Art. 164 **pleasure clause** was cited.
[39:3:14] # Hung Assembly – order of invitation (Sarkaria / Punchhi)
[39:3:15] - 1. **Pre-poll alliance** → 2. largest single party with support → 3. post-poll coalition → 4. post-poll alliance with outside support – then an **early floor test**.
[39:3:16] - **Tamil Nadu, May 2026**: Governor invited **C. Joseph Vijay** on **120 letters of support** in the 234-member House with an early floor test (Sarkaria-Punchhi order).
[39:3:17] - **Justice Kurian Joseph Committee (TN, 2026)**: proposes a **new Schedule** codifying the Governor's discretion, appointment from a State panel and removal by Assembly resolution.

(src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.10-14; Praveen CA360 2026 (src/current-affairs/)
## SUB 4 | President's Rule – Article 356
[39:4:0] # Provisions
[39:4:1] - Imposed when the government of a State **cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution** – on the **Governor's report** or **otherwise** (suo motu).
[39:4:2] - Second ground: **Art. 365** – a State **fails to comply with Union directions** (Art. 355 = Centre's duty to ensure States run per the Constitution).
[39:4:3] - Approval by both Houses within **2 months** (simple majority); **6 months** at a time; **maximum 3 years**.
[39:4:4] - **Beyond 1 year** only if a **National Emergency** is in force and the **Election Commission certifies** elections cannot be held (**44th Amendment**).
[39:4:5] - Effects: the President takes over the State executive, administered by the **Governor on his behalf**; the Legislature's powers go to **Parliament** (**Art. 357**) – **Parliament**, not the Union Cabinet, passes State Bills and budget; the Assembly is **suspended or dissolved** (not automatically dissolved); **Art. 19 is not suspended**; the High Court is untouched.
[39:4:6] - Under President's Rule there is **no State Council of Ministers** to advise the Governor (it exists even after dissolution or the CM's resignation, as caretaker).
[39:4:7] # Firsts and frequency
[39:4:8] TABLE head: Fact | Answer
  [39:4:8.0] First imposition | Punjab, 20 June 1951; PEPSU 1953 was second
  [39:4:8.1] First dismissal of an elected (non-Congress) government | Kerala, 1959
  [39:4:8.2] Never imposed | Telangana, Chhattisgarh
  [39:4:8.3] Most often | Manipur; latest spell from 13 Feb 2025, revoked Feb 2026 (Y. Khemchand Singh CM)
  [39:4:8.4] Times used | Over 125
[39:4:9] - **Ayodhya (Dec 1992)**: BJP governments of **UP, MP, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh** dismissed and Assemblies dissolved; **Bihar's was not** (Bihar had a brief spell in 1995).
[39:4:10] - **Former J&K**: 6 months of **Governor's Rule under Sec. 92** of the J&K Constitution (a provision **no other State had**), then Art. 356 (e.g. Dec 2018); **Art. 360** did not apply and the **right to property** stayed a FR there. Since **31 Oct 2019** J&K is a UT (Reorganisation Act 2019) – none of this survives.
[39:4:11] # Judicial review – S.R. Bommai (1994, 9 judges)
[39:4:12] - Proclamation **judicially reviewable**; Centre must disclose **relevant material**.
[39:4:13] - Majority tested on the **floor of the Assembly**, not in Raj Bhavan.
[39:4:14] - Assembly **not dissolved before Parliament approves**; a dismissed ministry **can be restored**.
[39:4:15] - Upheld dismissal of MP, Rajasthan, HP governments on **secularism**.
[39:4:16] TABLE head: Proper use | Improper use
  [39:4:16.0] Hung House with no alternative | Intra-party disputes
  [39:4:16.1] Flagrant defiance of constitutional directions | Maladministration alone
  [39:4:16.2] Physical breakdown | Ordinary law and order
[39:4:17] - **Rameshwar Prasad (2006)**: Bihar dissolution on unproven fears of horse-trading struck down.
[39:4:18] - **AP High Court (2020)**: "constitutional breakdown" observation – **stayed by the Supreme Court**.
[39:4:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Polity Part 2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt) p.12-14; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.265-275; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.296-297; Praveen CA360 2026 (src/current-affairs/)
## SUB 5 | Bills – Articles 200 and 201; Assent Cases
[39:5:0] # Governor's options – Art. 200
[39:5:1] - 1. **Assent**, 2. **withhold** assent, 3. **return** for reconsideration (**not a Money Bill**), 4. **reserve** for the President – **Art. 200**, not 201.
[39:5:2] - A returned Bill **re-passed** with or without amendment – the Governor **must assent**.
[39:5:3] - Constitution fixes **no time limit** ("as soon as possible") for returning a Bill.
[39:5:4] - **Must reserve**: a Bill that **derogates from the powers of the High Court**. **May reserve**: ultra vires Bills, against DPSP or national interest, compulsory acquisition (Art. 31A).
[39:5:5] - Reservation of State Bills is an example of **central control over the States**.
[39:5:6] # Reserved to get validity or protection
[39:5:7] TABLE head: Article | Bill
  [39:5:7.0] 288(2) | State tax on water / electricity of an inter-State river authority – has no effect unless reserved and assented
  [39:5:7.1] 31A / 31C | Compulsory acquisition; DPSP laws – reservation only for protection
  [39:5:7.2] 254(2) | Concurrent List law repugnant to a Union law – prevails only if reserved and assented
  [39:5:7.3] 304(b) | Restrictions on inter-State trade – previous sanction of the President before introduction
  [39:5:7.4] 360 | Money Bills during a Financial Emergency
[39:5:8] # President's options – Art. 201
[39:5:9] - Assent, withhold, or (non-Money Bill) direct the Governor to **return** it; the Legislature reconsiders **within 6 months**; the re-passed Bill goes **back to the President**, who is **not bound** to assent.
[39:5:10] - **No fixed time limit** for the President. A Bill reserved once can be reserved again only if **materially altered**.
[39:5:11] # Assent time-limit cases
[39:5:12] TABLE head: Date | Case | Holding
  [39:5:12.0] 2023 | State of Punjab v. Principal Secy to Governor | Act as soon as possible; cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely
  [39:5:12.1] 8 Apr 2025 | State of TN v. Governor of TN | Timelines 1 month / 3 months / 1 month on re-passage; referral of 10 re-enacted Bills unconstitutional; deemed assent under Art. 142
  [39:5:12.2] Nov 2025 | 16th Presidential Reference (Art. 143) | No court-fixed timelines; deemed assent rejected; only limited mandamus for prolonged delay; review limited to mala fides and procedure; Governor not bound by advice in choosing among Art. 200 options; Governor = "guide, philosopher and friend"
[39:5:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.296-297; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.9-10, p.40-41; Constitution of India Arts. 200, 201, 254, 288, 304 (legislative.gov.in)
## SUB 6 | Landmark Cases and Commissions on the Governor

  [39:6:0.0] Shamsher Singh (7 judges) | 1974 | Governor bound by aid and advice; public criticism of Cabinet policy an "unconstitutional faux pas"
  [39:6:0.1] S.R. Bommai (9 judges) | 1994 | Art. 356 reviewable; floor test; secularism

=== NOTES 2:40 | Chief Minister, State Council of Ministers and Advocate General
## SUB 0 | Appointment of the CM – Article 164 and the Six-Month Rule
[40:0:0] # Who appoints – Article 164(1)
[40:0:1] - **Appointed by:** the **Governor** under **Article 164(1)** (not Art. 163, 165 or 166; not the President, a High Court judge or the Attorney General). Other Ministers are appointed by the Governor **on the CM's advice**.
[40:0:2]   - Exception: in **Delhi (Art. 239AA)** and **Puducherry (Art. 239A / GUT Act 1963)** the **President** appoints the CM.
[40:0:3] - **Constitutional (nominal) executive head** of the State = the **Governor**; the **real executive** = the CM and the Council of Ministers (not the Chief Secretary or a Deputy CM).
[40:0:4] - **Hung Assembly:** the Constitution lays down **no criteria**; the Governor uses discretion. The principal consideration = the person **most likely to command a stable majority** (not simply the largest party), followed by an early **floor test**.
[40:0:5]   - **Sarkaria (1988) / Punchhi (2010) order:** 1. pre-poll alliance → 2. single largest party with support of others → 3. post-poll coalition (all partners join) → 4. post-poll alliance with some outside support.
[40:0:6] # Article 164 – clause by clause
[40:0:7] TABLE head: Clause | Provision
  [40:0:7.0] 164(1) | Governor appoints the CM; other Ministers on the CM's advice; Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor; Tribal Welfare Minister proviso
  [40:0:7.1] 164(1A) | Size: maximum 15% of the Assembly, minimum 12 (91st Amendment, 2003)
  [40:0:7.2] 164(2) | Council collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (not the Council or the Governor)
  [40:0:7.3] 164(3) | Oath of office and secrecy administered by the Governor
  [40:0:7.4] 164(4) | A non-member may be a Minister for six consecutive months; then he ceases to be a Minister
  [40:0:7.5] 164(5) | Salaries and allowances = as the State Legislature by law determines (until then, Second Schedule) – not the CM, Governor or Chief Secretary
[40:0:8] - **Six months, not 3 months, 1 year or 3 years:** a Minister (incl. the CM) can continue without being elected to the State Legislature for **six months** (Art. 164(4)).
[40:0:9] - **Case – P. Shanmugam (Puducherry):** a non-member CM, resigned in **October 2001** after failing to get elected within six months; N. Rangasamy succeeded him (27 Oct 2001). Jayalalithaa (Sept 2001) went after the Supreme Court annulled her appointment – a different ground.
[40:0:10] - **Term:** **not fixed** by the Constitution; the CM stays while he has the **Assembly's confidence** (on losing it – resign or be dismissed). Resignation is addressed to the **Governor**.
[40:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.298-299; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.31-32 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.17-27); app notes 2:40 (sub 1-2)

## SUB 3 | Size of the Council of Ministers and the Tribal Welfare Minister
[40:3:0] # 91st Amendment Act, 2003 – Article 164(1A)
[40:3:1] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [40:3:1.0] Subject of the 91st Amendment | Limiting the size of the Council of Ministers (and anti-defection changes) – not RTI, education or corruption
  [40:3:1.1] Maximum | 15% of the total strength of the Assembly, including the CM
  [40:3:1.2] Minimum | 12 Ministers including the CM (not 7, 10, 13, 14 or 15)
  [40:3:1.3] Andhra Pradesh (175 seats) | at most 26 Ministers
[40:3:2] - Date trap: the **91st Amendment is of 2003** (not 2001); the 90th, 92nd and 93rd are other subjects.
[40:3:3] # Tribal Welfare Minister – proviso to Article 164(1)
[40:3:4] - **Compulsory in:** **Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha** – of Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh and MP only **Madhya Pradesh** qualifies. He may also look after SC and backward class welfare.
[40:3:5] - **Bihar** was dropped by the **94th Amendment, 2006**.
[40:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.299; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.32 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.22-23); app notes 2:40 (sub 3, 4)
## SUB 4 | Position and Powers of the CM; Duties under Article 167
[40:4:0] # Position
[40:4:1] - CM = **real executive head** and head of the Government; State counterpart of the **PM (Arts. 74-75)**; the State has no counterpart of the Vice-President.
[40:4:2] - **Art. 163(1):** Council of Ministers headed by the CM aids and advises the Governor, **except in his discretionary functions**.
[40:4:3] - Council of Ministers: Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers; collectively answerable to the Assembly.
[40:4:4] # Powers
[40:4:5] - Recommends names of Ministers, **allocates portfolios**, can ask a Minister to resign.
[40:4:6] - Advises the Governor on **summoning and prorogation**; can recommend **dissolution** of the Assembly.
[40:4:7] # Article 167 – duties of the CM
[40:4:8] - **Article 167** defines the CM's duties towards the Governor (not Arts. 162, 164 or 165):
[40:4:9]   - 1. **Communicates** all Council decisions on administration and **proposals for legislation**.
[40:4:10]   - 2. **Furnishes information** the Governor calls for (a constitutional discretion of the Governor).
[40:4:11]   - 3. If the Governor requires, **submits for the Council's consideration** a matter decided by a single Minister.
[40:4:12] - CM = the **chief link** between the Governor and the Council of Ministers.
[40:4:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.298-299; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.31 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.17-21)
## SUB 5 | Deputy Chief Minister
[40:5:0] - **Not mentioned in the Constitution** – not in Art. 164, 74 or 52; a **political arrangement**; the Deputy CM is sworn in as a Minister ("None of the above" is the answer to "which Article").
[40:5:1] - **First Deputy CM of Andhra Pradesh:** **K.V. Ranga Reddy** (1956, Sanjiva Reddy ministry) – not J.V. Narsing Rao, B.V. Subba Reddy or C. Jagannadha Rao (later Deputy CMs).
[40:5:2] - AP had **five** Deputy CMs in 2019-24; **K. Pawan Kalyan** (Jana Sena) Deputy CM since June 2024.
[40:5:3] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.32 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.26); app notes 2:40 (sub 7)
## SUB 6 | Advocate General (Article 165) and the 130th Amendment Bill
[40:6:0] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [40:6:0.0] Article | 165 – State counterpart of the Attorney General (Art. 76)
  [40:6:0.1] Appointed by | Governor; holds office during his pleasure; no fixed term
  [40:6:0.2] Qualification | Qualified to be a High Court judge
  [40:6:0.3] Remuneration | Determined by the Governor
  [40:6:0.4] In the Legislature | Art. 177 – may speak and take part, no vote
[40:6:1] - **130th Constitution Amendment Bill, 2025:** amends **Arts. 75, 164 and 239AA** – a PM, CM or Minister in custody for **30 consecutive days** for an offence punishable with **5+ years** is removed on the **31st day**.
[40:6:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.299-300; app notes 2:40 (sub 8, 9)
