=== NOTES 2:41 | State Legislature – Assembly, Legislative Council and Article 169
## SUB 0 | Legislative Assembly – Strength, Term, Qualifications, Quorum
[41:0:0] # Strength – Article 170
[41:0:1] - **Article 170:** each Assembly = **not more than 500, not less than 60** members, **directly elected** from territorial constituencies (not 40/400, 50/450 or 450 maximum; not 545, the Lok Sabha figure). "No minimum" is wrong.
[41:0:2] - **Exceptions to the 60 minimum:** **Sikkim (32, Art. 371F)**, **Goa (40)**, **Mizoram (40)**; Arunachal Pradesh's minimum is 30 (Art. 371H) but it has 60.
[41:0:3] TABLE head: State / UT | Seats
  [41:0:3.0] Uttar Pradesh (largest) | 403
  [41:0:3.1] Andhra Pradesh / Telangana | 175 / 119 (united AP: 301 in 1956, later 294)
  [41:0:3.2] Himachal Pradesh | 68 – larger than Arunachal, Manipur, Meghalaya (60 each)
  [41:0:3.3] Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tripura (also Arunachal, Manipur) | 60 each
  [41:0:3.4] Goa, Mizoram | 40 each
  [41:0:3.5] Sikkim – smallest State | 32 – incl. one Sangha seat reserved for Buddhist monasteries (a religion-based reservation)
  [41:0:3.6] Puducherry (UT) | 30 elected + up to 3 nominated
[41:0:4] - **Smallest Assembly:** most keys say **Puducherry (30 elected seats)**; by total strength (33 with nominated members) the smallest is **Sikkim (32)**.
[41:0:5] # Term – Article 172
[41:0:6] - **5 years** (not 2, 4 or 6); can be **dissolved earlier by the Governor** (on the CM's advice) – not by the Speaker, CM or Vice-President.
[41:0:7] - **National Emergency:** **Parliament** may extend it by law **one year at a time**, not beyond **six months** after the Emergency ends (not the President, Governor or State Legislature).
[41:0:8] # Qualifications – Article 173
[41:0:9] - **Article 173** (not 175, 177 or 178): citizen of India; at least **25 years** for the Assembly (30 for the Council); other qualifications prescribed by Parliament.
[41:0:10] - UPSC 2008: "not more than 450 members" ✗ (500); "not qualified if less than 25" ✓ → **B only**.
[41:0:11] # Quorum – Article 189(3)
[41:0:12] - **Ten members or one-tenth** of the total membership, **whichever is greater** (not 30, one-half or one-fourth).
[41:0:13] - **Reservation:** SC/ST seats in proportion to population (Art. 332); Anglo-Indian nomination ended (104th Amendment, 2020); one-third for women after delimitation (106th Amendment, 2023).
[41:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.300-301; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.28-35); app notes 2:41 (sub 1)
## SUB 1 | Legislative Procedure – Money Bills, Ordinary Bills and Deadlock
[41:1:0] # Money Bills – Articles 198, 199, 207
[41:1:1] - Introduced **only in the Legislative Assembly** (not in either House or the Council), only by a **Minister**, only on the **Governor's recommendation** (**Art. 207(1)**) – not Parliament, the President or a committee.
[41:1:2] - **Art. 199:** defines a Money Bill; the **Speaker certifies** it (final).
[41:1:3] - **Art. 198:** the Council must return it within **14 days** (not 7, 10, 21 or 30); it cannot reject or amend it; the Assembly may accept or reject its recommendations.
[41:1:4] # Ordinary Bills – Article 197
[41:1:5] - A Bill passed by the Assembly can be held by the Council **not more than three months** on first passage and **one month** on second – the Council can only **interpose delay** (max. 4 months); it cannot permanently block a Bill.
[41:1:6] - **Final authority = the Legislative Assembly**; the Governor has no "final say" on a deadlock.
[41:1:7] - **Demands for grants** are voted **only by the Assembly**; the Council only discusses the budget.
[41:1:8] - **No joint sitting** in a State Legislature (unlike Art. 108 for Parliament).
[41:1:9] - **Bill originating in the Council** and **rejected by the Assembly** → the Bill **ends (dies)**; no joint sitting, no reconsideration, no reference to the Governor.
[41:1:10] TABLE head: Point | Council's power
  [41:1:10.0] Money Bill | Delay 14 days
  [41:1:10.1] Ordinary Bill (Assembly's) | Delay 3 + 1 months; Assembly prevails
  [41:1:10.2] Ordinary Bill (Council's own), rejected by Assembly | Bill ends
[41:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.303-305; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.47-52); app notes 2:41 (sub 3-4)
## SUB 2 | Legislative Council – Composition, Size and Tenure
[41:2:0] # Composition – Article 171
[41:2:1] TABLE head: Chosen by | Share
  [41:2:1.0] Local bodies (municipalities, district boards etc.) | 1/3
  [41:2:1.1] MLAs (from among non-members) | 1/3 – not 1/13
  [41:2:1.2] Graduates of 3 years' standing | 1/12
  [41:2:1.3] Teachers (secondary school and above) of 3 years' standing | 1/12
  [41:2:1.4] Nominated by the Governor (literature, science, art, co-operative movement, social service – co-operative movement is not a Rajya Sabha field) | 1/6
[41:2:2] - **Industrialists** are **not** a category. "1/13 elected by the Legislative Assembly" is the **wrong** statement (it is one-third).
[41:2:3] - Elections to the Council: **proportional representation by the single transferable vote**.
[41:2:4] - **Muthulakshmi Reddy** – India's first woman legislator (Madras Legislative Council).
[41:2:5] - **Article 171** = composition of the **Vidhan Parishad** (Art. 169 = creation / abolition; Art. 170 = Assembly).
[41:2:6] # Size
[41:2:7] - **Maximum one-third** of the Assembly's total membership (not one-half, two-thirds or one-fourth); **minimum 40** (not 44, 52 or 65). Parliament fixes the actual strength.
[41:2:8] - UPPSC 2023: "not more than one-third of the Assembly" ✓ and "at least forty members" ✓ → **both**.
[41:2:9] - UPSC 2015: the Council can be larger than half of the Assembly ✗; the Governor nominates the Chairman ✗ (the **Council elects** its Chairman, Art. 182) → **neither**.
[41:2:10] # Tenure
[41:2:11] - **Permanent body** – **cannot be dissolved, but can be abolished** (Art. 169); member's term **6 years**; **one-third retire every second year** – so its membership **changes every two years**.
[41:2:12] - The Assembly, Lok Sabha (House of the People) can be dissolved; the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is permanent and cannot be abolished by Parliament under Art. 169.
[41:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.300-301; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.29-31); app notes 2:41 (sub 2)
## SUB 3 | Article 169 – Creation and Abolition of Legislative Councils
[41:3:0] - **Article 169** (not 167, 168, 170, 171, 368 or 162): **Parliament** may by law **abolish** a Council or **create** one.
[41:3:1] - **Step 1 – Assembly resolution by special majority:** a majority of the **total membership** and **two-thirds of members present and voting** (not a simple majority; not the Lok Sabha).
[41:3:2] - **Step 2 – Parliament** passes the law by a **simple majority**; it is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368**.
[41:3:3] - The resolution is **recommendatory** – it **does not impose an obligation on the Union** (Parliament) to legislate. The **Governor has no role** (nor the Speaker).
[41:3:4] - Statements (NTR University): A – Art. 169 deals with creation/abolition ✓; B – resolution by **simple** majority ✗; C – Art. 171: not more than 1/3, not less than 40 ✓ → **A and C**.
[41:3:5] - **AP, January 2020:** the Assembly passed the resolution to abolish the Council under **Article 169(1)**; it was **withdrawn in November 2021**.
[41:3:6] - **AP Council history:** created 1958, **abolished 1985** (NTR), **revived 2007**; strength **50** under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014, **58** since the 2015 Amendment; Telangana **40**.
[41:3:7] > "Parliament ratifies the resolution passed by the Assembly with special majority" is the best of the loose options; Parliament itself needs only a simple majority.
[41:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.300-301; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.28-29); app notes 2:41 (sub 5, 7)
## SUB 4 | States with Legislative Councils
[41:4:0] TABLE head: State | Council seats
  [41:4:0.0] Uttar Pradesh – largest | 100
  [41:4:0.1] Maharashtra | 78
  [41:4:0.2] Bihar | 75
  [41:4:0.3] Karnataka | 75
  [41:4:0.4] Andhra Pradesh | 58
  [41:4:0.5] Telangana – smallest | 40
[41:4:1] - **Six States** have a Council (2026): AP, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, UP. In **2019 (before 31 October)** there were **seven** – J&K's Council was abolished by the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019**.
[41:4:2] - **No Council:** Arunachal Pradesh, Gujarat, **Rajasthan**, **Kerala**, Tamil Nadu (abolished 1986), West Bengal (abolished 1969), Punjab (abolished 1970).
[41:4:3] - **Telangana (2026):** Council Chairman **Gutha Sukender Reddy**; Assembly Speaker **Gaddam Prasad Kumar**.
[41:4:4] - **1956:** after the 7th Amendment, Art. 168 provided Councils for **8 States** – Bihar, Bombay, Madhya Pradesh (never set up), Madras, Mysore, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal; AP's Council came in 1958 (Legislative Councils Act, 1957).
[41:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.300; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.28); Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act 1956 s.8 (Art. 168); app notes 2:41 (sub 6)
## SUB 5 | Presiding Officers – Speaker and Chairman
[41:5:0] # Speaker – Articles 178-181, 189
[41:5:1] - **Officer of the Assembly** = the **Speaker** (and Deputy Speaker), elected by the Assembly from its members (**Art. 178**) – not the Governor, CM or a Minister.
[41:5:2] - **Resigns** by writing to the **Deputy Speaker** (**Art. 179**) – not the Governor, CM or President.
[41:5:3] - **Vacates office** if he **ceases to be a member**; is removed by a resolution of a majority of all the then members after **14 days' notice**.
[41:5:4] - **On dissolution** the Speaker **does not vacate** office; he continues until just before the **first meeting of the new Assembly**.
[41:5:5] - **Vote:** only a **casting vote in a tie** (**Art. 189**); during a resolution for his removal he **does not preside** but may speak and **vote in the first instance** (**Art. 181**).
[41:5:6] - Decides **Money Bill** certification (Art. 199(3)) and **Tenth Schedule** defection (subject to judicial review, Kihoto Hollohan 1992).
[41:5:7] - **K. Pratibha Bharati** – first woman Speaker of the AP Assembly (1999-2004).
[41:5:8] - **Immunity (Art. 194(2)):** no member is liable in any court for anything said or any vote given in the Legislature.
[41:5:9] # Chairman of the Council – Article 182
[41:5:10] - **Elected by the Council** from its members (not nominated by the Governor); resigns to the Deputy Chairman.
[41:5:11] > CDS 2006: continues after dissolution ✓, resigns to the Deputy Speaker ✓ → both. NDA 2012 / UPSC 2018: "vacates on dissolution" ✗.
[41:5:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.302-303; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.36-39); app notes 2:41 (sub 8)
## SUB 6 | Framework, Articles and Proceedings (Part VI)
[41:6:0] - **State Legislature = Part VI, Articles 168-212** (Parliament: Part V, Arts. 79-122).
[41:6:1] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [41:6:1.0] 168 | Constitution of State Legislatures (Governor + House/Houses)
  [41:6:1.1] 169 / 170 / 171 | Councils' creation-abolition / Assembly / Council composition
  [41:6:1.2] 172 / 173 / 174 | Duration / Qualifications / Sessions – gap less than six months
  [41:6:1.3] 175 / 176 | Governor's right of address and messages / special address – the Governor shall address the House(s) at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year
  [41:6:1.4] 178-187 | Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman, Deputy Chairman; Secretariat
  [41:6:1.5] 189 / 190-193 | Voting and quorum / vacation of seats and disqualification
  [41:6:1.6] 196-201; 202; 207 | Legislative procedure; budget; Money Bill recommendation
  [41:6:1.7] 208 | Each House makes rules to regulate its procedure and conduct of business (not 214, 352 or 368)
  [41:6:1.8] 211 / 212 / 213 | No discussion of a HC judge's conduct / courts barred / Ordinances
[41:6:2] - **Art. 208(2):** until a House makes its rules, the **pre-1950 provincial rules** apply with changes made by the Speaker / Chairman – **not** the Lok Sabha rules.
[41:6:3] - **Order of proceedings (MP Assembly):** **oath or affirmation → Governor's address → introduction of Ministers → mention of death** (3, 2, 4, 1).
[41:6:4] - **Art. 210:** language of business = the State's official language, **Hindi or English**.
[41:6:5] - **PRS Annual Review of State Laws 2025 (June 2026):** Assemblies sat on average **24 days** a year.
[41:6:6] - **Rajasthan** Assembly was the first to launch an online **question-answering information system (OASYS)** for MLAs' questions (2010).
[41:6:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.300-303; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.28-55); Constitution of India Art. 176, 208; The Hindu 11 Jan 2010 (Rajasthan online Assembly Q&A system); app notes 2:41 (sub 0, 10)
## SUB 7 | Disqualification of Legislators
[41:7:0] TABLE head: Ground | Decided by
  [41:7:0.0] Art. 191 – office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, not a citizen, disqualified by a law of Parliament (RPA 1951) | Governor – his decision is final, but he acts on the binding opinion of the Election Commission (Art. 192)
  [41:7:0.1] Tenth Schedule – defection | Speaker / Chairman
[41:7:1] - So for matters **other than the Tenth Schedule** the final authority is the **Governor** – not the Speaker, the ECI, the State Election Commission, the CM or the High Court.
[41:7:2] - **Art. 190 – vacation of seats:** no one can be a member of **both Houses** (or of two States' legislatures); a resignation takes effect only on the **Speaker's / Chairman's acceptance** (190(3)(b)); **60 days' absence** without permission → seat **vacated** (190(4)) – vacation, not an Art. 191 disqualification.
[41:7:3] - Compare MPs: **Art. 103** – the **President** decides, on the **Election Commission's** binding opinion.
[41:7:4] - **Conviction:** an MLA sentenced to **2 years or more** is disqualified **immediately** (RPA s.8(3); Lily Thomas, 2013).
[41:7:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.33 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.32-34); app notes 2:41 (sub 9)
## SUB 8 | MLAs and MLCs in Indirect Elections
[41:8:0] TABLE head: Election | Elected MLAs vote? | MLCs vote?
  [41:8:0.0] President (Art. 54) | Yes | No
  [41:8:0.1] Vice-President | No – only MPs | No
  [41:8:0.2] Rajya Sabha members | Yes (PR-STV) | No
  [41:8:0.3] Legislative Council | Yes – elect one-third of MLCs | –
[41:8:1] - The Assembly takes part in electing the **President, Rajya Sabha members and MLCs** (I, III, IV) – not the Vice-President.
[41:8:2] - A CM who is a **member of the Legislative Council** is **not eligible to vote** in the Presidential election (being an acting CM or yet to prove majority does not matter; an MLA, Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha elected member can vote).
[41:8:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.303 (Council has no part in the President's election); app notes 2:41 (sub 10)

  x: Under Articles 191–192 the Governor decides according to the Election Commission's opinion; defection goes to the Speaker or Chairman.
[nindian-polity-45-12] sub8
  Who elects the representatives of a State in the Rajya Sabha?
  Elected MLAs and MLCs | All MLAs including nominated members | The State's MPs | *Elected MLAs
  x: Elected MLAs choose them by PR-STV through secret ballot; nominated MLAs cannot vote.
[f6b405ff5885a] sub8
  In which of the following elections do the elected MLAs NOT vote?
  President | Rajya Sabha | Legislative Council | *Vice-President
  x: Only MPs elect the Vice-President; elected MLAs vote for the President, Rajya Sabha and one-third of the Legislative Council.
[n41418c135b9] sub8
  In which of the following elections do elected members of a State Legislative Assembly take part?
  Both the President and the Vice-President | The Vice-President only | Neither | *The President only
  x: Elected MLAs are in the President's electoral college (Article 54); the Vice-President is elected only by MPs.
[gd2c0bc43ec05] sub8
  Who among the following can vote in the election of the President of India?
  Nominated members of a State Legislative Assembly | Members of a Municipal Corporation | *Elected members of a State Legislative Assembly | Members of a State Legislative Council
  x: Only elected MLAs (with elected MPs) form the electoral college for the President; MLCs and nominated members do not vote.

=== NOTES 2:43 | Supreme Court – Composition, Appointment, Collegium, Njac and Jurisdictions
## SUB 0 | Jurisdiction – Original (Art. 131), Appellate (Arts. 132-136), Writ (Art. 32)
[43:0:0] # Jurisdictions at a glance
[43:0:1] TABLE head: Jurisdiction | Article | Key point
  [43:0:1.0] Original (federal) | 131 | Centre v. State(s), Centre + State(s) v. State(s), State v. State – exclusive: no other court
  [43:0:1.1] Writ | 32 | Fundamental Rights only; original but not exclusive (HCs also issue writs, Art. 226)
  [43:0:1.2] Appellate – constitutional | 132 (certificate under 134A) | Any case (civil, criminal or other) with a substantial question of constitutional interpretation
  [43:0:1.3] Appellate – civil | 133 | Substantial question of law of general importance, on HC certificate (₹20,000 limit removed by 30th Amendment, 1972)
  [43:0:1.4] Appellate – criminal | 134 | HC reversed acquittal and sentenced to death, or withdrew a case and sentenced to death – as of right; otherwise HC certificate
  [43:0:1.5] Special leave | 136 | Discretionary; any court or tribunal except military (136(2))
  [43:0:1.6] Review | 137 | Own judgments / orders
  [43:0:1.7] Advisory | 143 | President's references – opinion not binding
  [43:0:1.8] President / VP election disputes | 71 | Original, exclusive and final
[43:0:2] - The SC has **original, appellate and advisory** jurisdiction (plus writ, review and Court of Record powers) – "all the above" in the PYQs.
[43:0:3] # Original jurisdiction – Article 131
[43:0:4] - **SC as a federal court**: decides **Centre-State and inter-State** disputes that involve a **legal right** (question of law or fact); **exclusive** – no High Court shares it. It is the main forum for Centre-State **fiscal** disputes too.
[43:0:5] - First Art. 131 suit: **West Bengal v. Union (1961)** on the Coal Bearing Areas Act.
[43:0:6] - **Excluded from Art. 131**: disputes from **pre-Constitution treaties**, agreements, sanads (proviso – these can go to the President's reference under 143(2)); **inter-State river water disputes (Art. 262)**; matters referred to the **Finance Commission (Art. 280)**; adjustment of expenses and pensions (**Art. 290**); suits by **private persons** against the Union or a State; disputes between **private companies**; **Centre v. Union Territory**; **election disputes** of Parliament and State Legislatures (go to **High Courts**).
[43:0:7] > APPSC G1 2023 / UPSC 2012: NOT in Art. 131 = election disputes and Centre-UT disputes; included = Centre-State and State-State. APSLPRB 2019: water disputes and Finance Commission matters are outside it.
[43:0:8] # Appellate jurisdiction
[43:0:9] - **Highest court of appeal** (replaced the Privy Council); appeals in **constitutional, civil and criminal** cases from HCs.
[43:0:10] - **Art. 132 read with Art. 134A**: constitutional cases – HC certifies a substantial question of interpretation of the Constitution.
[43:0:11] - **Art. 134(1)**: appeal **as of right** when the HC has **on appeal reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death**, or has withdrawn a case from a subordinate court and convicted and sentenced him to death; otherwise only on HC certificate. No appeal as of right if the HC **reverses a conviction**.
[43:0:12] - **Art. 134(2)**: **Parliament may by law enlarge** the criminal appellate jurisdiction – done in **1970** (reversal of acquittal with life or 10 years) – so "Parliament has no power" is **wrong**.
[43:0:13] - **Art. 136 – Special Leave to Appeal**: the SC **may in its discretion** grant special leave from **any judgment, decree, order** of **any court or tribunal** (not only HCs), final or interlocutory, in any matter; **not** against **armed forces** courts or tribunals. A plenary, residual power – used "sparingly"; it is **not** about judges' leave or vacations.
[43:0:14] # Writ jurisdiction – Article 32
[43:0:15] - SC is the **guarantor and defender of Fundamental Rights**; a citizen may go **directly** to it (Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right).
[43:0:16] - **Not exclusive**: HCs issue writs under **Art. 226** for FRs **and** for other legal rights – so the HC's writ power is **wider**; "SC has exclusive power to issue writs" is **false**.
[43:0:17] # Enlarging jurisdiction
[43:0:18] - **Art. 138(1)**: **Parliament** may by law confer further jurisdiction on the SC for matters in the **Union List**; Art. 138(2) – other matters by special agreement of Centre and State.
[43:0:19] - **Art. 139**: Parliament may confer writ power for other purposes; **Art. 139A** (44th Amendment, 1978): SC may **withdraw** cases from HCs or **transfer** cases from one HC to another – so the **Supreme Court** can transfer a case anywhere in India.
[43:0:20] - Parliament **can enlarge but not curtail** the SC's jurisdiction – UPSC 2005 "Parliament cannot enlarge it" is **false**.
[43:0:21] > UPSC 2005: both statements wrong – Parliament can enlarge jurisdiction (Art. 138), and HC administrative expenses are charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State**, not of India.
[43:0:22] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.419-422, 425; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.322-325; Constitution of India Arts. 131-139A
## SUB 1 | Special Powers – Court of Record, Review, Arts. 141, 142, 144, 145; Guardian of the Constitution
[43:1:0] # Articles
[43:1:1] TABLE head: Article | Power
  [43:1:1.0] 129 | Court of Record – records of perpetual evidentiary value; power to punish contempt of itself (and, per 1991 ruling, of HCs and lower courts)
  [43:1:1.1] 137 | Review of its own judgments or orders – subject to Parliament's law and Art. 145 rules
  [43:1:1.2] 141 | Law declared by the SC binding on all courts within the territory of India
  [43:1:1.3] 142 | Decree or order for complete justice in any pending cause; enforceable throughout India
  [43:1:1.4] 144 | All authorities, civil and judicial, in India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court
  [43:1:1.5] 145 | Rules of practice and procedure – made with the approval of the President; 145(3): at least five judges for a substantial question of constitutional interpretation and for Art. 143 references
[43:1:2] - **Guardian / custodian of the Constitution** and **final interpreter** of it (judicial review); also guardian of **Fundamental Rights**, a **federal court** and the **highest court of appeal**. The Constitution's enforcement rests on the **Supreme Court** – not the President or Parliament.
[43:1:3] - **Not powers of the SC**: issuing **ordinances** (President, Art. 123), advising the President on **all** matters (only on references under Art. 143), striking down **any** law (only unconstitutional ones).
[43:1:4] - **Review (Art. 137)**: within **30 days**, before the same bench; grounds – new evidence, error apparent on the record, other sufficient reason. So the SC **can change its own judgment** – neither the President nor the Cabinet can review it.
[43:1:5] - **Curative petition**: **Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)**, after a review is dismissed; rests on **Arts. 129 and 142** (inherent power) – PYQ key **Art. 142**.
[43:1:6] - **Art. 142**: "prohibitions or limitations in **ordinary laws** cannot limit" it – the SC is **not constrained by ordinary laws** when doing complete justice. Uses: **ban on liquor shops within 500 m of highways (State of TN v. K. Balu, Dec 2016)**; deemed assent to 10 TN Bills (2025); Right to Safe Travel directives (27 May 2026).
[43:1:7] - **Rule-making (Art. 145)** needs the **President's approval** – "complete independence and autonomy to make rules" is **wrong**; it is the SC's own rule-making power, subject to that approval.
[43:1:8] - **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** (H.N. Sanyal Committee) defines civil and criminal contempt; the Constitution does not.
[43:1:9] - **V.V. Giri** (1970) – only sitting President to appear **in person** before the SC in a petition challenging his own election (Art. 71).
[43:1:10] - **e-SCR** (2023): free digital database of the SC's reported judgments.
[43:1:11] > APPSC G1 2019: correct statement = "all civil and judicial authorities shall act in aid of the SC" (Art. 144). Resignation goes to the President, the SC can review its judgments, and rules need the President's approval.
[43:1:12] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.417-419, 423-425; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.321, 324; Constitution of India Arts. 129, 137, 141-145

## SUB 3 | Composition, Appointment, Qualifications, Tenure; Acting, Ad Hoc and Retired Judges
[43:3:0] # Appointment – Art. 124(2)
[43:3:1] - **Every judge is appointed by the President** by warrant under his hand and seal – the collegium only recommends.
[43:3:2] - HC judges too are appointed by the **President** by warrant (Art. 217) – **not by the Governor**; both SC and HC judges resign to the President.
[43:3:3] - **CJI**: President after consulting such SC and HC judges as he deems necessary; by convention (and Second Judges Case) the **senior-most judge**.
[43:3:4] - **Other judges**: consultation with the **CJI is obligatory**; the President **may** consult other SC and HC judges.
[43:3:5] - The President acts on the advice of the **Union Council of Ministers headed by the PM** (Art. 74) – the file goes Law Minister → PM → President (Memorandum of Procedure).
[43:3:6] - Convention of seniority broken: **A.N. Ray (1973)**, superseding Shelat, Hegde and Grover; **M.H. Beg (1977)**.
[43:3:7] # Qualifications – Art. 124(3)
[43:3:8] - **Citizen of India** and either **5 years as an HC judge**, or **10 years as an HC advocate**, or a **distinguished jurist** in the **President's** opinion (never used so far). **No minimum age**.
[43:3:9] # Oath, salary, tenure, resignation
[43:3:10] - **Oath** before the **President** or a person appointed by him (form in the **Third Schedule**).
[43:3:11] - **Salaries** determined by **Parliament by law** (Art. 125); not reduced after appointment except in a **Financial Emergency** (Art. 360).
[43:3:12] - Holds office till **65**; age question decided as Parliament provides (Art. 124(2A)). **No fixed tenure** in years.
[43:3:13] - **Resigns by writing addressed to the President** (Art. 124(2)(a)) – not the CJI, PM or Law Minister.
[43:3:14] # Acting, ad hoc and retired judges
[43:3:15] TABLE head: Article | Who | Appointed / requested by
  [43:3:15.0] 126 | Acting CJI (office vacant, CJI absent or unable) | President appoints one of the other judges
  [43:3:15.1] 127 | Ad hoc judge – a qualified HC judge when there is no quorum | CJI with the President's previous consent, after consulting the HC Chief Justice
  [43:3:15.2] 128 | Retired SC (or qualified HC) judge to sit and act | CJI with the President's previous consent and the person's consent
[43:3:16] - **No additional judges** in the SC – additional and acting judges exist only in **High Courts (Art. 224)**; ad hoc judges are provided **only for the SC** (Art. 127).
[43:3:17] - **High Courts can review their own judgments** as **Courts of Record (Art. 215)** though no specific review power is given to them; the SC has the express power (Art. 137).
[43:3:18] > UPSC 2009 (asked again by APPSC): both statements correct – Art. 128 recall of retired judges, and the HC's power to review its own judgments.
[43:3:19] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.414-417; Laxmikanth (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) High Court chapter (Court of record); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.320-323
## SUB 4 | Collegium, Judges Cases and NJAC
[43:4:0] # Judges Cases
[43:4:1] TABLE head: Case | Year | Holding
  [43:4:1.0] First – S.P. Gupta | 1981 | Consultation ≠ concurrence; executive primacy
  [43:4:1.1] Second – SC Advocates-on-Record Association (SCAORA) | 1993 | Consultation = concurrence; collegium born (CJI + 2)
  [43:4:1.2] Third – Presidential Reference, Art. 143(1) | 1998 | Collegium of CJI + 4 senior-most judges; plurality of judges
  [43:4:1.3] Fourth – SCAORA (NJAC case) | 16 Oct 2015 | 99th Amendment and NJAC Act struck down 4:1; collegium revived
[43:4:2] # Collegium
[43:4:3] - **CJI + four senior-most SC judges** recommend SC appointments and HC transfers (CJI + 2 for HC appointments; HC collegium = HC CJ + 2 senior-most).
[43:4:4] - **Not in the Constitution or any Act** – it derives from **Supreme Court decisions** (Judges Cases); adopted **1993**, present form **1998**.
[43:4:5] - Formal appointment by the **President** (Art. 124(2) SC; Art. 217(1) HC); a reiterated name **must** be appointed.
[43:4:6] - Criticism: **"imperium in imperio"**, opacity.
[43:4:7] - **Art. 222**: the **President** transfers an HC judge (incl. a Chief Justice) after consulting the **CJI**; an HC Chief Justice's appointment starts with the **CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges** → Law Minister → State consulted → President.
[43:4:8] - **Collegium (June 2026)**: CJI **Surya Kant**, Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh, P.S. Narasimha (joined when **J.K. Maheshwari** retired, 29 Jun 2026).
[43:4:9] # NJAC – 99th Amendment, 2014
[43:4:10] - **Constitution (99th Amendment) Act, 2014** + **National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014** – inserted **Art. 124A-124C**; passed LS 13 Aug 2014, ratified by **16 States**, assent **31 Dec 2014**, in force **13 Apr 2015**.
[43:4:11] - **Six members**: **CJI (Chairperson)**, **two senior-most SC judges**, **Union Law Minister**, **two eminent persons** nominated by a committee of the **PM, CJI and Leader of Opposition** in the Lok Sabha (or leader of the largest opposition party). AG not a member.
[43:4:12] - **Struck down** by a **5-judge Constitution Bench** of the **Supreme Court** (Khehar J led) **4:1** – violated **judicial independence (Basic Structure)**; **J. Chelameswar** the **lone dissent** upholding the NJAC. India has no NJAC now.
[43:4:13] # Earlier proposals
[43:4:14] - **Constitution (98th Amendment) Bill, 2003** (NDA, Law Minister Arun Jaitley) – a **National Judicial Commission**. (The 98th Amendment **Act** of 2012 is different – Hyderabad-Karnataka, Art. 371J.)
[43:4:15] - **NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, report 2002)** and the **Malimath Committee (2003, criminal justice reforms)** proposed a **National Judicial Commission**; Malimath also suggested amending Art. 124 to make **impeachment of judges less difficult** (not Panchayati Raj).
[43:4:16] - **Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill, 2010** – passed by Lok Sabha (Mar 2012): a mechanism to **inquire into complaints against judges**; **lapsed** in 2014.
[43:4:17] - **Law Commission**: **14th Report (1958)** – appoint eminent Bar members directly, not strictly by seniority; **214th Report (2008)** – review of the appointment procedure.
[43:4:18] - Reform ideas: accountability law, a permanent disciplinary authority, asset disclosure, RTI on the administrative side – **not** abolishing the collegium by executive notification.
[43:4:19] - **P. Wilson's private member's Bill (19 Feb 2026)**: social diversity, a **90-day** limit for the Centre to notify collegium names, **regional benches**.
[43:4:20] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.414-415, 427; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.321-322; Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India (2015); PRS Legislative Research, Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill 2010
## SUB 5 | Advisory Jurisdiction – Article 143
[43:5:0] - **Art. 143(1)**: the **President** may refer a **question of law or fact** of **public importance** (arisen or likely) – the Court **may** give or **refuse** its opinion (e.g. Ram Janmabhoomi, 1993). Only the President can seek it – not the PM, a High Court, or the Court on its own; not limited to Fundamental Rights.
[43:5:1] - **Art. 143(2)**: disputes from **pre-Constitution treaties and agreements** (excluded from Art. 131) – the Court **must** give its opinion.
[43:5:2] - Opinion is **advisory, not binding on the President**; heard by at least **five judges** (Art. 145(3)).
[43:5:3] - Courts treat the law stated in a reference opinion as binding precedent (Art. 141) – the usual key "**not binding on the President, but binding on subordinate courts**".
[43:5:4] - **India v. USA**: advisory jurisdiction is the main difference – the **US Supreme Court has none**.
[43:5:5] - Also: India's review is under **'procedure established by law'** – narrower than the US **'due process of law'**; India blends **American judicial supremacy** with **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
[43:5:6] # References asked
[43:5:7] TABLE head: Year | Reference
  [43:5:7.0] 1960 | Berubari Union (ceding territory needs a constitutional amendment)
  [43:5:7.1] 1998 | Consultation process of the CJI – Third Judges Case, under Art. 143(1)
  [43:5:7.2] 2002 | Gujarat Assembly elections deferred by the EC – referred by President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
  [43:5:7.3] 2012 | 2G spectrum – auction of natural resources
  [43:5:7.4] Nov 2025 | 16th reference – timelines for assent to Bills
[43:5:8] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.422-423, 425-426; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.323
## SUB 6 | Removal of Judges, Independence Safeguards; Supreme Court v. High Court
[43:6:0] # Removal – Art. 124(4), (5)
[43:6:1] - Removed only by an **order of the President** after an **address by each House** of Parliament in the **same session**, by **special majority** (majority of **total membership** + **two-thirds present and voting**). The President **cannot remove** a judge on his own; nor can the CJI.
[43:6:2] - **Grounds**: **proved misbehaviour or incapacity** only – **not defined** in the Constitution; "violation of the Constitution" is the ground for the **President's** impeachment, not a judge's.
[43:6:3] - **Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968** gives the procedure: motion signed by **100 LS / 50 RS** members; **Speaker / Chairman may admit or reject** it; a **3-member committee** (CJI or SC judge, an HC Chief Justice, a distinguished jurist) – **not the President** – inquires; debate allowed on the motion.
[43:6:4] - **No judge removed so far**: **V. Ramaswami** (SC, 1993) – motion failed in the Lok Sabha; **Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC, 2011) – Rajya Sabha passed it, he **resigned (1 Sep 2011)** before the Lok Sabha vote.
[43:6:5] - CAG (Art. 148) and CEC (Art. 324(5)) are removed like an SC judge; Art. 218 applies these provisions to HC judges.
[43:6:6] - The Constitution says **"removal"** for judges; **"impeachment"** is used only for the President (Art. 61).
[43:6:7] - Lesser misconduct: **In-House Procedure (1999)**, after **C. Ravichandran Iyer (1995)**; **Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997)**.
[43:6:8] > UPSC 2019: correct = 3 and 4 (procedure in the 1968 Act; special majority in each House). Speaker can reject the motion; "misbehaviour" is not defined.
[43:6:9] # Independence safeguards
[43:6:10] TABLE head: Safeguard | Provision
  [43:6:10.0] Mode of appointment | President must consult the CJI – curtails executive discretion
  [43:6:10.1] Security of tenure | Removal only under Art. 124(4)
  [43:6:10.2] Expenses | Salaries, pensions and administrative expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund of India – non-votable
  [43:6:10.3] Conduct not discussed | In Parliament (Art. 121) / State Legislature (Art. 211), except on a removal motion
  [43:6:10.4] Ban on practice | Retired SC judge cannot plead in any court or authority in India (Art. 124(7))
  [43:6:10.5] Staff | CJI appoints SC officers and servants without executive interference (Art. 146)
  [43:6:10.6] Jurisdiction | Parliament can enlarge, not curtail it
[43:6:11] > UPSC 2012: safeguards = 1 and 3 (consulting the CJI; salaries on the CFI). Removal is not by the CJI, and staff are appointed by the CJI, not the Government.
[43:6:12] # Supreme Court v. High Court
[43:6:13] TABLE head: Point | Supreme Court | High Court
  [43:6:13.0] Strength fixed by | Parliament by law (Art. 124(1)) | President (Art. 216)
  [43:6:13.1] Retirement | 65 | 62
  [43:6:13.2] Removal | Art. 124(4) | Same mode (Art. 218)
  [43:6:13.3] Retired judge may plead | Nowhere in India | Only in the SC and other HCs (Art. 220)
  [43:6:13.4] Salary / pension | CFI / CFI | Consolidated Fund of the State / CFI
  [43:6:13.5] Court of Record | Art. 129 | Art. 215
  [43:6:13.6] Writs | FRs only (Art. 32) | FRs and other rights (Art. 226); superintendence (Art. 227)

## SUB 7 | Establishment, Seat and Strength
[43:7:0] # Establishment
[43:7:1] - **Part V, Chapter IV – Articles 124-147**; **Art. 124** establishes and constitutes the SC (Court of Record is Art. 129).
[43:7:2] - **Federal Court** (GoI Act 1935) set up **1937**; Privy Council appeals ended **1949**; the SC replaced both and was **inaugurated on 28 January 1950** (two days after the Republic, 26 Jan **1950**); moved to **Tilak Marg in 1958**.
[43:7:3] - **Art. 130 – Seat**: **Delhi**, or elsewhere as the **CJI** decides **with the President's approval**.
[43:7:4] - **Art. 348(1)(a)**: all proceedings in the SC and every HC in **English** (Art. 145 only lets the SC frame rules).
[43:7:5] # Strength – Art. 124(1)
[43:7:6] - **Parliament** fixes and increases the number by **ordinary law** – **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956** – not the President, the CJI, the collegium or the Law Commission.
[43:7:7] TABLE head: Year | Strength incl. CJI
  [43:7:7.0] 1950 (Constitution) | 8 (CJI + 7)
  [43:7:7.1] 1956 / 1960 | 11 / 14
  [43:7:7.2] 1977 / 1986 | 18 / 26
  [43:7:7.3] 2008 Act (2009) | 31
  [43:7:7.4] 2019 | 34 (CJI + 33)
  [43:7:7.5] 16 May 2026 | 38 (CJI + 37) – Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 (Art. 123); replacing Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha (Jul 2026)
[43:7:8] - Benches are usually of 2-3 judges; a **Constitution Bench** has at least **five** (Art. 145(3)); the largest was **13** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
[43:7:9] - **Pendency**: the main cause given in PYQs is the **shortage of judges** (vacancies, low judge-population ratio) – the reason for the 2026 increase.
[43:7:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.414, 417, 426-427; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.320; Praveen CA360 May 2026 (src/current-affairs/praveen-ca360-2026-05-magazine.txt); PMF Lens Jul 2026 (src/current-affairs/pmf-lens-2026-07-01.txt)

=== NOTES 2:44 | High Courts, Subordinate Judiciary, Judicial Review, Activism and Pil
## SUB 0 | High Court Judges – Appointment, Tenure, Transfer, Removal
[44:0:0] # Appointment and qualifications (Art. 217)
[44:0:1] - Every HC judge is appointed by the **President** by warrant (not the Governor, not the CJI). The **Governor cannot appoint or remove** HC judges – but he does appoint the **CM, SPSC members and the Advocate General**.
[44:0:2] - **Chief Justice**: President after consulting the **CJI and the Governor**. **Other judges**: also the **Chief Justice of that HC** → consultees = **HC CJ, CJI, Governor** (not the Attorney General). Common HC: **Governors of all the States** concerned.
[44:0:3] - **Collegium**: HC CJ + **2** senior-most HC judges propose → **CJI + 2** senior-most SC judges (Third Judges case, 1998); NJAC (99th Amendment) struck down in **2015**.
[44:0:4] - **Qualifications**: citizen; **10 years judicial office** or **10 years HC advocate**; no minimum age; **no "distinguished jurist" route** (only SC, Art. 124(3)(c)).
[44:0:5] - **Strength** of each HC: fixed by the **President** (Art. 216) – not Parliament, Cabinet, PM or Governor; strength differs from HC to HC. (SC strength: Parliament by law.)
[44:0:6] - Sanctioned strength (18 Sep 2025): **1,122** for all HCs, **804** filled. **8 Aug 2026**: 30 HC judges appointed (Madras 15, Karnataka 6).
[44:0:7] - **Justice H.R. Khanna** (8th Law Commission, **80th Report**, 1979): at least **one-third** of HC judges should be from another State.
[44:0:8] # Oath, tenure, resignation
[44:0:9] - **Oath** before the **Governor** or a person appointed by him (Art. 219) – not the President or CJI.
[44:0:10] - Holds office till **62** – raised from **60** by the **15th Amendment, 1963**; the **114th Amendment Bill (2010)** sought **65**. Not "during pleasure", not "as long as they desire". (SC judges: **65**.)
[44:0:11] - **Resignation** in writing to the **President** (Art. 217(1)(a)) – not the CJI, HC CJ or Governor.
[44:0:12] # Transfer (Art. 222)
[44:0:13] - HC judges **can be transferred**; the **President** transfers after consulting the **CJI** (Art. 222(1)) – the CJI/collegium only advises; the PM or Law Minister has no power. Only **HC judges**: **no provision to transfer SC judges**.
[44:0:14] # Removal
[44:0:15] - Same manner and grounds as an SC judge (Arts. **217(1)(b), 218**, 124(4)): **President's order** after an address by **both Houses** with special majority. Grounds only **proved misbehaviour or incapacity** – **difference of opinion with the Chief Justice** is never a ground; neither the Governor nor the State Legislature can remove.
[44:0:16] - Procedure: **Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968** – motion by 100 LS / 50 RS members; 3-member committee (SC judge, HC CJ, jurist). No HC judge impeached so far.
[44:0:17] TABLE head: Judge | Fact
  [44:0:17.0] Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC) | Resigned 2011 after Rajya Sabha voted for removal
  [44:0:17.1] G.R. Swaminathan (Madras HC) | Removal motion noticed by 107 MPs, Dec 2025
  [44:0:17.2] Yashwant Varma (formerly Allahabad HC, not Madras) | Inquiry report to be tabled despite resignation (Jul 2026)
[44:0:18] # Acting, additional and retired judges
[44:0:19] TABLE head: Article | Who | Rule
  [44:0:19.0] 223 | Acting (ad hoc) Chief Justice | Appointed by the President from the HC judges
  [44:0:19.1] 224(1) | Additional judge | Temporary rise in work / arrears; up to 2 years, not beyond 62
  [44:0:19.2] 224(2) | Acting judge | For an absent judge or one acting as CJ; ends at 62
  [44:0:19.3] 224A | Retired HC / SC judge sitting | HC CJ requests, with the President's previous consent and the judge's consent (inserted by the 15th Amendment, 1963)
[44:0:20] # HC Chief Justice in administrative capacity
[44:0:21] - Dual capacity – judicial and administrative. Administrative acts (staff appointments, postings) are **subject to the writ jurisdiction (Art. 226) of the other judges of the same HC** – not "special control of the CJI", the Governor or the CM (UPSC 1996).

## SUB 1 | High Courts in India – Number, History, Jurisdiction
[44:1:0] # Constitutional basis
[44:1:1] - HCs: **Part VI, Chapter V, Articles 214–231**. **Art. 214**: a HC for each State. **Art. 231** (7th Amendment, 1956): **Parliament by law** may set up a **common HC** for two or more States (or States + a UT) – not the President's order, an SC order or an amendment. **Art. 230**: Parliament extends/excludes HC jurisdiction over a UT (7th Amendment, 1956). **Art. 241**: Parliament may constitute a HC for a UT.
[44:1:2] - A **new HC** is created by a **law of Parliament** and brought into being by a **Presidential notification** (e.g. AP HC from 1 Jan 2019 under the AP Reorganisation Act).
[44:1:3] # History
[44:1:4] - **Indian High Courts Act, 1861** → first three in **1862**: **Calcutta (2 July 1862, oldest), Bombay, Madras**. Fourth: **Agra 1866**, shifted to **Allahabad 1869** – **150th anniversary in 2016**.
[44:1:5] - First HCs **after independence (1948)**: **Orissa** (Cuttack) and **Assam/Gauhati** (Assam HC, renamed Gauhati 1971); Rajasthan 1949. Punjab HC 1947; Delhi 1966; HP 1971; Sikkim 1975.
[44:1:6] # Number of High Courts
[44:1:7] TABLE head: Year | Number
  [44:1:7.0] 2000 (Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand) | 18 → 21 (so 21 in 2002–2012: "25 HCs" was false in UPSC 2002/2005, "24" false in CDS 2007)
  [44:1:7.1] Jan–Mar 2013 (Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura) | 21 → 24
  [44:1:7.2] 1 Jan 2019 (separate Andhra Pradesh HC) | 24 → 25 (still 25, as of 2026)
[44:1:8] - Only **three HCs cover more than one State**: **Punjab and Haryana**, **Gauhati**, **Bombay** (Maharashtra + Goa). **Delhi** alone among UTs has its own HC (since 1966); **J&K and Ladakh** share one.
[44:1:9] # Jurisdiction and seats
[44:1:10] TABLE head: High Court | States / UTs | Seat and benches
  [44:1:10.0] Bombay | Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu | Mumbai; benches Nagpur, Panaji, Aurangabad (+ Kolhapur circuit bench, 2025)
  [44:1:10.1] Calcutta | West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar | Kolkata; circuit benches Port Blair, Jalpaiguri
  [44:1:10.2] Gauhati | Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh | Guwahati; benches Kohima, Aizawl, Itanagar (before 2013 also Imphal, Agartala, Shillong – then the most benches)
  [44:1:10.3] Madras | Tamil Nadu and Puducherry | Chennai; bench Madurai
  [44:1:10.4] Kerala | Kerala, Lakshadweep | Ernakulam
  [44:1:10.5] Punjab and Haryana | Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh | Chandigarh
  [44:1:10.6] J&K and Ladakh | Both UTs | Jammu (winter), Srinagar (summer)
  [44:1:10.7] Uttarakhand | Uttarakhand | Nainital
  [44:1:10.8] Sikkim | Sikkim (own HC since 1975) | Gangtok
  [44:1:10.9] Manipur / Tripura / Meghalaya | Own HCs since 2013 | Imphal / Agartala / Shillong
[44:1:11] - **A&N → Calcutta HC** (in **West Bengal**), not Madras; Puducherry → Madras; Lakshadweep → Kerala.
[44:1:12] - **Not under the Gauhati HC**: **Sikkim** (own HC since 1975) – and since 2013 also **Manipur and Tripura**.
[44:1:13] - **Manipur** had no HC of its own until **2013** (UPPCS 2005 answer); Orissa, Sikkim and HP had theirs.

## SUB 2 | Judicial Review – Meaning, Origin, Basis
[44:2:0] - **Meaning**: power of the **SC and HCs** to pronounce upon the **constitutionality of laws and executive orders** (Centre and States) and declare them **void** – not questioning the **wisdom** of laws, not pre-assent review, not reviewing its own judgments (that is Art. 137 review), not hearing appeals from lower courts. Hence the SC "can declare illegal any law of the State".
[44:2:1] - Examines the **constitutional validity of laws** – not a "periodic review of the Constitution" or "review of the functioning of the judiciary".
[44:2:2] - Enjoyed by the **Supreme Court as well as the High Courts** (Arts **32** and **226**; NextGen: Arts **13 and 226** confer it on HCs) – not all courts.
[44:2:3] - The term is **not used in the Constitution**; part of the **basic structure** (**Kesavananda 1973**; **L. Chandra Kumar 1997**).
[44:2:4] - **Origin USA**: **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**, CJ **John Marshall**; India borrowed it from the **USA**. Prevalent in **both India and the USA**; **UK** – parliamentary sovereignty, courts cannot void Acts.
[44:2:5] - **Indian vs British parliamentary system**: the difference is **judicial review** (India) – both have real and nominal executives, collective responsibility and bicameral legislatures.
[44:2:6] - **Checks legislative excesses** of Parliament and State Assemblies (not President/Governor, no-confidence or elections); **restricts the sovereignty of Parliament** – laws cannot break the Basic Structure.
[44:2:7] - India = **balance of parliamentary sovereignty (British) and judicial supremacy (American)** – neither pure parliamentary sovereignty, judicial supremacy nor cabinet supremacy.
[44:2:8] - **Custodian / guardian of Fundamental Rights**: the **Supreme Court** (Art. 32) – with the **High Courts** (Art. 226); not the President, PM, Parliament or Rajya Sabha.
[44:2:9] - Basis: written Constitution + **federalism** + FRs. **Symbol of federal government** (APPSC key) – courts as umpire of the Centre-State division. **Theory**: **supremacy of the Constitution** / limited government.
[44:2:10] - **Grounds**: violation of FRs; lack of **legislative competence**; repugnance to the Constitution / Basic Structure – not disagreement with majority policy.
[44:2:11] - FRs held amendable first in **Shankari Prasad (1951)**.
[44:2:12] # Constitutional basis → Article
[44:2:13] TABLE head: Article | Role
  [44:2:13.0] 13(2) | Laws abridging FRs void – primary textual basis (incl. pre-Constitution laws)
  [44:2:13.1] 32 | SC writs – "heart and soul" (Ambedkar); basic structure
  [44:2:13.2] 131 | Centre-State disputes
  [44:2:13.3] 132-136 | Appeals; 136 Special Leave
  [44:2:13.4] 137 | SC reviews its own judgments
  [44:2:13.5] 139A | SC may transfer cases to itself (42nd/44th era)
  [44:2:13.6] 141 / 142 | SC law binding / complete justice
  [44:2:13.7] 143 | Advisory
  [44:2:13.8] 226 / 227 | HC writs / superintendence
  [44:2:13.9] 245 / 246 | Legislative powers subject to the Constitution
  [44:2:13.10] 251, 254 | Repugnancy
  [44:2:13.11] 372(1) | Pre-Constitution laws continue, subject to review
[44:2:14] - APPSC-G2 2023 match: 137 – review; 226 – HC writs; 13 – void laws; 32 – SC writs.
[44:2:15] # Actions of President and Governor
[44:2:16] TABLE head: Provision | Effect
  [44:2:16.0] 74(2) | Ministers' advice to the President cannot be inquired into
  [44:2:16.1] 163(3) | Same for advice to the Governor
  [44:2:16.2] 361 | President / Governor not answerable to courts
[44:2:17] - Yet their decisions are reviewable on **mala fides or irrelevant grounds** – Art. 361 protects only the office-holder (**S.R. Bommai, 1994**).
[44:2:18] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch.27 Judicial review (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt p.431-437) and ch.34 (laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.64); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.330 (nextgen-polity-appsc-19.txt p.15); app notes 2:44 (sub 6-7)
## SUB 3 | Judicial Activism and PIL
[44:3:0] # Terms
[44:3:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [44:3:1.0] Judicial activism (= judicial dynamism) | Proactive role of courts protecting rights and filling gaps; opposite of restraint
  [44:3:1.1] PIL | "A legal action initiated in a court of law for the enforcement of public interest or general interest in which the public or a class of the community have pecuniary or some other interest" (SC definition)
  [44:3:1.2] Social Action Litigation | Other name of PIL (also SIL, Class Action Litigation)
  [44:3:1.3] Locus standi relaxed | Any member of the public with "sufficient interest" can move court for others' rights
  [44:3:1.4] Epistolary jurisdiction | Letters, postcards, newspaper reports treated as petitions
[44:3:2] - **Why activism arises**: mainly the **failure of the legislature and executive** to discharge their duties – not judges' wish for supremacy or populism.
[44:3:3] - **PIL = outcome of judicial activism** (its most popular form) – not of judicial restraint; "intertwined with" activism. PIL evolved by **judicial initiative / activism** – **not** by a constitutional amendment, Act of Parliament or Presidential order.
[44:3:4] - PIL under **Art. 32 (SC)** or **Art. 226 (HC)**; in line with **Art. 39A**.
[44:3:5] - **Example of activism**: SC decision on the **rights of the third gender** (**NALSA, 2014**) – not routine river-water, tax-appeal or land-ownership decisions.
[44:3:6] # Origin and pioneers
[44:3:7] - **Judicial activism**: originated in the **USA**; term coined **1947** by **Arthur Schlesinger Jr.**; in India from the **mid-1970s** (post-Emergency). PIL: originated in the **USA in the 1960s**; in India early **1980s** (first cases 1979).
[44:3:8] - **Pioneers of PIL**: **Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati** – the first SC judges to admit PILs; with O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai they laid the foundation of activism. Judge "who introduced PIL" = **P.N. Bhagwati**.
[44:3:9] - **V.R. Krishna Iyer** was **never Chief Justice of India** (UPSC 2008: only "progenitor of PIL" is correct). Bhagwati was CJI 1985-86.
[44:3:10] - **First PIL**: **Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979)** – **undertrial prisoners spending long years in Bihar jails** (speedy trial); filed by **Kapila Hingorani ("Mother of PILs")**.
[44:3:11] # Doctrines in a match
[44:3:12] TABLE head: Doctrine | Application
  [44:3:12.0] PIL | Any member of the public with sufficient interest can approach the court for others' rights
  [44:3:12.1] Writ jurisdiction | Writs for enforcing FRs and correcting injustices
  [44:3:12.2] Proportionality | Government action balanced; no branch abuses power
  [44:3:12.3] Separation of powers | Keeps the judiciary independent of legislature and executive
[44:3:13] # Instruments and SC evolutions
[44:3:14] - **Suo motu cognisance**; **continuing mandamus** (case kept open to monitor); **guidelines** filling a vacuum (**Vishaka 1997** → POSH Act 2013); **Art. 142**; expert committees.
[44:3:15] - Genuine SC evolutions: **Basic Structure**, **PIL**, **removal of handcuffs**, continuing mandamus, expansion of Art. 21. **Not** an SC evolution: "**exemptions to FRs**" (Arts **31A–31C, 33**) – constitutional text.
[44:3:16] TABLE head: Case | Year | Associated with
  [44:3:16.0] Hussainara Khatoon | 1979 | First PIL, speedy trial
  [44:3:16.1] Olga Tellis | 1985 | Livelihood of pavement dwellers (Art. 21)
  [44:3:16.2] M.C. Mehta | 1980s on | Environment – activism, not restraint
  [44:3:16.3] Vishaka | 1997 | Workplace harassment guidelines
  [44:3:16.4] Prakash Singh | 2006 | Police reforms
  [44:3:16.5] Puttaswamy | 2017 | Privacy a fundamental right
  [44:3:16.6] Swaraj Abhiyan | 2016 | Drought management guidelines
  [44:3:16.7] State of Rajasthan v. UoI | 1977 | Declined political question – restraint
  [44:3:16.8] Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass | 2007 | Judges not to encroach on legislature/executive – restraint
[44:3:17] - **DPSPs are non-justiciable (Art. 37)**: for their non-enforcement a citizen cannot approach any court.
[44:3:18] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch.28 Judicial activism p.438 and ch.29 PIL p.446 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); app notes 2:44 (sub 9)
[44:3:19] - **CJI when PIL began**: the first PILs (1979-81) came under CJI **Y.V. Chandrachud** (1978-85); exams key **P.N. Bhagwati** (CJI 1985-86), the judge who introduced PIL.

## SUB 5 | Court of Record and Contempt of Court
[44:5:0] - **Arts 129 (SC) and 215 (HC)**: the **SC and the HCs** are Courts of Record (not district courts). Two powers: records of **perpetual memory and testimony**, of **evidentiary value**, not questioned in lower courts, recognised as **legal precedents**; and power to **punish for contempt of itself**.
[44:5:1] - So only the **SC or a HC** can punish for its own contempt (not any court, tribunal or quasi-judicial body); under the 1971 Act a HC also punishes contempt of **subordinate courts**.
[44:5:2] - "Contempt of court" is **not defined in the Constitution** – defined by the **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971**. **Parliament** makes laws on contempt (Union List entry 77; Concurrent List entry 14).
[44:5:3] - **Contempt of Court Act, 1926** – first major law; **H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961)** → **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** (UPSC 2022: statements 1, 2 and 4 correct; 3 wrong).
[44:5:4] TABLE head: Type | Meaning
  [44:5:4.0] Civil contempt | Wilful disobedience of a judgment/order or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court
  [44:5:4.1] Criminal contempt | Scandalising or lowering the court's authority; prejudicing or interfering with judicial proceedings; obstructing the administration of justice
[44:5:5] - **Not contempt**: a **complaint against a court to a higher court**, fair criticism, fair reporting.
[44:5:6] - Purpose: to secure **public respect and confidence** in the judicial process – A-R: both true and R explains A.
[44:5:7] - **Justice C.S. Karnan** (Calcutta HC): first sitting HC judge to **appear personally before the SC** in a contempt case (March 2017); sentenced to **six months** for **contempt of court** (May 2017).
[44:5:8] - Jul 2026: SC (CJI Surya Kant bench) shifted "bulldozer justice" contempt pleas to HCs. Sep 2026: SC refused to stay Bombay HC contempt proceedings over a judicial officer's outburst.
[44:5:9] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch.34 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt p.64); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.321 (nextgen-polity-appsc-19.txt p.6, Court of Record); Contempt of Courts Act 1971 s.2; app notes 2:44 (sub 3)
## SUB 6 | Subordinate Judiciary – Articles 233–237
[44:6:0] TABLE head: Article | Provision
  [44:6:0.0] 233 | District judges – appointed, posted, promoted by the Governor in consultation with the HC; direct recruit: not in Union/State service, 7 years advocate or pleader, recommended by the HC
  [44:6:0.1] 233A | Validation of appointments (20th Amendment, 1966)
  [44:6:0.2] 234 | Other judicial officers – Governor's rules after consulting the SPSC and the HC
  [44:6:0.3] 235 | Control over district and subordinate courts vested in the High Court
  [44:6:0.4] 236 | "District judge" includes city civil court judge, additional/joint/assistant district judge, chief judge of a small cause court, chief presidency magistrate, sessions judge – not a tribunal judge
  [44:6:0.5] 237 | Governor may extend these provisions to magistrates
[44:6:1] - "District Judge" is first mentioned in **Article 233**.
[44:6:2] - **District Judge** = **highest judicial authority in the district**; highest civil court; as **Sessions Judge**, highest criminal court; has judicial, administrative and **supervisory powers** over all subordinate courts (A-R: R explains A).
[44:6:3] - A **death sentence** by a Sessions Judge must be **confirmed by the HC** (now under the **BNSS 2023**, from 1 July 2024) → UPSC 2004: all four statements correct.
[44:6:4] - **AIJS**: enabled by **Art. 312** (42nd Amendment) but **not yet created**.
[44:6:5] - **National Judicial Academy** (judicial education, research and training) – **Bhopal**.
[44:6:6] - **Mobile courts**: idea of **Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam**; first **August 2007** at **Punhana (Mewat), Haryana**.
[44:6:7] - **Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008** (in force 2 Oct 2009): **Nyayadhikari** (JMFC rank); mobile court at the **intermediate panchayat** level.

## SUB 8 | High Court Powers – Jurisdiction and Writs
[44:8:0] - Jurisdictions of a HC: **original, writ, appellate, supervisory**, control over subordinate courts, court of record, judicial review – **no advisory jurisdiction** (that is the SC's, Art. 143).
[44:8:1] - **Art. 226**: writs for **FRs "and for any other purpose"** (ordinary legal rights) – **wider than Art. 32**; to **any person, authority or government** within its territory, and **even outside** if the **cause of action** arises within. So "a HC cannot issue orders to any government except its own" is **wrong**. Art. 226 is discretionary; Art. 32 itself is an FR (R does not explain A).
[44:8:2] - **Art. 227**: **administrative and judicial superintendence** over all courts and tribunals in its territory; may act **suo motu**; **227(4)** – not over **Armed Forces** courts/tribunals. The SC has no Art. 227-type power.
[44:8:3] - **Appellate**: a HC is primarily a court of appeal; second civil appeals only on a **substantial question of law**; Sessions Court death sentences need HC confirmation (**BNSS 2023**).
[44:8:4] - Four HCs (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Delhi) have **original civil jurisdiction** in high-value cases.
[44:8:5] TABLE head: Article | Provision
  [44:8:5.0] 214 | A High Court for each State
  [44:8:5.1] 215 | Court of Record
  [44:8:5.2] 216 | Constitution of HCs – President fixes strength
  [44:8:5.3] 217 | Appointment and conditions; retirement 62
  [44:8:5.4] 218 | SC removal provisions applied to HC judges
  [44:8:5.5] 219 | Oath before the Governor
  [44:8:5.6] 220 | Restriction on practice after being a permanent judge
  [44:8:5.7] 221 | Salaries
  [44:8:5.8] 222 | Transfer of judges
  [44:8:5.9] 223 | Acting Chief Justice
  [44:8:5.10] 224 | Additional and acting judges
  [44:8:5.11] 224A | Retired judges at sittings
  [44:8:5.12] 226 / 227 | Writs / superintendence
  [44:8:5.13] 230 | Extension of HC jurisdiction to UTs
  [44:8:5.14] 231 | Common HC
  [44:8:5.15] 241 | HC for a UT
[44:8:6] - Wrong pairs seen in MCQs: "Art. 131 – HC superintendence" (131 = Centre-State disputes); "Art. 226 – complete justice" (= Art. 142); "Art. 137 – SC writs" (= Art. 32).

## SUB 10 | Limits of Judicial Review and Overcoming a Judgment
[44:10:0] - **Narrower than the USA**: Art. 21 "**procedure established by law**" vs US "**due process of law**" (US SC = "third chamber" shaping policy). Presidential system first formed in the **USA**.
[44:10:1] - **Political questions** avoided; delimitation review possible if capricious (**Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod, 2024**).
[44:10:2] TABLE head: Amendment | Effect
  [44:10:2.0] 1st (1951) | After land-reform / reservation rulings; created the Ninth Schedule
  [44:10:2.1] 38th (1975) | President's / Governor's satisfaction (Arts 123, 213, 352) non-justiciable
  [44:10:2.2] 39th (1975) | Art. 329A(4) shielded PM's election – struck down in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
  [44:10:2.3] 42nd (1976) | Barred HCs from reviewing central laws
  [44:10:2.4] 43rd (1977) | Restored that power
  [44:10:2.5] 44th (1978) | Reversed the 38th bar
[44:10:3] - Basic Structure first propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**. Judicial review **limits Parliament's sovereignty**; Parliament **cannot** amend away the Basic Structure.
[44:10:4] - Legislature **cannot simply overrule** a judgment by resolution. Permissible: a **validating law removing the basis** of the judgment (even retrospectively); a constitutional amendment (subject to the Basic Structure); review (Art. 137) / curative petition.
[44:10:5] - **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021** re-enacted struck-down conditions → struck down again in **Madras Bar Association (2025)**.
[44:10:6] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch.27 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt p.433-437); app notes 2:44 (sub 8)
## SUB 11 | Judicial Overreach Debate
[44:11:0] TABLE head: Basis | Review / restraint | Activism
  [44:11:0.0] Nature | Interpretative, legalistic | Creative, proactive, reform-oriented
  [44:11:0.1] Question | "Is the law valid?" | "Is the law just?"
[44:11:1] - **Overreach**: courts entering the executive / legislative domain → strains (blurs) **separation of powers**.
[44:11:2] - Concerns: courts doing executive work, weak enforcement, flood of letter petitions, **delays in other cases** (not a reduction), PIL misuse; Art. 142 "**complete justice**" undefined and may bypass democratic scrutiny.
[44:11:3] - **Justice A.S. Anand**: activism must not become **judicial adventurism**. **Upendra Baxi**: courts should **fill a vacuum**, not replace democratic institutions.
[44:11:4] - PIL rethink debate (May 2026) – curbing misuse, **not abolishing access to justice**.
[44:11:5] - **Mar 2026**: SC ban on an NCERT chapter on judicial delay and corruption criticised as **censorship under Art. 19**.
[44:11:6] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch.28 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt p.438-445); app notes 2:44 (sub 10)

=== NOTES 2:46 | Federal Structure of India – Federalism, Unitary Bias, Seventh Schedule and Residuary Powers
## SUB 0 | Seventh Schedule – the Three Lists, Article 246 and Counts
[46:0:0] # Where the division of powers sits
[46:0:1] - The **Seventh Schedule** (with **Article 246**, Part XI) distributes **legislative powers/subjects** between the Union and the States in **three Lists** – it reflects the **federal structure**; it was part of the original Constitution (not added later) and has **three** Lists, not two.
[46:0:2] - Other Schedules are distractors: **Sixth** = tribal areas of the North-East, **Eighth** = languages, **Ninth** = protected laws, **Eleventh** = Panchayats, **Fifth** = Scheduled Areas, **Third** = oaths.
[46:0:3] TABLE head: List | Who legislates | Original | Now (live entries)
  [46:0:3.0] I – Union | Parliament – exclusive (Art. 246(1)) | 97 | 98
  [46:0:3.1] II – State | State Legislature – exclusive "in normal circumstances" (Art. 246(3)) | 66 | 59
  [46:0:3.2] III – Concurrent | Both Parliament and State Legislatures (Art. 246(2)) | 47 | 52
[46:0:4] - **Counts settled:** Laxmikanth 8th ed. gives **98 / 59 / 52** (entries now in force); NextGen gives **100 / 61 / 52** (it counts inserted numbers such as 2A, 92A, 92B and not all omissions). Both agree on **Concurrent = 52 (originally 47)**; old exam keys "47" and "97" are the **original** figures.
[46:0:5] - The **Union List has more subjects than the State List** – one reason the Centre is called strong.
[46:0:6] # Conflicts between Lists and laws
[46:0:7] - Precedence: **Union List > Concurrent List > State List** when entries overlap.
[46:0:8] - Concurrent List conflict (**Art. 254**): the **Union law prevails** – but **not always**: a State law **reserved for and assented to by the President** prevails in that State (Art. 254(2)), until Parliament legislates again.
[46:0:9] - So "Union law **always** prevails" is **false**, and "**only States** can legislate on the Concurrent List" is **false**; under special circumstances (Arts 249, 250, 252, 253, 356) Parliament **can** legislate on the State List.
[46:0:10] - **Central sector schemes** are mostly framed on Union List subjects.
[46:0:11] - Entry numbering still ends at 97 / 66 / 47 because entries were inserted (e.g. **Union Entry 92A**, inter-State sales tax, by the **6th Amendment, 1956**) or omitted.
[46:0:12] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.215, p.222-223; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text, src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.157; Constitution of India Arts 246, 254 and Seventh Schedule (legislative.gov.in); app notes 2:46 sub 4
