## SUB 2 | Federal vs Unitary Features
[46:2:0] # Classification
[46:2:1] TABLE head: Federal features | Unitary (non-federal) features
  [46:2:1.0] Dual polity – two sets of governments | Strong Centre – more and weightier Union subjects, Centre's overriding Concurrent power, residuary power with Centre
  [46:2:1.1] Written Constitution | Single Constitution for Union and States (only ex-J&K had its own)
  [46:2:1.2] Division of powers (Seventh Schedule) | Flexibility – most provisions amended by Parliament alone; States not indestructible (Art. 3)
  [46:2:1.3] Supremacy of the Constitution | Unequal representation of States in the Rajya Sabha
  [46:2:1.4] Rigid Constitution – federal provisions need ratification by half the States | Emergency provisions
  [46:2:1.5] Independent judiciary | Single citizenship; integrated judiciary
  [46:2:1.6] Bicameralism – Rajya Sabha represents the States | All India Services; integrated audit (CAG); integrated election machinery
  [46:2:1.7]  | Appointment of Governor by the Centre; veto over State Bills (President's approval); Parliament's authority over the State List (Art. 249)
[46:2:2] - **Independence of the judiciary** is the **essential** federal feature (UPSC 2021) – it interprets the Constitution and settles Centre-State disputes.
[46:2:3] - India is federal because of the **distribution of powers** between the Union and the States (UPSC 1994); the **Rajya Sabha** signifies the **federal structure**.
[46:2:4] - "Not a federal feature" answers: **Office of the Governor** (APPSC G1 2018), **CAG** (APPSC G2), "**result of an agreement among the federating units**" (UPSC 2017).
[46:2:5] - The **Rajya Sabha's unequal representation** is counted as a unitary feature by Laxmikanth, but UPSC 2017 listed it among the features of Indian federalism – it is never the "not a feature" answer.
[46:2:6] - **Violating federal principles:** **Governor, CAG, Emergency powers (esp. Art. 356)**; **Central Services** serve only the Union and are not a violation – it is the **All India Services** (Art. 312) that Laxmikanth says "violate the principle of federalism".
[46:2:7] - **Not violative of federalism:** the **three-List division** and **residuary power with Parliament** (Canadian model); President taking over a State under emergency **is** violative.
[46:2:8] - Unitary features in a code: **Appointment of Governor, All India Services, President's approval on State Bills, constitutional crisis (emergency)**; written/rigid Constitution, supremacy, decentralisation are federal.
[46:2:9] - **Governor** is appointed by the President (**Arts 155-156**); **All India Services** (**Art. 312**) are recruited through the **UPSC** and controlled by the Centre (Art. 312 has nothing to do with the Concurrent List).
[46:2:10] - **Constitutional amendment affecting the federal structure** needs ratification by **at least half the States** (Art. 368(2) proviso).
[46:2:11] # Borrowed features linked to federalism
[46:2:12] TABLE head: Feature | Source
  [46:2:12.0] Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre, Governor appointed by the Centre, "Union" | Canada
  [46:2:12.1] Concurrent List | Australia
  [46:2:12.2] Federal scheme, Office of Governor, emergency provisions, judiciary | GoI Act, 1935
  [46:2:12.3] Suspension of FRs during emergency | Weimar (Germany)
  [46:2:12.4] Single citizenship, parliamentary system | UK
[46:2:13] - The Indian federal system is based on the **Canadian model**, not the American (formation by disintegration, the term "Union", centralising tendency).
[46:2:14] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.214-218 (federal and unitary features), ch. Salient Features/Sources; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text, src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.159-162; app notes 2:46 sub 2, sub 5
[46:2:15] - **'One Nation One Tax'** (GST, 2017) is a uniform, centralising arrangement – **not** a feature of a true federation; independent judiciary and bicameralism are.
[46:2:16] - **Bicameral State legislatures:** only **six** States (AP, Telangana, UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka) have a Legislative Council – 'bicameral legislature at all State level' is false; **dual government** is the federal item, Governor and integrated services are unitary.
[46:2:17] - **Features and their Parts:** Bicameralism (Parliament) – **Part V**; Emergency – **Part XVIII**; Welfare State (DPSP) – **Part IV**; Single citizenship – **Art. 9** (no dual citizenship).
## SUB 3 | Who Said What – Nature of Indian Federalism
[46:3:0] TABLE head: Scholar | Description
  [46:3:0.0] K.C. Wheare | "Quasi-federal" – "a unitary state with subsidiary federal features rather than a federal state with subsidiary unitary features"
  [46:3:0.1] Ivor Jennings | "A federation with a strong centralising tendency"
  [46:3:0.2] Granville Austin | "Cooperative federalism"; author of *The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation*
  [46:3:0.3] Morris-Jones | "Bargaining federalism"
  [46:3:0.4] Paul Appleby | "Extremely federal"
  [46:3:0.5] Alexandrowicz | "A case sui generis"
  [46:3:0.6] B.R. Ambedkar | Constitution "avoids the tight mould of federalism" and "could be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances"
  [46:3:0.7] K. Santhanam | Unitary bias grew from financial dependence of States and the Planning Commission
  [46:3:0.8] K.M. Nambiar | Emergency powers a "fraud on the Constitution"
  [46:3:0.9] H.V. Kamath | "Elephantine" Constitution (the CA's seal was an elephant)
  [46:3:0.10] Carl Friedrich | India "not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope" (APPSC G1 key)
[46:3:1] - Standard book label: "**federal system with unitary bias**" / "**federal in form, unitary in spirit**" (Laxmikanth, NextGen); Wheare's own phrase is the reverse – "unitary with federal features". The unitary features tilt **the balance of power in favour of the Centre** (Laxmikanth), so India is a **quasi-federation**.
[46:3:2] - **D.D. Basu:** neither purely federal nor purely unitary but a combination of both → "quasi-federal because neither federal nor unitary" (UPPSC 2007: A and R true, R explains A).
[46:3:3] - **Supreme Court:** "fundamentally federal with **pronounced unitary elements**".
[46:3:4] - The **Preamble** does **not** describe India as federal, unitary or quasi-federal – it says "**Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic**".
[46:3:5] - India **is** a federal system with a very strong Centre: "India is not a Union" is false; in the UPPSC 1998 A-R the key took "federalism is not practical in India" as true and "India is not a federal State" as false (A true, R false).
[46:3:6] > Harold Laski and Lord Bryce have no label for Indian federalism – pure distractors. "Centralising tendency" = Jennings, not Wheare.
[46:3:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.218-219 (critical evaluation), ch. Salient Features (elephantine size); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text, src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.159, p.163; app notes 2:46 sub 3
## SUB 4 | India – a "Union of States" (Article 1)
[46:4:0] - **Art. 1(1):** "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**" – the Constitution's names for the country are **India and Bharat** only (not Hindustan, Bharatvarsh).
[46:4:1] - The word "**Federation**" is **nowhere** used in the Constitution; India is described neither as a federation nor as a confederation.
[46:4:2] - "**Union of States**" is taken from the **British North America Act, 1867** (Canada).
[46:4:3] - **Ambedkar's two reasons** for "Union": (i) the federation is **not the result of an agreement** among the States (unlike the USA); (ii) the States have **no right to secede** – the Union is **indestructible**.
[46:4:4] - The Union of India is an **indissoluble Union of States**; it is not formed at the will of States and cannot be dissolved by Parliament, State Assemblies or plebiscite.
[46:4:5] - **Indestructible Union of destructible States:** Parliament can alter the area, boundaries or name of any State **without its consent** by a **simple majority** (Art. 3); USA = indestructible Union of indestructible States.
[46:4:6] - **Secession:** the Constitution gives **no right of self-determination/secession** to any region; advocacy of secession is **not protected** by free speech – the **16th Amendment (1963)** allows restrictions in the interest of **sovereignty and integrity of India**.
[46:4:7] - Territory of India = States + UTs + acquired territories; "**Union of India**" = the **States** only; both listed in the **First Schedule**.
[46:4:8] - **Art. 2** = admission/establishment of new States not part of India; laws under Arts 2-3 that change the First and Fourth Schedules are **not** Art. 368 amendments (Art. 4); an Art. 3 Bill needs the **President's recommendation**.
[46:4:9] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.214, p.216 (States not indestructible); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text, src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.162; Constitution of India Arts 1-4, Art. 19(2) as amended by the 16th Amendment; app notes 2:46 sub 1
## SUB 5 | Federalism – Meaning, Types and Federal Countries
[46:5:0] - **Federalism:** two sets of governments **co-exist** with a **constitutional distribution of powers**, under a **written Constitution**, with an independent judiciary as umpire.
[46:5:1] - **Unitary government:** one supreme central government; local units are its creations with delegated powers; **no constitutional division of powers**.
[46:5:2] - **Confederation:** a loose league of **sovereign States** that keep the **right to secede**.
[46:5:3] - A **federal polity** involves Union-State relations, inter-State relations, mechanisms for **cooperation** and mechanisms for **resolving disputes**.
[46:5:4] # Unitary government – merits and demerits
[46:5:5] TABLE head: Merits | Demerits
  [46:5:5.0] Quick (swift) decisions, uniformity of laws, flexibility | Over-centralisation; local needs neglected
  [46:5:5.1] Strong state – firm crisis response | Not suited to large, diverse countries
[46:5:6] - "**Ideal for large countries**" is NOT a characteristic of unitary government; adaptability, wide participation and less authoritarianism are federal/democratic merits.
[46:5:7] - **Power sharing** is justified because it reduces conflict, prevents majority imposition and consults all affected – it does **not** speed up decision-making.
[46:5:8] # Coming-together vs holding-together
[46:5:9] TABLE head: Type | Meaning | Examples
  [46:5:9.0] Coming-together | Independent States pool sovereignty | USA, Switzerland, Australia
  [46:5:9.1] Holding-together | A large country divides power; stronger Centre | India, Spain, Belgium
[46:5:10] # Federal and unitary countries
[46:5:11] TABLE head: Federal | Unitary
  [46:5:11.0] USA, Canada, Australia, Argentina, Switzerland, Germany, Russia, Brazil, Belgium (since 1993) | Britain (UK), France, Italy, Japan, China, Cuba, Sri Lanka
[46:5:12] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.213-214 (federal vs unitary government); NCERT Class X Democratic Politics ch. Power Sharing/Federalism (OnlyIAS NCERT summaries, src/polity/onlyias-ncert-polity-*.txt); Constitution of Argentina and Belgium (federal states); app notes 2:46 sub 0
## SUB 6 | 42nd Amendment Transfers and Residuary Powers
[46:6:0] # 42nd Amendment, 1976 – State List → Concurrent List
[46:6:1] - **Five** subjects moved: **education**, **forests**, **weights and measures**, **protection of wild animals and birds**, **administration of justice** (constitution and organisation of all courts except the SC and HCs).
[46:6:2] - Inserted **Entry 20A – population control and family planning**.
[46:6:3] - **Education** was originally a **State** subject; it went to the **Concurrent List (Entry 25)** by the **42nd Amendment** – not the 24th, 25th or 44th.
[46:6:4] - **Public order, police, agriculture** were **not** transferred.
[46:6:5] - Union use of Concurrent entries is debated – **farm laws** (Entry 33), **NEP** and **NMC Act** (education).
[46:6:6] # Residuary powers – Article 248
[46:6:7] - **Residuary powers** = matters **not enumerated in any of the three Lists**; Parliament has **exclusive** power over them (**Art. 248** and **Union Entry 97**), including **residuary taxes** (gift tax, wealth tax, expenditure tax).
[46:6:8] - Art. 248 is in **Part XI** (Chapter I, Legislative Relations); the **101st Amendment, 2016** made it "subject to **Article 246A**" (GST).
[46:6:9] TABLE head: Model | Residuary powers with
  [46:6:9.0] India, Canada | Centre
  [46:6:9.1] USA, Australia | States
  [46:6:9.2] GoI Act, 1935 | Governor-General
[46:6:10] - Former **J&K** (Art. 370): residuary powers lay with the **State** until August 2019.
[46:6:11] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.222-223; Constitution of India Arts 246A, 248 and Seventh Schedule; app notes 2:46 sub 5, sub 6
## SUB 7 | Switching to Unitary Mode – Emergency and Overriding Powers
[46:7:0] - During an **emergency** the Centre becomes all-powerful and the federal structure **converts into a unitary one without a formal amendment** – unique among federations; so the Indian polity is described as **unitary** under the Emergency provisions.
[46:7:1] - Only during a **National Emergency (Art. 352)** – declared in **any part** of the country – does the Union assume **full legislative and executive control**; President's Rule covers one State only, and ordinances or martial law (Art. 34) do not.
[46:7:2] - Emergency provisions are in **Part XVIII (Arts 352-360)**; **three** kinds: National (352), State/President's Rule (356), Financial (360).
[46:7:3] # Overriding powers
[46:7:4] TABLE head: Article | Power
  [46:7:4.0] 249 | Rajya Sabha resolution (2/3 present and voting) in national interest → Parliament legislates on a State subject (1 year, renewable)
  [46:7:4.1] 250 | During National Emergency Parliament legislates on the State List; laws lapse 6 months after it ends
  [46:7:4.2] 252 | Two or more States request Parliament to legislate
  [46:7:4.3] 253 | Laws to implement international agreements
  [46:7:4.4] 354 | President may modify revenue distribution during a National Emergency – the order lasts till the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends (not six months)
[46:7:5] # Emergencies compared
[46:7:6] TABLE head: Basis | 352 National | 356 President's Rule | 360 Financial
  [46:7:6.0] Ground | War, external aggression, armed rebellion (44th replaced "internal disturbance") | Failure of constitutional machinery | Threat to financial stability
  [46:7:6.1] Approval | 1 month, special majority | 2 months, simple | 2 months, simple
  [46:7:6.2] Duration | 6 months at a time, no maximum | 6 months at a time, max 3 years (beyond 1 year: National Emergency + EC certificate) | Until revoked
  [46:7:6.3] Used | 3 times – 1962, 1971, 1975 | Many times (AP 1973, Jai Andhra) | Never
[46:7:7] - **44th Amendment (1978):** Cabinet's **written advice**; **1/10th** of Lok Sabha members can seek a sitting to disapprove; **Arts 20-21** never suspended; **Art. 19** suspended automatically only in war/external aggression; **38th Amendment** had barred judicial review.
[46:7:8] - During a National Emergency Parliament can extend the **Lok Sabha/Assembly term by 1 year at a time**, at most **6 months** after it ends; a proclamation survives **30 days** after a new Lok Sabha's first sitting if the old one was dissolved.
[46:7:9] - **Only a National Emergency** affects Fundamental Rights; President's Rule and Financial Emergency do not.
[46:7:10] - **Financial Emergency:** financial directions, **salary cuts** (incl. judges), State **Money Bills reserved** for the President.
[46:7:11] - **1975 Emergency:** 25 June 1975 – **Samvidhan Hatya Diwas (25 June)**; withdrawn **21 March 1977**.
[46:7:12] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.216-217 (emergency as unitary feature), ch. Emergency Provisions; Constitution of India Arts 249-253, 352-360; app notes 2:46 sub 7
[46:7:13] - **Art. 353:** during a National Emergency the Centre can give **executive directions to a State on any matter**; FRs other than Arts 20-21 are suspended only by a **Presidential order under Art. 359** (Art. 19 automatically under Art. 358 only in war/external aggression) – so **not all FRs** are suspended.
[46:7:14] - **Grounds used:** **1962** (Chinese aggression, Oct; in force till Jan 1968) and **1971** (Pakistan, Dec) – **external aggression**; **1975** – **internal disturbance** (made while the 1971 one was in force).
[46:7:15] - **Art. 354 in practice:** the President can **reduce or cancel** (never increase) the transfer of finances – tax shares and grants – from the Centre to the States; a National Emergency may cover **all of India or any part** (42nd Amendment).
## SUB 8 | Courts, Rajya Sabha and Asymmetric Federalism
[46:8:0] # Supreme Court on federalism
[46:8:1] TABLE head: Case | Holding
  [46:8:1.0] State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962) | Not truly federal; States not sovereign
  [46:8:1.1] Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Federal character is a basic feature
  [46:8:1.2] S.R. Bommai (1994) | Federalism = basic structure; Art. 356 open to judicial review
  [46:8:1.3] MADA v SAIL (July 2024, 9 judges, 8:1) | Royalty is not a tax; States can tax mineral rights
[46:8:2] - **Judicial review** (incl. of **executive orders**) reinforces the federal principle; it does not question policy wisdom.
[46:8:3] # Representation and amendment
[46:8:4] - Rajya Sabha seats: **Fourth Schedule**, by population (**UP 31**); US Senate **2 per State**.
[46:8:5] - Parliamentary form: Council of Ministers **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha** (Art. 75(3)); the Constitution is **neither wholly rigid nor wholly flexible**.
[46:8:6] - **Article 368** is in **Part XX**; federal provisions need ratification by **half the State Legislatures**.
[46:8:7] - **India vs USA:** India – single citizenship, integrated judiciary, three Lists, residue with Centre; USA – dual citizenship, dual courts, residue with States; both have a written Constitution, division of powers and a federal Supreme Court.
[46:8:8] # Asymmetric federalism
[46:8:9] TABLE head: Provision | State / area
  [46:8:9.0] Former Art. 370 | J&K – own constitution and flag; inoperative Aug 2019, upheld by SC Dec 2023
  [46:8:9.1] 371A | Nagaland
  [46:8:9.2] 371D | Andhra Pradesh – equal opportunities in public employment and education
  [46:8:9.3] 371F / 371J | Sikkim / Karnataka
  [46:8:9.4] Fifth / Sixth Schedule | Scheduled Areas / tribal areas of the North-East
[46:8:10] # Federal practice and current debates
[46:8:11] - Phases: 1952-67 Congress dominance; 1967-77 confrontation (**Rajamannar Committee 1969**, Tamil Nadu); 1977-89 (**Sarkaria Commission 1983**); **1989-2014 coalition era** (**Inter-State Council 1990**); 2014 on NITI Aayog (2015), **GST (2017)**.
[46:8:12] - **Feb 2026:** Tamil Nadu's **Justice Kurian Joseph** committee – Part 1 report on Union-State relations.
[46:8:13] - **May 2026:** Lok Sabha **defeated** the **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026** – Lok Sabha maximum **550 → 850**; **AP 25 → 38** seats.
[46:8:14] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) ch. Federal System, Basic Structure, Special Provisions; app notes 2:46 sub 8, sub 9, sub 10 (2026 current affairs from the app's CA)
[46:8:15] - **Single citizenship** (Art. 9; from the UK) despite a dual polity; **USA** (national + State) and **Switzerland** (federal, canton and commune) have more than one level of citizenship.

=== NOTES 2:47 | Centre-state Legislative Relations – Articles 245-255, Repugnancy, Parliament on the State List
## SUB 0 | Parliament on the State List – Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 and 356
[47:0:0] # The five situations
[47:0:1] TABLE head: Article | Trigger | Area / duration
  [47:0:1.0] 249 | Rajya Sabha resolution, 2/3 of members present and voting, national interest | Resolution in force up to 1 year, renewable 1 year at a time; law ceases 6 months after the resolution lapses
  [47:0:1.1] 250 | National Emergency (Proclamation under Art. 352 in operation) | Whole or any part of India; law ceases 6 months after the Emergency ends
  [47:0:1.2] 252 | Resolutions of the legislatures of two or more States | Only the consenting States (others may adopt later); only Parliament can amend or repeal
  [47:0:1.3] 253 | To implement international treaties, agreements, conventions | Whole or any part of India; no State's consent needed
  [47:0:1.4] 356/357 | President's Rule in a State | Parliament (or its delegate) makes the State's laws; they continue after PR ends until the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts them
[47:0:2] - **Normal rule:** Parliament cannot legislate on the State List except under **Arts 249, 250, 252, 253 and 356** – "on its own in the national interest" is **wrong** (needs the Rajya Sabha resolution).
[47:0:3] - **Articles are the grant, emergencies the occasion:** the power during a National Emergency is given by **Art. 250** (Art. 352 only proclaims the Emergency).
[47:0:4] # Article 249 – Rajya Sabha resolution
[47:0:5] - **Majority:** **two-thirds of members present and voting** – not total membership, not the Lok Sabha (the Lok Sabha has **no role**).
[47:0:6] - **Duration:** resolution in force for a period **not exceeding one year** (Art. 249(2)); can be renewed any number of times.
[47:0:7] - A **special power of the Rajya Sabha** (with Art. 312 – new All India Services).
[47:0:8] - The State **may still legislate**, but the **Parliamentary law prevails** in a conflict (**Art. 251**).
[47:0:9] # Article 250 – Emergency
[47:0:10] - During a Proclamation of Emergency **Parliament** (not the President or a minister) legislates on State List matters; State power is **not suspended**, Union law prevails on conflict.
[47:0:11] - Laws cease **6 months after the Proclamation ceases** – they do **not** continue indefinitely.
[47:0:12] # Article 252 – consent of States
[47:0:13] TABLE head: Act passed under Article 252 | Year
  [47:0:13.0] Prize Competition Act | 1955
  [47:0:13.1] Wild Life (Protection) Act | 1972
  [47:0:13.2] Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act | 1974
  [47:0:13.3] Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act | 1976
  [47:0:13.4] Transplantation of Human Organs Act | 1994
[47:0:14] - A request by **one State** is not enough; the requesting States **lose the power to amend or repeal** the law.
[47:0:15] - **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** is **not** an Art. 252 law (made under Art. 253 after the Stockholm Conference).
[47:0:16] # Article 253 – international agreements
[47:0:17] - Parliament can make **any law for the whole or any part of India** to implement treaties, agreements, conventions or decisions of international bodies – **even on State List subjects** and **without the consent of any State** (UPSC 2013; UPPCS 2006, 2016).
[47:0:18] - So "the Union can legislate on State List subjects to implement an international agreement" is the statement that reflects India's federal design.
[47:0:19] > Statement angle: State List law possible on – request of 2+ States ✓, Rajya Sabha 2/3 resolution ✓, international agreements ✓, Emergency ✓, President's Rule ✓; a **Lok Sabha** resolution ✗.
[47:0:20] > Wrong-answer angle: "Both Union and States have absolute freedom on the Concurrent List" ✗ – Union law prevails in conflict.
[47:0:21] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.223-225; NextGen Polity APPSC 18 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-18.txt) p.10; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.10, p.34; Constitution Arts 249-253, 357 (indiacode.nic.in); app notes 2:47 (sub 6, 13)
## SUB 1 | Residuary Powers – Article 248
[47:1:0] # The rule
[47:1:1] - **Article 248** (Part XI) + **Entry 97 of the Union List**: matters in **no list** belong **exclusively to Parliament** – Parliament **only**, not the States, the President, the Supreme Court or "both jointly".
[47:1:2] - Art. 248 itself says Parliament has **exclusive power** to make any law on any matter **not enumerated in the Concurrent or State List** – so both "residuary powers are in Art. 248" and "Parliament has exclusive power over items not in the State or Concurrent List" are correct.
[47:1:3] - Includes **residuary taxation** (e.g. gift tax, wealth tax, expenditure tax); examples: **space research**, **cyber law**.
[47:1:4] TABLE head: Country | Residuary power with
  [47:1:4.0] India, Canada | Centre (Union / Parliament)
  [47:1:4.1] USA, Australia | States
[47:1:5] - **Sarkaria Commission (1988):** residuary powers **except taxation** to the **Concurrent List**; residuary taxation to stay with Parliament.
[47:1:6] - **Rajamannar Committee (1971):** residuary powers (legislation and taxation) to the **States**.
[47:1:7] # Jammu and Kashmir (till 5 August 2019)
[47:1:8] - Under Art. 370 and the 1954 Presidential Order, residuary power for J&K lay with the **State Legislature** (except a few matters such as terrorism) – not Parliament (APPSC 2001, DAO 2011).
[47:1:9] - Other J&K facts asked: J&K was part of the territory of India (Art. 1, First Schedule), but not all provisions on States applied to it; by accession India got **Defence, External Affairs and Communications**.
[47:1:10] - **⚠ Now:** Art. 370 provisions ceased in Aug 2019; the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019** made J&K and Ladakh **Union Territories** (31 Oct 2019), so residuary power now rests with **Parliament** (upheld by the SC, Dec 2023).
[47:1:11] > Trap: "Like other States, J&K's residuary powers vest in Parliament" was the WRONG statement (pre-2019).
[47:1:12] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.223, p.238, p.240; NextGen Polity APPSC 18 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-18.txt) p.9, p.12; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.10; J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 (indiacode.nic.in); app notes 2:47 (sub 5)
## SUB 2 | Part XI and the Article Map 245-255
[47:2:0] # Where it sits
[47:2:1] - **Part XI** (Relations between the Union and the States) = **Articles 245-263**: Chapter I **legislative relations = Arts 245-255**; Chapter II administrative relations = Arts 256-263.
[47:2:2] - Distribution of legislative powers is regulated by **Articles 245 and 246** (with the **Seventh Schedule**); scheme borrowed from **Canada**, plus a third **Concurrent List** (from the GoI Act, 1935).
[47:2:3] TABLE head: Articles | Subject
  [47:2:3.0] 245-255 (Part XI, Ch. I) | Legislative relations
  [47:2:3.1] 256-263 (Part XI, Ch. II) | Administrative relations; 263 Inter-State Council
  [47:2:3.2] 264-293 (Part XII) | Finance; 268-281 distribution of revenues; 280 Finance Commission; 281 its recommendations
  [47:2:3.3] 301-307 (Part XIII) | Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse
[47:2:4] - Arts **265, 266** (taxes by authority of law; Consolidated Fund) are in **Part XII**, not Part XI Chapter I.
[47:2:5] # Article by article
[47:2:6] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [47:2:6.0] 245 | Extent of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures
  [47:2:6.1] 246 | Subject-matter division: three Lists of the Seventh Schedule
  [47:2:6.2] 246A | GST – Parliament and States together (101st Amendment, 2016)
  [47:2:6.3] 247 | Parliament may set up additional courts for Union laws
  [47:2:6.4] 248 | Residuary powers – Parliament
  [47:2:6.5] 249 | State List in the national interest (Rajya Sabha resolution)
  [47:2:6.6] 250 | State List during a National Emergency
  [47:2:6.7] 251 | Union law under 249/250 prevails over an inconsistent State law
  [47:2:6.8] 252 | Law for two or more States by consent
  [47:2:6.9] 253 | Laws to implement international agreements
  [47:2:6.10] 254 | Inconsistency (repugnancy) between Union and State laws
  [47:2:6.11] 255 | Requirements of recommendation / previous sanction = matters of procedure only
[47:2:7] # Article 255
[47:2:8] - An Act is **not invalid** merely because a required **recommendation or previous sanction** was not given, **if assent was later given** by the Governor or the President – so courts cannot strike down a law on that ground alone.
[47:2:9] > Match angle: 245 extent – 248 residuary – 254 inconsistency – Part XI relations (245-263).
[47:2:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.221-225; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.10; Constitution Part XI (indiacode.nic.in); app notes 2:47 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 3 | Seventh Schedule – Lists and Subjects
[47:3:0] # Article 246 scheme
[47:3:1] TABLE head: Clause | Who | List
  [47:3:1.0] 246(1) | Parliament – exclusive | List I (Union)
  [47:3:1.1] 246(2) | Both – concurrent | List III (Concurrent)
  [47:3:1.2] 246(3) | State – exclusive, subject to (1) and (2) | List II (State)
  [47:3:1.3] 246(4) | Parliament for areas not in a State (UTs) | All three Lists
[47:3:2] - **Art. 246 / Seventh Schedule** divide all subject areas (incl. environment-related subjects) into the three Lists, and is also the source of the power to impose **taxes and fees** (tax entries are in the Lists).
[47:3:3] - **Order of predominance:** **Union List > Concurrent List > State List** – in a Concurrent-State conflict the **Concurrent List prevails**; no reference to the President or the Speaker.
[47:3:4] - **Limits on Parliament:** it legislates subject to the **distribution of powers** (and the Constitution) – not the UN Charter, conventions or public opinion.
[47:3:5] - **Art. 246A (GST)** breaks the strict division: **simultaneous** power; **only Parliament** for **inter-State supply (IGST)**.
[47:3:6] TABLE head: List | Original | Now
  [47:3:6.0] Union | 97 | 98
  [47:3:6.1] State | 66 | 59
  [47:3:6.2] Concurrent | 47 | 52
[47:3:7] - **State List 66 → 59:** entries 11, 19, 20, 29 omitted/moved (**42nd CAA, 1976**), 36 (**7th CAA, 1956**), 52 and 55 (**101st CAA, 2016**).
[47:3:8] - **Union List 97 → 98:** 92A, 92B, 92C were added, then 92 and 92C omitted by the **101st CAA, 2016**.
[47:3:9] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen prints "Union List 100 subjects"; Laxmikanth 8th ed. gives **98** – the current count.
[47:3:10] # Subject → List
[47:3:11] TABLE head: Union List | State List | Concurrent List
  [47:3:11.0] Defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, railways | Public order (Entry 1), police, prisons | Education (Entry 25)
  [47:3:11.1] Banking, RBI, currency, foreign loans, Post Office Savings Bank | Public health and sanitation | Forests
  [47:3:11.2] Census, broadcasting | Agriculture (Entry 14), markets and fairs (Entry 28), fisheries | Social security
  [47:3:11.3] Inter-State trade (Entry 42) | Trade within a State (Entry 26) | Economic and social planning (Entry 20)
  [47:3:11.4] Organisation of High Courts | Local government – Panchayati Raj / Municipalities (Entry 5) | Marriage, divorce, adoption (Entry 5)
  [47:3:11.5] Technical institutions of national importance (Entry 64) | Taxes on mineral rights (Entry 50) | Criminal law, civil procedure, succession
  [47:3:11.6]  | Elections to State Legislature (Entry 37) | Adulteration of foodstuffs, drugs, electricity, newspapers
  [47:3:11.7]  | Land (Entry 18); livestock (Entry 15) | Prevention of cruelty to animals (Entry 17)

[47:3:13] - **Composition of Panchayats** is decided by the **State Legislature** (Art. **243-C(1)**).
[47:3:14] - **Farm Laws (2020)** used **Concurrent Entry 33** in a field linked to **agriculture (State Entry 14)**.

  [47:3:15.2] Preventive detention – defence, foreign affairs, security of India | Union Entry 9
  [47:3:15.3] Preventive detention – State security, public order | Concurrent Entry 3

## SUB 4 | Territorial Extent – Article 245 and Territorial Nexus
[47:4:0] TABLE head: Legislature | Extent
  [47:4:0.0] Parliament | Whole or any part of India; alone can make extra-territorial laws
  [47:4:0.1] State Legislature | Own State only; outside reach only with a real territorial nexus
[47:4:1] - **Art. 245(2):** no law of Parliament is invalid because it has **extra-territorial operation** – so the power of extra-territorial legislation = **Parliament only** (not a House alone, the President, the State or any UN approval).
[47:4:2] - Parliament's laws apply to persons and property in India and to **Indian citizens and their property anywhere** in the world.
[47:4:3] - **Doctrine of territorial nexus:** decides the **scope of a State Legislature's extra-territorial power** – a State law with extra-territorial operation is valid if there is a **sufficient, real (not illusory) nexus** between the State and the object (Wallace 1948; R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla 1957; TISCO 1958).
[47:4:4] - **⚠ Do not confuse:** "what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly" = **colourable legislation**, not territorial nexus.
[47:4:5] # Exceptions to Parliament's reach
[47:4:6] - **Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu (Art. 240):** **President's regulations** have the force of Acts of Parliament.
[47:4:7] - **Scheduled Areas:** the **Governor** may **bar or modify** Acts of Parliament; Governor of **Assam** likewise for tribal areas.
[47:4:8] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.221; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch94 Doctrine of territorial nexus (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-03.txt) p.61-62; NextGen Polity APPSC 18 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-18.txt) p.9; app notes 2:47 (sub 2)
## SUB 5 | Repugnancy, Paramountcy and Central Control
[47:5:0] # Article 254
[47:5:1] - Applies to a Central vs State law on a **Concurrent** subject.
[47:5:2] - **254(1):** **Union law prevails**; the State law is **void to the extent of repugnancy** – the **doctrine of paramountcy** (reconciles conflicting laws where both levels can legislate on the same matter).
[47:5:3] - **254(2):** a State law **reserved for and assented to by the President** prevails **only in that State**.
[47:5:4] - **Proviso:** Parliament can later **override** it by a fresh law.
[47:5:5] - **Art. 251** (not 254) covers conflict with laws made under **Arts 249/250**; Art. 250 is **not** the repugnancy article.
[47:5:6] # Central control over State legislation
[47:5:7] - **Governor may reserve** State Bills for the President (Art. 200/201); Art. 254(2) reservation is an exception to aid and advice.
[47:5:8] - **State Bill** with **reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade** in the public interest needs the **President's previous sanction** (Part XIII, Art. 304(b)).
[47:5:9] - **Arts 301-303:** Parliament cannot **prefer or discriminate** between States in trade laws, except in **scarcity**.
[47:5:10] - **Nov 2025 SC advisory opinion (Presidential Reference):** **rejected "deemed assent"** and **judicially fixed timelines** for Governors and the President.
[47:5:11] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.223-225; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); app notes 2:47 (sub 7, 8)
## SUB 6 | Doctrines of Interpretation
[47:6:0] - Most doctrines are **judicially evolved**, not written in the Constitution.
[47:6:1] TABLE head: Doctrine | Meaning | Case
  [47:6:1.0] Pith and substance | True nature of a law decides; incidental encroachment on another List is fine (Art. 246) | Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v Bank of Commerce (1947, Privy Council); State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951) – prohibition law valid
  [47:6:1.1] Colourable legislation | "What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly" | Kameshwar Singh (1952); K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa (1953)
  [47:6:1.2] Harmonious construction | Overlapping entries read together so both operate | —
  [47:6:1.3] Severability | Only the unconstitutional part void, if separable (Art. 13) | A.K. Gopalan (1950); F.N. Balsara (1951)
  [47:6:1.4] Eclipse | Pre-Constitution law conflicting with an FR is dormant; revives if the right is amended | Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v State of M.P. (1955)
  [47:6:1.5] Territorial nexus | Scope of State extra-territorial laws (Art. 245) | Chamarbaugwalla (1957)
  [47:6:1.6] Basic structure | Parliament cannot destroy basic features | Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
  [47:6:1.7] Judicial review | Courts test legislative acts and executive actions (Arts 13, 32, 226) | Marbury v Madison (1803, USA)
[47:6:2] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch94 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-03.txt) p.55-87; NextGen Polity APPSC 18 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-18.txt) p.9-10; app notes 2:47 (sub 9)
## SUB 7 | Current Debates on Legislative Relations
[47:7:0] - **Demand for review of Centre-State relations:** growing, because the **States lack adequate resources** for development – both true, the reason explains it (UPPCS 2007 A-R).
[47:7:1] - **MMDR (Amendment) Bill, 2026:** limits State tax on **mineral rights** and mineral-bearing land; **Kerala** says it enters **State Entries 18 and 50** (Aug 2026).
[47:7:2] - Centralising tools criticised: Art. 254(2) override, use of Arts 249/252, frequent ordinances, Union List dominance, GST disputes.

=== NOTES 2:50 | Centre-state Financial Relations – Articles 264-293; Taxes, Grants-in-aid, Borrowing
## SUB 0 | Distribution of Tax Revenues – Articles 268 to 271 and State Taxes
[50:0:0] # Who levies, who collects, who keeps (present position, after the 80th and 101st Amendments)
[50:0:1] TABLE head: Article | Levied by | Collected / kept by | Taxes
  [50:0:1.0] 268 | Union | States collect and appropriate | Stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes, insurance policies, share transfers; proceeds not part of the CFI
  [50:0:1.1] 269 | Union | Union collects, assigned to the States | Taxes on inter-State sale or purchase of goods (not newspapers) and on inter-State consignment; net proceeds do not form part of the CFI
  [50:0:1.2] 269A | Union | Shared as Parliament provides on GST Council advice | IGST on inter-State supplies (101st Amendment)
  [50:0:1.3] 270 | Union | Shared with States on Finance Commission advice (divisible pool) | All Union List taxes – income tax (non-agricultural), corporation tax, customs, CGST … – except 268, 269, 269A taxes, surcharges (271) and cesses
  [50:0:1.4] 271 | Union | Union only – States get no share | Surcharges on 269 and 270 taxes (not on GST)
  [50:0:1.5] 268A (omitted) | Union | Union + States | Service tax – inserted by 88th (2003), omitted by 101st (2016)
  [50:0:1.6] 272 (omitted) | Union | Shared by law | Union excise – omitted by the 80th (2000)
[50:0:2] - **Income tax:** the Union **levies, collects and distributes** it between itself and the States (Art. 270) – it is neither kept wholly by the Union nor given wholly to the States; only the **surcharge** stays with the Union.
[50:0:3] - **Before 2000** (old Art. 269) the Union levied and collected but **assigned to the States** taxes on **railway fares and freights**, **stock-exchange and futures-market transactions** (other than stamp duty), estate and succession duty, newspapers and their advertisements; the **80th Amendment** moved these into the **Art. 270 pool**. Only **income tax** was shared from 1950; **corporation tax and customs** became shareable only from **1996** (80th).
[50:0:4] - **Art. 268 before GST** also covered **excise on medicinal and toilet preparations containing alcohol** – levied by the Union, **collected and kept by the States**; the 101st Amendment removed it (now under GST).
[50:0:5] # Taxes levied, collected and retained by the States (State List, 18 heads)
[50:0:6] - **Land revenue**, **agricultural income tax** (Entry 46 – the **Constitution**, not the Finance Commission, assigns it), duties on succession to agricultural land, taxes on **lands and buildings**, mineral rights.
[50:0:7] - **State excise on alcoholic liquor** for human consumption, opium and narcotics; taxes on **sale of petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, ATF and liquor** (outside GST – levied **by the States**, not the Centre).
[50:0:8] - Electricity, goods and passengers by road/inland waterways, **vehicles**, animals and boats, **tolls**, **professions** (Art. 276), capitation, **entertainment tax by local bodies**, stamp duty on other documents.
[50:0:9] - **Profession tax (Art. 276(2)):** the **only tax whose total per person is capped by the Constitution** – **₹2,500 a year** (₹250 till the **60th Amendment, 1988**).
[50:0:10] # Local bodies
[50:0:11] - **Art. 243H / 243X:** the State Legislature may let Panchayats/Municipalities **levy, collect and appropriate** taxes, duties, tolls and fees, and may **assign** to them taxes collected by the State.
[50:0:12] - **Assigned revenues:** taxes **assigned to local bodies by statute but collected by the State** and passed on to the Panchayats.
[50:0:13] - **Gram Panchayat taxes:** house tax, **tax/fee on fairs and markets ("fair tax")**, water and lighting rates, vehicle and animal fees – **not** sales tax, customs or excise.
[50:0:14] > Asked as: which tax is levied by the Union but collected and kept by the States (stamp duty); levied and collected by the Union but assigned (Art. 269); levied by the Centre and shared (income tax, Art. 270); State-only taxes (land revenue, liquor excise); statements on 269/270/271 (APPSC Group-I 2024); profession tax cap.
[50:0:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 16 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-16.txt) p.12-15; NextGen Polity APPSC Part 17 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-17.txt) p.6; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.229-232; app notes 2:50 sub 1, 3
## SUB 1 | Finance Commission and Devolution – Article 280
[50:1:0] # The body
[50:1:1] - **Art. 280:** a **quasi-judicial** body constituted by the **President** every **fifth year** or earlier; chairman + 4 members (Finance Commission Act, 1951); **Art. 281:** its report and the action taken are laid before Parliament.
[50:1:2] - Called the **"balancing wheel of fiscal federalism"**; its advice is **not binding**.
[50:1:3] # What it recommends (Art. 280(3))
[50:1:4] - **Distribution of the net proceeds of taxes** between the Union and the States (**vertical**) and **among the States inter se** (**horizontal distribution**).
[50:1:5] - **Principles governing grants-in-aid** to the States out of the **Consolidated Fund of India** (Art. 275).
[50:1:6] - Measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund for **Panchayats and Municipalities** (73rd/74th Amendments), and any matter referred by the President.
[50:1:7] - It does **not** attract foreign capital, distribute funds among PSUs or audit financial administration (UPSC 2011 – "none of these").
[50:1:8] - Tax sharing is **not** fixed by the Finance Ministry, RBI, NABARD, NITI Aayog, the Inter-State Council, NDC or the GST Council; the **CAG certifies the net proceeds** (Art. 279).
[50:1:9] # Shares
[50:1:10] TABLE head: FC | Period | States' share of divisible pool
  [50:1:10.0] 10th | 1995-2000 | Alternative Scheme of Devolution – 29% of gross Union taxes (80th Amendment)
  [50:1:10.1] 14th (Y.V. Reddy) | 2015-20 | 42% – "compositional shift" from grants to devolution
  [50:1:10.2] 15th (N.K. Singh) | 2020-26 | 41%
  [50:1:10.3] 16th (Arvind Panagariya) | 2026-31 | 41% retained; State fiscal deficit 3% of GSDP; end off-budget borrowing
[50:1:11] - **Compositional shift:** more tax devolution and fewer conditional grants → **increase in the share of unconditional (untied) transfers** to States and more fiscal autonomy (APPSC Group-I 2017).
[50:1:12] - **Cesses and surcharges** (~18% of gross tax) stay outside the pool, so effective devolution is about **31-32%**; southern States' **"Chalo Delhi" (2024)** opposed population-based criteria. Tax devolution 2024-25: **₹12.87 lakh crore**.
[50:1:13] > Asked as: who recommends distribution of net tax proceeds / principles of grants-in-aid (Finance Commission – 6 PYQs); horizontal distribution; effect of the compositional shift.
[50:1:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.10; NextGen Polity APPSC Part 20 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-20.txt) p.6; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.234; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.65-66; app notes 2:50 sub 5, 6
## SUB 2 | Part XII Framework – Key Articles 264 to 293
[50:2:0] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [50:2:0.0] 265 | No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law
  [50:2:0.1] 266 | Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts of India and the States – CFI receives all Union revenues, loans raised and loan repayments
  [50:2:0.2] 267 | Contingency Funds
  [50:2:0.3] 268 | First Article of Chapter I "Distribution of Revenues" (Arts 268-281)
  [50:2:0.4] 274 | President's prior recommendation for Bills affecting taxes in which States are interested / "agricultural income"
  [50:2:0.5] 275 | Statutory grants-in-aid to States
  [50:2:0.6] 276 | Profession tax
  [50:2:0.7] 279 / 279A | Net proceeds (certified by the CAG) / GST Council
  [50:2:0.8] 280 / 281 | Finance Commission / its recommendations
  [50:2:0.9] 282 | Discretionary grants – any public purpose
  [50:2:0.10] 285 / 289 | Union property exempt from State taxes / State property exempt from Union taxes
  [50:2:0.11] 292 / 293 | Borrowing by the Union / by the States
[50:2:1] - **Part XII** (Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits) = Arts **264-300A**; Centre-State financial relations = Arts **268-293**; **distribution of revenues = Arts 268-281** (UPPCS 2014).
[50:2:2] - Budget procedure is in **Part V** (Arts 112-117), not Part XII.
[50:2:3] > Asked as: Article number recall – 265 (4 PYQs incl. APPSC HWO), 268 (scheme of distribution), 275, 280, 282, range 268-281.

## SUB 3 | GST and the GST Council
[50:3:0] # Framework
[50:3:1] - **101st Amendment Act, 2016** (the **122nd Amendment Bill**) – GST from **1 July 2017**; **destination-based**; inserted **Arts 246A, 269A, 279A**, omitted 268A; replaced about **17** indirect taxes.
[50:3:2] - **Subsumed:** Central excise, service tax, CVD/SAD, **State VAT/sales tax**, **entry tax and octroi**, **entertainment tax (except by local bodies)**, luxury, purchase and lottery taxes.
[50:3:3] - **Not subsumed:** **land revenue** (not a tax on supply at all), **State excise on alcohol for human consumption** (liquor is outside GST), stamp duty, electricity duty, basic customs; petroleum products zero-rated till the Council decides.
[50:3:4] - **Art. 246A:** Parliament and States both make GST laws; **only Parliament** for **inter-State supply**; **Art. 269A:** IGST, revenue to the **destination State**.
[50:3:5] # GST Council – Art. 279A
[50:3:6] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [50:3:6.0] Chair | Union Finance Minister
  [50:3:6.1] Members | Union MoS (Revenue/Finance) + every State's Finance Minister
  [50:3:6.2] Votes | Centre 1/3, all States together 2/3; decision by 3/4 of weighted votes
  [50:3:6.3] Status | Mohit Minerals (2022): recommendations persuasive, not binding
[50:3:7] - **53rd GST Council (22 June 2024):** monetary limits for departmental appeals – **₹20 lakh GSTAT, ₹1 crore High Court, ₹2 crore Supreme Court** (CBIC Circular 207/1/2024-GST).
[50:3:8] - **GST and federalism:** "**pooled sovereignty**" – Centre and States decide **jointly** in the Council as partners (cooperative federalism); critics note the Centre's effective veto. Compensation cess on luxury/sin goods for **5 years (2017-22)**; **GST 2.0** from **September 2025**.
[50:3:9] > Asked as: Amendment number (101st – 2 PYQs); Council chair; tax not subsumed; 2024 Council decisions; GST and Centre-State relations.
[50:3:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.231, p.233-234; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.66; GST Council 53rd meeting press release (pib.gov.in, 22-06-2024); CBIC Circular 207/1/2024-GST (gstcouncil.gov.in); app notes 2:50 sub 4
## SUB 4 | Grants-in-aid, Plan Transfers and Special Category Status
[50:4:0] # Statutory vs discretionary grants
[50:4:1] TABLE head: Feature | Statutory (Art. 275) | Discretionary (Art. 282)
  [50:4:1.0] To whom | States in need (not every State); ST welfare, Scheduled Areas | Any State – any public purpose, even outside legislative competence
  [50:4:1.1] Recommended by | Finance Commission | Earlier the Planning Commission; now Union ministries
  [50:4:1.2] Charged on CFI | Yes | No
[50:4:2] - Statutory grants are on the **Finance Commission's** advice, **not NITI Aayog's**.
[50:4:3] # Plan-transfer formulas
[50:4:4] TABLE head: Formula | Year | Weights (%)
  [50:4:4.0] Gadgil (D.R. Gadgil) | 1969, 4th Plan | Population 60, per-capita income 10, tax effort 10, irrigation/power 10, special problems 10
  [50:4:4.1] Gadgil-Mukherjee | 1991, 8th Plan | Population 60, per-capita income 25, performance 7.5, special problems 7.5
[50:4:5] - **Gadgil formula** = allocation of **Central Plan assistance** to States, i.e. **devolution of funds** – not tax division, borrowing, river waters or LoC. Both ended with the **Planning Commission (2015)**.
[50:4:6] # Special Category Status (NDC, 1969)
[50:4:7] - Benefits: Central assistance as **90% grant : 10% loan**, **excise-duty and tax concessions** for industry – so "all of these".
[50:4:8] - Parameters: **hilly terrain**, **low population density / large tribal share**, **strategic border location**, economic backwardness, **non-viable State finances** – not high per-capita income.
[50:4:9] - **AP:** post-2014 demand for SCS (never written into APRA 2014).
[50:4:10] > Asked as: Article for grants (275/282); Gadgil formula (2 PYQs); SCS benefits.
[50:4:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 17 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-17.txt) p.2-3; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.233; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.66; app notes 2:50 sub 7, 8
## SUB 5 | Borrowing – Articles 292 and 293
[50:5:0] TABLE head: Article | Rule
  [50:5:0.0] 292 | Union borrows on the security of the CFI, within or outside India, within limits fixed by Parliament by law
  [50:5:0.1] 293(1) | A State borrows only within India, on the security of its Consolidated Fund, within limits fixed by the State Legislature – no direct foreign loans
  [50:5:0.2] 293(2) | Union may lend to States or guarantee their loans
  [50:5:0.3] 293(3) | A State owing the Union needs the Union's consent (with conditions) for a fresh loan
[50:5:1] - **Net Borrowing Ceiling** (~3% of GSDP) is imposed via **293(3)** and counts off-budget borrowing; **Kerala v Union of India (2024)** – Art. 131 suit, referred to a **five-judge bench**.
[50:5:2] - AP net borrowings **2024-25: ₹60,485.40 crore**.
[50:5:3] > Asked as: can a State take foreign loans directly? – **No** (UPPCS 2012).
[50:5:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch15 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.235; NextGen Polity APPSC Part 17 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-17.txt) p.4; app notes 2:50 sub 9
## SUB 6 | Amendments, Emergencies and Fiscal Disputes
[50:6:0] TABLE head: Amendment | Year | Change
  [50:6:0.0] 60th | 1988 | Profession tax ceiling ₹250 → ₹2,500
  [50:6:0.1] 80th | 2000 (in force 1 April 1996) | 10th FC Alternative Scheme – 29% of gross Union taxes; omitted Art. 272; all Union taxes shareable
  [50:6:0.2] 88th | 2003 | Inserted Art. 268A (service tax)
  [50:6:0.3] 101st | 2016 | GST – Arts 246A, 269A, 279A; omitted 268A
[50:6:1] - 268A and 272 were **not** omitted by the same Amendment (272 – 80th; 268A – 101st).
[50:6:2] - **Art. 354:** in a National Emergency the President may **modify revenue distribution**, till the end of the **financial year** in which the Emergency ends.
[50:6:3] - **Art. 360:** Union may direct States on **financial propriety**; State **Money/Financial Bills reserved** for the President.
[50:6:4] - **Disputes:** Supreme Court's original jurisdiction (**Art. 131**); matters referred to the **Finance Commission are excluded**.

=== NOTES 2:52 | Emergency Provisions – National Emergency (352), President's Rule (356), Financial Emergency (360); S.r. Bommai Case
## SUB 0 | National Emergency (Article 352) – Grounds, Proclamation, Approval
[52:0:0] # Grounds
[52:0:1] - Proclaimed by the **President** when the security of India or any part is threatened by **war, external aggression or armed rebellion** – also on **imminent danger**; for the whole of India or a part.
[52:0:2] - **44th Amendment, 1978** substituted "**armed rebellion**" for "**internal disturbance**" – internal disturbance / threat to internal peace is **no longer a ground**.
[52:0:3] - War / external aggression = "**External Emergency**"; armed rebellion = "**Internal Emergency**".
[52:0:4] # Proclamation
[52:0:5] - Only when the **Union Cabinet's decision is communicated in writing** – **Art. 352(3)**, inserted by the **44th Amendment** – not on the PM's or the Home Minister's advice alone, not suo motu, not on the CJI's advice.
[52:0:6] - The word "**Cabinet**" (mantrimandal) appears **only once** in the Constitution – in **Art. 352(3)**.
[52:0:7] - **Judicial review:** the 38th Amendment (1975) made the President's satisfaction **non-justiciable**; the **44th** removed that bar and **Minerva Mills (1980)** held a proclamation **reviewable** (mala fide / irrelevant grounds) – so "it cannot be challenged in any court" is **wrong**.
[52:0:8] # Approval, duration, revocation
[52:0:9] TABLE head: Point | Rule
  [52:0:9.0] Approval | Both Houses within one month (two months till 1978)
  [52:0:9.1] Majority | Special majority – 2/3 present and voting + majority of total membership, in each House separately (no joint sitting)
  [52:0:9.2] Duration | 6 months at a time, extendable indefinitely
  [52:0:9.3] Lok Sabha dissolved | Survives 30 days from the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha if Rajya Sabha has approved
  [52:0:9.4] Revocation | President any time; must revoke if Lok Sabha disapproves by simple majority
  [52:0:9.5] Special sitting | 1/10 of total Lok Sabha members give written notice to the Speaker (President if not in session) → sitting within 14 days
[52:0:10] > Asked as: Article (352 – 9 PYQs); grounds / not a ground (internal disturbance – 9 PYQs); whose advice (written Cabinet decision – 6 PYQs); approval period (1 month – 4 PYQs); 44th Amendment changes; statements on approval/revocation.
[52:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 23 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-23.txt) p.9-10; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch17 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.259-261, p.274; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.10, p.117-119; app notes 2:52 sub 1
[52:0:12] - **Art. 85:** not more than **six months** between two sessions of Parliament (the six-month cycle often paired with the Emergency's six-month extensions).
## SUB 1 | President's Rule (Article 356) – State or Constitutional Emergency
[52:1:0] # Grounds and approval
[52:1:1] - Imposed when the President is satisfied, **on the Governor's report or otherwise**, that the government of a State **cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution** (Art. 356) or the State **fails to comply with Union directions** (Art. **365**).
[52:1:2] - Called "**State Emergency**" or "**Constitutional Emergency**" – it leads to **President's Rule / Governor's Rule**, not suspension of freedoms, salary cuts or mid-term polls.
[52:1:3] - **No consent** of the State Legislature; the Governor reports when **he is convinced** the government cannot run per the Constitution.
[52:1:4] TABLE head: Point | Rule
  [52:1:4.0] Approval | Both Houses within two months, simple majority
  [52:1:4.1] Each approval | 6 months
  [52:1:4.2] Maximum | 3 years
  [52:1:4.3] Beyond 1 year | Only if a National Emergency is in operation AND the Election Commission certifies elections cannot be held (Art. 356(5))
  [52:1:4.4] Revocation | President any time – no parliamentary approval
[52:1:5] # Consequences
[52:1:6] TABLE head: Organ | Effect
  [52:1:6.0] Executive | President assumes State functions; Council of Ministers dismissed (necessarily); Governor administers with advisers
  [52:1:6.1] Legislature | Assembly suspended or dissolved (not necessarily dissolved); Parliament makes laws on State List matters for the State, or delegates to the President (President's Acts)
  [52:1:6.2] Laws | Laws made during PR continue after it ends until altered by the State Legislature
  [52:1:6.3] High Court | Unaffected
  [52:1:6.4] Local bodies | Not dissolved
[52:1:7] # Proper and improper use (Sarkaria → Bommai)
[52:1:8] - **Proper:** hung assembly; no party able to form a ministry; **constitutional direction of the Centre disregarded**; internal subversion; physical breakdown.
[52:1:9] - **Improper:** loss of majority without probing an alternative; no floor test; Lok Sabha defeat of the ruling party; **maladministration or corruption** of the ministry; intra-party problems.
[52:1:10] # Misuse debate
[52:1:11] - Used **more than 125 times**, often arbitrarily for political reasons – hence among the **most controversial** provisions.
[52:1:12] - **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** hoped it would remain a "**dead letter**", used only as a **measure of last resort**.
[52:1:13] - **AP High Court (Dec 2020)** asked whether it could record a "breakdown of constitutional machinery" – **Art. 356**.
[52:1:14] > Asked as: Article (356 – 6 PYQs); maximum period (3 years); approval period (2 months); extension beyond 1 year (EC certificate + Emergency); consequences (statements); who reports (Governor); Ambedkar's "dead letter".
[52:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 23 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-23.txt) p.10; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch17 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.265-270; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.23, p.119; app notes 2:52 sub 3
[52:1:16] - **Art. 355:** the Union's **duty** to ensure that every State's government is carried on **in accordance with the Constitution** (and to protect it against external aggression and internal disturbance) – the basis of Art. 356.
## SUB 2 | Scheme of Emergency Provisions – Three Emergencies Compared
[52:2:0] - **Part XVIII**, Arts **352-360**; source: **Government of India Act, 1935** (also the ordinance power, Arts 123/213); suspension of FRs from the **Weimar Constitution** (Germany).
[52:2:1] - The Constitution provides **three** emergencies; it has **no "President's Rule at Union level"**, though it does provide martial law (Art. 34) and special provisions for States (Art. 371 series).
[52:2:2] TABLE head: Feature | National (352) | President's Rule (356) | Financial (360)
  [52:2:2.0] Ground | War, external aggression, armed rebellion | Failure of constitutional machinery in a State | Threat to financial stability or credit
  [52:2:2.1] Approval within | 1 month | 2 months | 2 months
  [52:2:2.2] Majority | Special | Simple | Simple
  [52:2:2.3] Duration | 6 months, indefinite | 6 months, max 3 years | No maximum
  [52:2:2.4] Effect on FRs | Yes (358/359) | None | None
  [52:2:2.5] Used | 3 times (1962, 1971, 1975) | 125+ times; first Punjab 1951 | Never
[52:2:3] - Federal statement + reason "Art. 352 deals with failure of constitutional machinery" → the reason is **false** (that is Art. 356).
[52:2:4] > Asked as: Articles 352-360; how many types (three); which emergency for which ground (SSC); what the Constitution does not provide.
[52:2:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch17 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.259, p.267-268; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.10, p.23; app notes 2:52 sub 0
[52:2:6] - **Art. 352** deals with the **proclamation of Emergency** (on actual or imminent danger); 'an emergency may take place at any time' is true but does not explain the Article.
## SUB 3 | Effects of National Emergency – Fundamental Rights, Terms, State List
[52:3:0] # Article 358 vs Article 359
[52:3:1] TABLE head: Basis | Article 358 | Article 359
  [52:3:1.0] What | Suspends the six freedoms of Art. 19 | Suspends the right to move courts for FRs named in the order
  [52:3:1.1] How | Automatic | Needs a Presidential Order
  [52:3:1.2] Ground | Only war or external aggression | Any National Emergency
  [52:3:1.3] Limit | Only Emergency-related laws protected | Arts 20 and 21 can never be suspended (44th Amendment)
[52:3:2] - FRs can be suspended **only during a National Emergency**, by the **President** – not by Parliament's law, a government notification, the PM or the Supreme Court.
[52:3:3] # Centre-State and terms
[52:3:4] - **Art. 250:** **Parliament** (not a minister) makes laws on **State List** subjects for any part of India; they lapse **6 months** after the Emergency.
[52:3:5] - **Lok Sabha term (Art. 83(2)):** Parliament **by law** may extend it **one year at a time**, not beyond **6 months** after the Emergency ends; same for State Assemblies.
[52:3:6] - **Art. 353** executive directions; **Art. 354** revenue distribution modified.
[52:3:7] > Asked as: who can suspend FRs (5 PYQs); Art. 359; Lok Sabha extension (2 PYQs); who legislates on the State List.
[52:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 23 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-23.txt) p.9; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch17 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.261-264; app notes 2:52 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Financial Emergency (Article 360)
[52:4:0] - Ground: threat to the **financial stability or credit of India** or any part; proclaimed by the **President**.
[52:4:1] - Approval within **two months**, **simple majority**; once approved it continues **indefinitely – no maximum period** – till revoked.
[52:4:2] - **Effects:** directions to States on **canons of financial propriety**; **reduction of salaries and allowances** of State employees and of all persons serving the Union **including Supreme Court and High Court judges**; State **Money and Financial Bills reserved** for the President – the Centre gains full control over States' finances.
[52:4:3] - **Never declared** so far (nearest: the 1991 crisis) – Art. 360 is the emergency "never implemented".
[52:4:4] > Asked as: statements (2-month approval true; "excluding judges" false – 3 PYQs); effects (all four); never declared; no maximum period.
[52:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 23 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-23.txt) p.11; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch17 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.271-273; app notes 2:52 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Instances of National Emergency and the 1975 Emergency
[52:5:0] TABLE head: Instance | Date | Ground | President
  [52:5:0.0] 1st | 26 Oct 1962 | Chinese aggression (war) | S. Radhakrishnan
  [52:5:0.1] 2nd | 3 Dec 1971 | Indo-Pak war (external aggression) | V.V. Giri
  [52:5:0.2] 3rd | 25 June 1975 | "Internal disturbance" (while the 1971 one was still on) | Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
[52:5:1] - **Trigger of 1975:** the **Allahabad High Court** (12 June 1975, *Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain*) voided Indira Gandhi's 1971 election – not the railway strike, Nav Nirman or inflation, which were background.
[52:5:2] - **Twenty Point Programme:** launched by Indira Gandhi in **1975** during the Emergency; restructured 1982, 1986, 2006; monitored by **MoSPI**.
[52:5:3] - **25 June** – "**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas**" since 2025.
[52:5:4] > Asked as: how many times (3); date of the internal-disturbance proclamation (25 June 1975); trigger; 20-point programme year.
[52:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 23 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-23.txt) p.9; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch17 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.264; app notes 2:52 sub 1
## SUB 6 | President's Rule in Andhra Pradesh and Other States
[52:6:0] TABLE head: Spell | Period | Context
  [52:6:0.0] Andhra State | Nov 1954 – Mar 1955 | Fall of the Prakasam ministry
  [52:6:0.1] AP 1st (longest) | 18 Jan 1973 – 10 Dec 1973 | Jai Andhra agitation; CM P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned; ended when Jalagam Vengala Rao became CM; Six-Point Formula → 32nd Amendment (Art. 371D)
  [52:6:0.2] AP 2nd | 1 Mar 2014 – 8 Jun 2014 | CM Kiran Kumar Reddy resigned over bifurcation
[52:6:1] - **First PR in India:** Punjab, **1951**; **never under PR:** Chhattisgarh and Telangana.
[52:6:2] - **Most times:** **Manipur – 11** (latest Feb 2025), then **Uttar Pradesh – 10**.
[52:6:3] - **Longest total period:** **Jammu & Kashmir** (~12¾ years); among States, **Punjab** (~10½ years, incl. the continuous 1987-92 spell).
[52:6:4] - **Manipur:** PR from **13 Feb 2025** after **N. Biren Singh** resigned; revoked **4 Feb 2026** – **Yumnam Khemchand Singh** sworn in as CM.
[52:6:5] - **J&K:** under the former State Constitution (s.92) the **Governor** imposed Governor's Rule for 6 months, followed by President's Rule under Art. 356; since the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019** the UT comes under President's Rule by the **President (s.73)**.

## SUB 7 | S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994) and Other Cases
[52:7:0] - **9-judge bench**; the landmark case on **Art. 356** and **Centre-State relations**.
[52:7:1] - Proclamation is subject to **judicial review**; majority to be tested on the **floor of the Assembly**; Assembly only **suspended** until Parliament approves; court may **restore** a dismissed government.
[52:7:2] - **Secularism and federalism** are **basic features**.
[52:7:3] TABLE head: Case | Year | Ruling
  [52:7:3.0] ADM Jabalpur | 1976 | Right to life unenforceable in Emergency – overruled by K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)
  [52:7:3.1] Minerva Mills | 1980 | Art. 352 proclamation reviewable
  [52:7:3.2] S.R. Bommai | 1994 | Art. 356 – review, floor test, secularism + federalism
  [52:7:3.3] Rameshwar Prasad | 2006 | Bihar Assembly dissolution struck down
  [52:7:3.4] Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Basic structure
[52:7:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch17 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.268-270; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.59, p.110; app notes 2:52 sub 5

[52:8:0] TABLE head: Amendment | Change
  [52:8:0.0] 38th (1975) | President's satisfaction made non-justiciable
  [52:8:0.1] 39th (1975) | Election disputes of PM and Speaker beyond courts
  [52:8:0.2] 42nd (1976) | "Mini-Constitution"; Lok Sabha/Assembly terms 6 years
  [52:8:0.3] 44th (1978) | "Internal disturbance" → "armed rebellion"; written Cabinet decision; approval 1 month; special majority; Lok Sabha disapproval; Art. 358 only for war/external aggression; Arts 20, 21 beyond Art. 359

  x: President's Rule, like a Financial Emergency, is approved by a simple majority; only a National Emergency needs a special majority.
