## SUB 3 | Delimitation – Commission, Freeze and Amendments
[63:3:0] # Meaning and basis
[63:3:1] - **Delimitation** = fixing the **number and boundaries** of Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies, and the **SC/ST reserved seats**, on the latest **census** – "**one person, one vote, one value**".
[63:3:2] - The body that decides the number and size of constituencies = **Delimitation Commission** (not the ECI, NITI Aayog or MHA); purpose = revising **constituency** boundaries, **not State boundaries** (Parliament, Art. 3).
[63:3:3] - Basis: **Art. 82** (Lok Sabha), **Art. 170** (Assemblies) – readjustment after each census; seats go to States on **population, not area**.
[63:3:4] # Delimitation Commission
[63:3:5] - Set up by the **Central Government** under an **Act of Parliament**; can be set up for **select States/UTs** (2020: J&K, Assam, Manipur, Arunachal, Nagaland). Nodal ministry: **Ministry of Law and Justice** (Legislative Department).
[63:3:6] - Members (2002 Act): a retired **Supreme Court judge** (chair), the **CEC** or an EC he nominates, and the **State Election Commissioner** – ex officio.
[63:3:7] - Orders have the **force of law**: **cannot be questioned in any court** and **cannot be modified** when laid before the Lok Sabha/Assembly (UPSC 2012: both correct).
[63:3:8] TABLE head: Act | Commission | Chair
  [63:3:8.0] 1952 | 1952 (first) | Justice N. Chandrasekhara Aiyar
  [63:3:8.1] 1962 | 1963 | Justice J.L. Kapur
  [63:3:8.2] 1972 | 1973 | Justice J.L. Kapur
  [63:3:8.3] 2002 | 2002 | Justice Kuldip Singh
  [63:3:8.4] J&K | 2020 (orders 2022) | Justice Ranjana Desai
[63:3:9] - **Four** Delimitation Commissions (1952, 1963, 1973, 2002) till December 2023 (UPSC 2024).
[63:3:10] # Freeze
[63:3:11] TABLE head: Amendment | Effect
  [63:3:11.0] 42nd (1976) | Froze State seat shares on the 1971 Census till 2000
  [63:3:11.1] 84th (2001) | Freeze extended till the first census after 2026; lifted the freeze for redrawing boundaries (on 1991 Census)
  [63:3:11.2] 87th (2003) | Boundaries redrawn on the 2001 Census, total seats unchanged
[63:3:12] - Present constituencies (2001 Census) continue till the **first census after 2026**. Lok Sabha: **543** elected; ceiling **550 (530 States + 20 UTs)**.
[63:3:13] - AP Reorganisation Act, 2014, **Sec. 26**: AP Assembly **175 → 225**, Telangana 119 → 153, subject to Art. 170 – waits for the **first census after 2026**. The **RPA 1950** deals with **allocation of seats and electoral rolls**.
[63:3:14] - 2026: **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill** – Lok Sabha ceiling 550 → **850**; **defeated** in the Lok Sabha for want of a special majority. Southern States fear seats shifting to **UP, Bihar, Rajasthan**; Tamil Nadu Assembly resolution (Aug 2026) sought a permanent freeze at 543 and women's quota from 2029 not tied to delimitation.
[63:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Polity 02 p.23; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams 02 p.1; Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch. Delimitation Commission; app's current notes row 63
## SUB 4 | Electoral Systems and Types of Elections
[63:4:0] # Who is elected how
[63:4:1] TABLE head: Office / House | Electorate | Method
  [63:4:1.0] Lok Sabha / Legislative Assembly | Citizens directly (adult suffrage) | First past the post, single-member territorial constituencies
  [63:4:1.1] Rajya Sabha | Elected MLAs; seats allotted to States by population | PR – single transferable vote
  [63:4:1.2] President | Elected MPs + elected MLAs (incl. Delhi, Puducherry – 70th Amendment) | PR-STV
  [63:4:1.3] Vice-President (Art. 66) | All MPs – elected and nominated; State Legislatures have no role | PR-STV
  [63:4:1.4] Legislative Council | MLAs, local bodies, graduates, teachers + Governor's nominees | PR-STV
[63:4:2] - India uses **direct election on adult suffrage** and **PR by single transferable vote**; the **list system** and **cumulative vote** are not used.
[63:4:3] # First past the post vs proportional representation
[63:4:4] - **FPTP** (plurality): the candidate with **more votes than any other** wins – no 50% needed. Vote-seat distortion, e.g. **Karnataka 1994**: Janata Dal 116 seats on 36% votes.
[63:4:5] - **PR** gives seats in proportion to votes → **representation of minorities**; not needed where a **two-party system** has developed (UK). Rejected for the Lok Sabha: complex, fragmentation, **unstable governments**, no by-elections.
[63:4:6] # Types of elections and special constituencies
[63:4:7] TABLE head: Type | Meaning
  [63:4:7.0] General | All seats, at normal end of term
  [63:4:7.1] Mid-term | After the House is dissolved before its term ends
  [63:4:7.2] By-election | A single vacancy; within 6 months (Sec. 151A) – not if the remaining term is under one year
[63:4:8] - **Floating constituency**: no fixed geographical boundary – **Sangha (Sikkim)**: only registered **Buddhist monks** vote and contest (both statements correct).
[63:4:9] - **Security deposit** is forfeited if a candidate does not get **more than one-sixth** of the valid votes (Sec. 158).
[63:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams 01 p.14-15, 02 p.1; Laxmikanth 8th ed. p.301 (Vice-President), p.328 (Rajya Sabha); NextGen Rocket Polity 01 p.64
[63:4:11] - **Minimum age to contest:** Lok Sabha/Assembly **25**, Panchayats and Municipalities **21**.
## SUB 5 | EVM-VVPAT, NOTA and Indelible Ink
[63:5:0] # EVM and VVPAT
[63:5:1] - EVM = electronic vote-recording and counting device (not an electoral system). **First used: Parur (Kerala), 1982**; older EVMs recorded up to **3,840** votes – current ECI EVMs up to **2,000**.
[63:5:2] - **VVPAT first used: Noksen Assembly by-poll, Nagaland, 4 September 2013** (not LS 2014, Goa 2017).
[63:5:3] - **N. Chandrababu Naidu v UoI (2019)**: VVPAT slips tallied in **5 polling stations per Assembly segment**. **ADR v ECI (2024)**: SC rejected **100% VVPAT** counting; 2nd/3rd-placed candidates may seek checks of 5% of EVMs.
[63:5:4] # NOTA
[63:5:5] - **PUCL v Union of India, 27 September 2013** – SC ordered a NOTA button on all EVMs (secret negative vote, **Art. 19(1)(a)**). NOTA introduced in **2013** – first used in the **Nov-Dec 2013 Assembly polls**; first Lok Sabha use **2014 = 16th Lok Sabha** (1.1% votes). The 12th-15th Lok Sabha polls had no NOTA, and it was not used in 2009.
[63:5:6] - Symbol: ballot paper with a **black cross**, designed by **NID Ahmedabad**. NOTA votes are **not counted as valid votes** for result/deposit; even if NOTA tops, the leading candidate **wins** – no fresh poll; using NOTA is **voting, not abstention**.
[63:5:7] - **Not** for **Rajya Sabha / Legislative Councils** (SC struck it down, **2018**) – only direct elections.
[63:5:8] - Old **Rule 49-O**: voter refused to vote before the Presiding Officer, noted in **Form 17-A** – broke secrecy.
[63:5:9] # Indelible ink
[63:5:10] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [63:5:10.0] Maker | Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd
  [63:5:10.1] Formula | National Physical Laboratory
  [63:5:10.2] Chemical / finger | Silver nitrate / left forefinger
  [63:5:10.3] First used | 1962 general election
[63:5:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams 20 p.9, 26 p.3; NextGen Rocket Polity 02 p.24, p.57-58, p.80-81; ECI EVM FAQ (CEO Haryana)
## SUB 6 | Model Code of Conduct, Polls and Voter Facilitation
[63:6:0] # Model Code of Conduct
[63:6:1] - **ECI guidelines** evolved by **consensus of parties** – **not enacted by Parliament**, not in the Constitution, IPC or RPA (voluntary compliance); authority: **Art. 324**.
[63:6:2] - In force from the **announcement of the election schedule** (**Harbans Singh Jalal v UoI, 1997**) till results (A true, "enacted by Parliament" false).
[63:6:3] TABLE head: Year | Milestone
  [63:6:3.0] 1960 | First drafted and used in the Kerala Assembly election
  [63:6:3.1] 1968 | Formalised by the ECI
  [63:6:3.2] 1979 | Part VII ("party in power") added
  [63:6:3.3] 1991 | Strictly enforced by CEC T.N. Seshan
[63:6:4] - Part VII: ministers may **not combine official visits with campaigning**; ordinary official visits are allowed.
[63:6:5] - On violation the ECI can **warn / censure** a candidate or party (it cannot disqualify, cancel results or fine); recognition can be suspended under **Para 16A, Election Symbols Order, 1968**.
[63:6:6] # Exit polls and opinion polls
[63:6:7] - **Exit poll** = **post-election survey** of voters just after leaving the booth, by private agencies; **Sec. 126A**: barred from the first phase till **half an hour after the last phase**. **Opinion poll** = pre-poll survey; **Sec. 126**: 48-hour silence. They are not the same.
[63:6:8] # Voter days, apps and facilitation
[63:6:9] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [63:6:9.0] National Voters' Day | 25 January (ECI founded 1950); 9th NVD (2019) theme "No Voter to be Left Behind"
  [63:6:9.1] NETA app | Voters rate representatives – built by a private start-up, not the ECI
  [63:6:9.2] Sahulat app | Jammu and Kashmir (Rajouri, 2019) – elderly voters
  [63:6:9.3] Braille ballots | Meghalaya – first State at all booths
  [63:6:9.4] cVIGIL | Report MCC violations with geo-tagged photo/video; action in 100 minutes
  [63:6:9.5] ECINET | One platform for 40+ ECI apps
  [63:6:9.6] Saksham | Voters with disabilities
  [63:6:9.7] SVEEP (2009) | Voter education; ECI partnered Indian Railways
[63:6:10] - Postal ballot: service voters, poll staff, **preventive detenus**; home voting for seniors **85+**.
[63:6:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Polity 01 p.63, 02 p.24; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams 02 p.3, 26 p.3; app's current notes row 63
## SUB 7 | Candidates, RPA Acts, Machinery and Election Petitions
[63:7:0] # Candidates and the RPA
[63:7:1] - Lok Sabha nomination: **any citizen of India whose name is on the electoral roll of any constituency**, aged **25+** (residence in that constituency not needed).
[63:7:2] - **Sec. 8 RPA 1951** (made by **Parliament**): conviction with **2+ years** → disqualified during the sentence + **6 years** after release (not permanently). A non-member minister must be **qualified for membership**, not merely a voter.
[63:7:3] TABLE head: Basis | RPA 1950 | RPA 1951
  [63:7:3.0] Deals with | Allocation of seats, delimitation framework, voter qualifications, electoral rolls | Conduct of elections, disqualifications, party registration (Sec. 29A), corrupt practices, election petitions
  [63:7:3.1] Linked Articles | 81, 82, 170, 171, 325, 326 | 84, 102, 173, 191, 324, 329
[63:7:4] - **Sec. 14 / 15**: **President** (Lok Sabha) / **Governor** (Assembly) issue the formal notification on ECI's recommendation; the ECI notifies the schedule, scrutinises nominations, allots symbols. **Validity of an election** is settled only by the **courts**.
[63:7:5] - **Sec. 77-78**: expense accounts to the **DEO** within **30 days**.
[63:7:6] # Rolls, machinery and parties
[63:7:7] - Rolls: four **qualifying dates** – 1 Jan, 1 Apr, 1 Jul, 1 Oct (not 1 December); **Special Intensive Revision** rebuilds the roll (**Bihar** SIR removed about 70 lakh names).
[63:7:8] - Officers: **CEO** (State), **DEO** = usually the **District Collector**, **Returning Officer** conducts the poll and declares the result; observers (Sec. 20B) – general, police, **expenditure**. The ECI controls officers on poll duty.
[63:7:9] - Parties: **registered** by the **ECI** under **Sec. 29A RPA 1951**; **recognised** by the ECI under the **Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968**. National party: State party in **4** States, or 6% votes in 4 States + 4 LS seats, or 2% LS seats from 3 States; State party: 3% of Assembly seats or **3** seats. **Six** national parties (2025): BJP, INC, BSP, CPI(M), AAP, NPP (not TMC). ECI delisted **808** registered unrecognised parties.
[63:7:10] # Election petitions
[63:7:11] TABLE head: Section (RPA 1951) | Content
  [63:7:11.0] 80 | No election can be questioned except by an election petition (Art. 329(b))
  [63:7:11.1] 80A | Tried by the High Court (original jurisdiction); to try to decide in 6 months
  [63:7:11.2] 81 | Filed within 45 days of the result
  [63:7:11.3] 100 | Grounds for declaring an election void (disqualification, corrupt practice, improper rejection of nomination – not a small margin)
[63:7:12] - Appeal: **Supreme Court**. **President / Vice-President** election disputes: **only the Supreme Court** (Art. 71) – not Parliament or the ECI.
[63:7:13] - Electoral offences (bribery, undue influence, personation): from **1 July 2024 BNS Chapter IX (Secs. 169-177)**.
[63:7:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Polity 02 p.22-24, 01 p.64; Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch.81-83; app's current notes row 63

## SUB 0 | Committees and Commissions on Electoral Reform
[64:0:0] TABLE head: Committee / Report | Year | Subject – the answer word
  [64:0:0.0] Tarkunde Committee (unofficial, set up by Jayaprakash Narayan in his "Total Revolution") | 1974-75 | Electoral reforms: 3-member ECI; voting age 18; EC chosen by a panel of PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI (not the Speaker)
  [64:0:0.1] Dinesh Goswami Committee (V.P. Singh's National Front govt; Goswami was Law Minister) | 1990 | Electoral reforms (broadest review): government (State) funding of Parliamentary elections (partly, in kind), EVMs, curb booth capturing, rotate SC/ST seats → many reforms enacted in the RP (Amendment) Act, 1996
  [64:0:0.2] Vohra Committee | 1993 | Nexus between crime and politics (criminals, politicians, officials)
  [64:0:0.3] Indrajit Gupta Committee (8 members, BJP-led govt) | 1998 (report 1999) | State funding of elections – partial, in kind, only to national/State parties with a symbol; held "constitutionally and legally justified"; not adopted
  [64:0:0.4] Law Commission 170th Report | 1999 | Reform of electoral laws: simultaneous polls, internal party democracy, some list (PR) seats

  [64:0:0.10] Law Commission 255th Report | 2015 | Electoral reforms: election finance, paid news, collegium for CEC, ECI power to deregister parties, one candidate one seat, totaliser

## SUB 1 | EVM, VVPAT, NOTA and the Chronology of Reforms
[64:1:0] # EVM – firsts and law
[64:1:1] TABLE head: Date | Milestone
  [64:1:1.0] 19 May 1982 | First EVM use – Parur (Kerala) Assembly seat; challenged in A.C. Jose v Sivan Pillai
  [64:1:1.1] 1989 | Section 61A, RPA 1951 – statutory backing to EVMs (not Art. 328/329)
  [64:1:1.2] 1998 | Experimental use in selected Assembly seats of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi – not Gujarat
  [64:1:1.3] 1999 | Goa – first entire State Assembly election on EVMs
  [64:1:1.4] 2004 | 14th Lok Sabha – first national election held entirely on EVMs
  [64:1:1.5] 4 Sep 2013 | VVPAT first used – Noksen (Nagaland) Assembly by-election
[64:1:2] - **Makers:** **BEL** (Bengaluru) and **ECIL** (**Hyderabad**).
[64:1:3] - **M3** (third-generation) EVM and **VVPAT M3** are in use: up to **2,000 votes**; one control unit takes **24 ballot units = 384 candidates incl. NOTA**; **tamper detection and self-diagnostics**. **M2**: 4 ballot units, **64** candidates.
[64:1:4] # VVPAT
[64:1:5] - The printed slip (serial no., name, symbol) is visible through a window for **7 seconds** (not 30), then is cut and drops into a **sealed box** – it is **never handed to the voter**; it gives the voter instant feedback that the vote went to the chosen candidate.
[64:1:6] - **Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013):** VVPAT "an indispensable requirement of free and fair elections", to be brought in **in phases**.
[64:1:7] - **N. Chandrababu Naidu (2019):** VVPAT-EVM tally raised from **1 to 5 polling stations** per Assembly segment.
[64:1:8] - **ADR v ECI (April 2024):** no 100% slip count and **no return to paper ballots**; **symbol-loading units sealed 45 days**; 2nd/3rd-placed candidates may seek a check of **5% of EVMs** within 7 days.
[64:1:9] - Slips are counted wherever EVM data and **Form 17C** do not match. Counting order: **postal ballots → penultimate EVM round → final round**.
[64:1:10] - **Remote EVM (RVM)** prototype (Jan 2023): lets **domestic migrants** vote for up to **72 constituencies** from one remote polling station. **Totaliser** (Law Commission 255th): pools several machines to **hide booth-wise trends**.
[64:1:11] # NOTA and other reforms
[64:1:12] - **NOTA** = a voter's choice to **reject all the contesting candidates** while keeping the ballot secret – **PUCL v UoI, 27 Sep 2013** (Art. 19(1)(a)); introduced on EVMs in **2013** (Assembly polls of **Chhattisgarh, Mizoram, Rajasthan, MP, Delhi**); first Lok Sabha use **2014**. Even if NOTA tops the poll, the candidate with the most votes wins.
[64:1:13] TABLE head: Year | Reform
  [64:1:13.0] 1988-89 | 61st Amendment – voting age 21 → 18
  [64:1:13.1] 1993 | EPIC (photo identity cards) under CEC T.N. Seshan
  [64:1:13.2] 2010 | Overseas (NRI) electors
  [64:1:13.3] 2021 | Election Laws (Amendment) Act – Aadhaar-roll linking, four qualifying dates, "spouse" for "wife", requisition of premises
  [64:1:13.4] 2023 | CEC and ECs Act – selection panel = PM, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM, Leader of Opposition; CJI dropped
  [64:1:13.5] 2025-26 | ECINET; max 1,200 electors per polling station; SIR of rolls (AP: Alluri Sitharama Raju district – 100% digitisation of SIR forms, Jul 2026); ECI–SEC declaration of 26 Feb 2026 under CEC Gyanesh Kumar
[64:1:14] - **Chronology:** **EVM (1982) → EPIC (1993) → VVPAT (4 Sep 2013) → NOTA (27 Sep 2013)**; and Sec. 61A (1989) → EPIC (1993) → two-seat cap (1996) → Aadhaar linking (2021).
[64:1:15] > Asked as: legal basis of EVMs (Sec. 61A RPA); EVM firsts (Goa 1999 true, Gujarat 1998 false – APPSC Group-II); VVPAT version (M3), first use (Nagaland 2013) and display time (7 s, not 30 s); NOTA meaning and year (2013); chronology EVM-EPIC-VVPAT-NOTA (UPPSC 2025).
[64:1:16] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch81 p.364 and Ch83 p.374, 378-379 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt); NextGen Rocket Polity Part 2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt) p.24, 80; NextGen Polity APPSC Part 18.1 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.3; app notes 2:64 sub 7-8
## SUB 2 | Electoral Bonds and Party Funding
[64:2:0] - **Electoral Bond Scheme:** announced in Budget 2017 (**Finance Act, 2017**), notified **2 January 2018**; stated aim – **clean money and transparency** in political funding.
[64:2:1] - **Instrument:** a **bearer** banking instrument like a promissory note, without the buyer's or payee's name; sold **only by SBI** branches; denominations **₹1,000, ₹10,000, ₹1 lakh, ₹10 lakh, ₹1 crore**; valid **15 calendar days**; credited to the party's account **the same day**.
[64:2:2] - **Buyer:** a **citizen of India** or a body **incorporated or established in India** (alone or jointly).
[64:2:3] - **Recipient:** only a party registered under **Sec. 29A, RPA 1951** that secured **not less than 1%** (not 2%) of the votes in the last Lok Sabha or Assembly election; encashed only through its bank account with SBI.
[64:2:4] - **ADR v Union of India, 15 Feb 2024:** a **five-judge bench, unanimously, struck the scheme down as unconstitutional** – it violated voters' **right to information, Art. 19(1)(a)**; also struck down the **removal of the corporate donation cap** (Companies Act); **SBI** had to give donor data to the **ECI**. (2024 = bonds struck down, not introduced.)
[64:2:5] - **Other funding rules:** anonymous cash donation cap cut **₹20,000 → ₹2,000** (Budget 2017); donations above ₹2,000 only by cheque/bank transfer; parties report contributions above **₹20,000** to the ECI; tax exemption – now **Sec. 12, Income-tax Act 2025** (earlier Sec. 13A, 1961 Act); 2017 removed the **7.5% of net profit** cap on corporate donations.
[64:2:6] - **ADR:** about **60% (₹19,083 crore)** of party funds in 2004-23 came from undisclosed sources.
[64:2:7] > Asked as: SC ruling (struck down – APPSC 2024-25); statements on buyer, value, 15-day life, 29A party, 1% threshold (AP 2023: all correct; RAS 2018: 2% statement false).
[64:2:8] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch83 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.380; PMF Polity Part 4 (src/polity/pmf-polity-04.txt) p.54, 59; Electoral Bond Scheme 2018 notification (PIB, 2 Jan 2018); app notes 2:64 sub 4-5
## SUB 3 | Representation of the People Act, 1951 – Key Sections
[64:3:0] TABLE head: Section | Provision
  [64:3:0.0] 8 | Conviction with 2+ years' jail → disqualified, plus 6 years after release; 8(4) struck down (Lily Thomas, 2013)
  [64:3:0.1] 29A | Registration of parties with the ECI
  [64:3:0.2] 33(7) | Contest from at most two constituencies (added 1996)
  [64:3:0.3] 33A | Disclosure of criminal antecedents
  [64:3:0.4] 34 | Security deposit: ₹25,000 Lok Sabha, ₹10,000 Assembly; SC/ST half (raised in 2009)
  [64:3:0.5] 61A | Use of EVMs (inserted 1989)
  [64:3:0.6] 70 | Vacate one of two seats within 14 days
  [64:3:0.7] 77 / 78 | Keep an account of election expenses / file it with the DEO within 30 days
  [64:3:0.8] 81 | Election petition in the High Court within 45 days
  [64:3:0.9] 123 | Corrupt practices – bribery, undue influence, appeal on grounds of religion, race, caste, community or language (123(3))
  [64:3:0.10] 126 / 126A | Campaign silence 48 hours / ban on exit polls
  [64:3:0.11] 135B / 135C | Paid holiday on polling day / liquor ban 48 hours before the poll
  [64:3:0.12] 151A | By-election within six months
[64:3:1] - **Deposit forfeited** if a candidate fails to secure **more than one-sixth (1/6) of the valid votes polled**; so if even the **winner** loses his deposit, **a very large number of candidates** contested and votes were split.
[64:3:2] - **Abhiram Singh v C.D. Commachen (Jan 2017):** a 7-judge bench read **Sec. 123(3)** widely – votes cannot be sought in the name of religion, race, caste, community or language (of candidate or voter).
[64:3:3] - **Two-seat cap:** in **1991 Devi Lal** contested **three** Lok Sabha seats; the **RP (Amendment) Act, 1996** capped it at **two** (Sec. 33(7)). No rule makes a party or candidate bear by-poll costs – that is only an ECI/Law Commission ("one candidate, one seat") proposal.
[64:3:4] - **1996 Act (Goswami):** two-seat cap; higher deposits; 10 proposers for independents/unrecognised-party candidates; poll **not countermanded** on a candidate's death (a recognised party may name a substitute within 7 days); paid holiday; liquor ban; by-polls in 6 months; 6-year bar for offences under the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971**.
[64:3:5] - **2003:** Rajya Sabha domicile requirement removed (any elector in India; upheld in **Kuldip Nayar, 2006**) and **open ballot** introduced.
[64:3:6] - **1990s:** the **most Lok Sabha and Assembly elections** were held in the **1990s** (Lok Sabha 1991, 1996, 1998, 1999 – frequent changes of government and hung Houses).
[64:3:7] > Asked as: deposit (1/6 of valid votes – twice); section interpreted in the religion/caste ruling (123); UPSC 2021 statements (Devi Lal 1991 true; "no law" and "party bears by-poll cost" false); EVM provision (61A).
[64:3:8] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch82-83 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.369-370, 374-375, 378; NextGen Rocket Polity Part 2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt) p.22-23; PMF Polity Part 4 (src/polity/pmf-polity-04.txt) p.57-58; app notes 2:64 sub 1-2
## SUB 4 | Election Expenditure Limits and Money Power
[64:4:0] TABLE head: Category | Lok Sabha | Assembly
  [64:4:0.0] Larger States/UTs (2022) | ₹95 lakh (₹70 lakh from 2014; ₹40 lakh from Feb 2011; ₹25 lakh before) | ₹40 lakh (earlier ₹28 lakh; ₹16 lakh in 2011)
  [64:4:0.1] Smaller States/UTs (2022) | ₹75 lakh (earlier ₹54 lakh) | ₹28 lakh (earlier ₹20 lakh)
[64:4:1] - **Basis:** **Rule 90, Conduct of Election Rules, 1961**; raised by the **Conduct of Elections (Amendment) Rules, 2022**. **₹1 crore was never the limit.**
[64:4:2] - The ceiling applies to **candidates only**, not parties (**Sec. 77** loophole) – there is **no limit on expenditure by political parties**; star campaigners' travel is excluded. Failure to file accounts → ECI can **disqualify for 3 years**.
[64:4:3] - **RUPPs:** over **2,800**, only about 750 contested in 2024; the ECI delisted **808** non-compliant ones.
[64:4:4] > Asked as: expenditure limit for a Lok Sabha seat in big States (₹40 lakh in 2011-12 – now ₹95 lakh).
[64:4:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch83 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.377; PMF Polity Part 4 (src/polity/pmf-polity-04.txt) p.58; ECI press note 28 Feb 2011 and Conduct of Elections (Amendment) Rules, 2022 (eci.gov.in; PIB 7 Jan 2022); app notes 2:64 sub 4
## SUB 5 | State Funding of Elections
[64:5:0] TABLE head: Type | Meaning
  [64:5:0.0] Partial | The State meets some costs, in cash or in kind (airtime, fuel, rallies)
  [64:5:0.1] Full | The State bears all legitimate costs; private donations banned
[64:5:1] - **Recommended by:** **Indrajit Gupta (1998)** – partial, in kind, to recognised parties; **Dinesh Goswami (1990)** – government funding of Parliamentary polls; **2nd ARC** – partial.
[64:5:2] - **Law Commission 170th Report:** full State funding desirable **only if parties are barred** from taking funds from other sources.
[64:5:3] - **Practised in:** Germany, Sweden, Japan, Canada.
[64:5:4] - **For:** curbs black money and quid-pro-quo; **level field for resource-poor candidates (Art. 14)**. **Against:** fiscal burden; does not stop off-book cash.
[64:5:5] - **State of Karnataka v Prathik Parasrampuria (2026):** eliminating black money from elections is a core duty of the **Election Commission of India**. Idea (Jan 2026): a pooled **National Election Fund**.
[64:5:6] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch83 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.381 fn.1; PMF Polity Part 4 (src/polity/pmf-polity-04.txt) p.60; app notes 2:64 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Criminalisation of Politics – Cases and Steps
[64:6:0] TABLE head: Case | Year | Holding
  [64:6:0.0] ADR v UoI | 2002 | Candidates disclose criminal cases, assets, liabilities, education
  [64:6:0.1] PUCL v UoI | 2003 | Voter's right to know (Art. 19(1)(a)); struck down Sec. 33B
  [64:6:0.2] Lily Thomas v UoI | July 2013 | Struck down Sec. 8(4); a convicted MP/MLA is disqualified immediately, no 3-month appeal shield
  [64:6:0.3] Krishnamurthy v Sivakumar | 2015 | Hiding serious cases vitiates the nomination
  [64:6:0.4] Public Interest Foundation | 2018 | 5 judges; did not disqualify on framing of charges – left it to Parliament; parties must publish records
[64:6:1] - **Patna High Court (2004):** jailed persons (no right to vote) cannot contest; SC upheld (2013); Parliament amended the RPA (2013) to let them contest.
[64:6:2] - **Tenth Schedule** disqualification is decided by the **Speaker/Chairman**, subject to **judicial review** (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).
[64:6:3] - **ECI rule:** parties fielding candidates with criminal records must publish the records and the **reasons for selecting** them.
[64:6:4] - **Data:** **31%** of Lok Sabha MPs elected in 2024 face serious criminal charges (ADR; 14% in 2009); **12 special courts** for MP/MLA cases; "**bahubali culture**" = **muscle power**.
[64:6:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch83 and Ch86 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.376, 379, 393; PMF Polity Part 4 (src/polity/pmf-polity-04.txt) p.58; app notes 2:64 sub 3
## SUB 7 | One Nation One Election – Simultaneous Polls
[64:7:0] - Lok Sabha and Assembly polls were held together **1951-52 to 1967**; backed by the Law Commission **170th (1999)** and its 2018 draft report.
[64:7:1] - **High-Level Committee** (set up **2 Sep 2023**), chair **Ram Nath Kovind**; members include **Amit Shah, Ghulam Nabi Azad**, N.K. Singh, Subhash C. Kashyap, Harish Salve, Sanjay Kothari. Lok Sabha + Assemblies first, **local bodies within 100 days**; safeguard idea – the **German constructive vote of no-confidence**.
[64:7:2] - **Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024** (Dec 2024, referred to a **Joint Parliamentary Committee**): inserts **Art. 82A** and amends **Art. 83** (duration of Parliament), **Art. 172** (duration of State Legislatures) and **Art. 327** – not Art. 246 or 280.
[64:7:3] - **Art. 356** (President's Rule) is also named in the debate (Law Commission 2018 draft listed 83, 85, 172, 174, 356) because a mid-term dissolution breaks the cycle.
[64:7:4] > Asked as: which Article needs amendment (83 and 172 – the CGPSC 2024 printed key gave 356).
[64:7:5] ~~ Sources: Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 (prsindia.org); Report of the High-Level Committee on Simultaneous Elections (onoe.gov.in, March 2024); app notes 2:64 sub 9

  On which date was the Electoral Bond Scheme notified?
  *2 January 2018 | 15 February 2024 | 1 April 2017 | 2 January 2019
  x: The scheme was notified on 2 January 2018 and struck down on 15 February 2024.
[f5a5a92e2a15a] sub2

  x: A five-judge bench unanimously held the scheme unconstitutional.
[gd3155bdca4ac] sub2

  *Finance Act, 2017 | Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996 | Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 | Companies Act, 2013
  x: The Electoral Bond Scheme was notified on 2 January 2018 on the basis of the Finance Act, 2017.
[n95a0bbaf615] sub3
  Which Section of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 bans exit polls?

  x: Section 126A of the RPA, 1951 concerns the ban on exit polls.
[nindian-polity-25-31] sub3

  One-third | One-fourth | One-half | *One-sixth
  x: A candidate loses the security deposit if they win no more than one-sixth of the valid votes.
[nindian-polity-25-13] sub3
  Under Section 33(7) of the RPA, 1951, from how many constituencies at most can a candidate contest a Lok Sabha or Assembly election?
  One constituency | *Two constituencies | Three constituencies | Four constituencies
  x: Section 33(7), added in 1996, limits a candidate to two constituencies.
[n23e870ce7e5] sub3
  Disclosure of criminal antecedents of candidates is dealt with in which Section of the RPA, 1951?
  Section 8 | Section 29A | Section 123 | *Section 33A
  x: Section 33A concerns disclosure of criminal antecedents; Section 8 is disqualification, 29A registration and 123 corrupt practices.
[n239f32561b3] sub3
  Which one of the following is NOT included among the corrupt practices covered by Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951?
  *Failure to file an election expenditure account within 30 days | Bribery | Appeal on the grounds of religion or caste | Undue influence
  x: Section 123 covers corrupt practices such as bribery, undue influence and appeals based on religion or caste. Filing the expenditure account within 30 days is governed by Section 78.
[na6776d883fb] sub3
  Within how many days must a person elected from two constituencies vacate one of them?
  10 days | *14 days | 30 days | 60 days
  x: Under Section 70 one seat must be vacated within 14 days; the two-constituency cap in Section 33(7) came with the 1996 amendment.
[nc255b81140e] sub3
  Which Section of the RPA, 1951 requires a candidate to keep an account of election expenses?
  *Section 77 | Section 78 | Section 70 | Section 123
  x: Section 77 requires the account to be kept; Section 78 requires it to be filed with the DEO within 30 days.
[n5b0a369112f] sub3
  Under Section 34 of the RPA 1951, what is the security deposit for a general-category Lok Sabha candidate?
  ₹10,000 | ₹12,500 | *₹25,000 | ₹50,000
  x: It is ₹25,000 for the Lok Sabha and ₹10,000 for an Assembly; SC/ST candidates pay half.
[n54bbd019382] sub3
  What does Section 81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 relate to?
  Registration of political parties | Corrupt practices during an election campaign | The maintenance of election expenditure accounts | *Election petitions presented in the High Court within 45 days of the result
  x: Section 81 concerns election petitions, which are presented in the High Court within 45 days of the election result.
[nf4aeee141bb] sub3

  x: Section 151A concerns holding a by-election within six months. Section 135B provides for a paid holiday, Section 135C concerns the liquor ban, and Section 70 deals with vacating one of two seats.
[nindian-polity-73-19] sub3

  2013 | 1982 | *1989 | 1993

[fdd5568537002] sub3

  *1 only | 2 only | Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2

[fc7c62d1587ac] sub3

[nindian-polity-53-9] sub3
  Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the death of a contesting candidate?

[neba772ed4bf] sub3

  Criminalisation of politics | State funding of elections | Paid news | *Candidates contesting from more than one constituency
  x: The Law Commission proposed 'one candidate, one seat' for candidates contesting from more than one constituency; the ECI proposed the vacating candidate bear by-election costs.
[n3014713e66a] sub3

  x: The 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies, increased security deposits, and required more proposers for independents and unrecognised parties.
[nindian-polity-53-24] sub3

  Indrajit Gupta | Dinesh Goswami | *Devi Lal | V.P. Singh
  x: The 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies after Devi Lal stood from three Lok Sabha seats in 1991.
[nindian-polity-53-8] sub3

Reason (R): The 2003 Amendment removed the requirement that the candidate be an elector in the particular State.
  *Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A | Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A | A is true, but R is false | A is false, but R is true
  x: Both are true: since a 2003 amendment removed the rule that a candidate must be a voter in that State, any registered voter in India can contest a Rajya Sabha seat from any State. R explains A.
[f80c680d5c033] sub3

[g88b4a2e09883] sub3

[n1fe38e89a68] sub3

[ne2203077099] sub4
  Why is Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 criticised in the context of party expenditure?
  Prohibits all expenditure on election campaigns | *Places a ceiling only on the expenditure of candidates, not on the election expenditure incurred directly by political parties | Places a ceiling only on political parties, not on candidates | Requires all campaign expenditure to be incurred in cash
  x: The perceived loophole is that Section 77 caps candidate expenditure while not imposing a comparable ceiling on the parties’ own election spending.

  x: The level-field argument rests on equality under Article 14; curbing black money is another argument in favour, while the fiscal burden is an argument against.

  x: The Supreme Court described elimination of black money from elections as a core responsibility of the Election Commission of India.

  x: Bearing all legitimate costs while banning private donations describes full funding; funding may be full or partial, in cash or in kind.

[na96026b9b52] sub6

  x: The Speaker or Chairman decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, but the decision remains subject to judicial review, as recognised by the Supreme Court in 1992.
[nc0475c8910d] sub6
  The judgment in Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) is associated with which of the following conclusions?
  Disqualification of legislators was transferred from Parliament to the Election Commission. | Only a sitting legislator can be disqualified after a three-month period. | A convicted legislator remains protected until the disposal of the appeal. | *A convicted legislator is disqualified immediately, without protection during the pendency of an appeal.
  x: The Lily Thomas judgment held that conviction leads to immediate disqualification and that an appeal does not provide protection against that disqualification.
[nf872a3ef75d] sub6
  In which case was mandatory disclosure by candidates of criminal cases, assets, liabilities and education laid down?
  Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India | Lily Thomas v. Union of India | Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India | *ADR v. Union of India (2002)
  x: ADR (2002) made such disclosure mandatory; PUCL placed the voter's right to know in Article 19(1)(a).
[nb6ab69977e5] sub6

  x: The Court did not itself impose disqualification on framing of charges; it left the issue to Parliament.
[nc191234fd0c] sub6

  x: The expression refers to the use of muscle power and its adverse effect on trust in legislatures.
[f7a65ae5b5fa9] sub6

  x: PUCL (2003) upheld the voter's right to know under Article 19(1)(a) and struck down Section 33B.
[fc0fbd8deec2f] sub6

  x: Lily Thomas struck down Section 8(4), the three-month appeal buffer, making disqualification immediate on conviction.
[f414486d56360] sub6

  Ordered immediate disqualification | *Left the matter to Parliament | Made it a ground under Section 8 | Directed the ECI to bar such candidates
  x: The five-judge bench did not disqualify on framing of charges and left it to Parliament, but required parties to publish criminal records.
[gc6b06c08b638] sub6

  x: The Patna High Court so ruled in 2004 and the Supreme Court upheld it in 2013; Parliament then amended the RPA to let detained persons contest.
[ge7f3942ddd16] sub6

  x: ADR data show MPs with serious charges rose from 14% (2009) to 31% (2024); 29% is the figure for MLAs.
[ge7284fcab41f] sub6

  x: In Krishnamurthy v Sivakumar (2015) the Court held that concealing serious cases vitiates the nomination.
[n377a64cc072] sub7

  x: Simultaneous polls were held from 1951-52 to 1967; both the 170th Law Commission Report and the 2018 draft report backed them.

  x: Former President Ram Nath Kovind chaired it; Amit Shah and N.K. Singh were members, and Dinesh Goswami headed the 1990 electoral reform committee.

[nbfff8799655] sub7

  x: The Bill proposes amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327, not Article 280.
[n2e5a965ec94] sub7

  x: The 129th Amendment Bill (introduced December 2024, referred to a JPC) aims at simultaneous Lok Sabha and Assembly elections (APPSC 2024 key); it inserts Art 82A and amends Arts 83, 172 and 327. ## SUB 2 | Indian National Congress – History Facts Asked
[65:2:0] - **"National"** in the name reflected the **reaction against British rule** (an all-India national identity).
[65:2:1] - **1891 Nagpur session (7th):** president **P. Anandacharlu** – the first Andhra to be INC President.
[65:2:2] - **1934:** **Congress Socialist Party** founded (Patna/Bombay) within the INC.
[65:2:3] - **1936:** the INC set up a **Foreign Department** under Nehru with **Ram Manohar Lohia** as its secretary.
[65:2:4] - **At Independence (1947)** the INC President was **J.B. Kripalani**.
[65:2:5] - **Mahatma Gandhi** advised that the INC be **disbanded as a political party** after Independence (and turned into a Lok Sevak Sangh).
[65:2:6] - **Kamaraj Plan (1963):** by **K. Kamaraj** – senior ministers resigned to work for the party, to **make the INC vibrant**.
[65:2:7] - INC = the "**grand old party**" of India in media usage; the standard nickname **GOP ("Grand Old Party")** belongs to the **US Republican Party**.
[65:2:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Modern India) via app notes 2:65 sub 3 and 5; aicc.org.in (INC presidents); Britannica, "Republican Party" (GOP)
## SUB 3 | Ideology, Classification and Party Concepts
[65:3:0] - **Ideological spectrum (Laxmikanth):** **left** – CPI, CPI(M); **centre** – Congress; **right** – BJP. Types: reactionary, conservative, liberal, radical.
[65:3:1] - **Communist parties' social base:** agricultural and industrial working class, the educated, youth – **not the business class**.
[65:3:2] - **Partyless democracy:** **Jayaprakash Narayan** (1950s; "A Plea for Reconstruction of Indian Polity", 1959) is the usual answer; it grew from **Gandhi's** ideas, and **M.N. Roy** also argued for a party-less "radical democracy".
[65:3:3] - **Inner-party democracy:** **periodic elections within the party** to choose office-bearers.
[65:3:4] - **Pressure groups** = the "**Anonymous Empire**" – seek influence, not power.
[65:3:5] - **Problems of parties:** money power, criminalisation (**Vohra Committee, 1993**), casteism, personality cult, defections, weak ideology.
[65:3:6] - **Largest party in the world** by primary membership: **BJP** (claimed 18 crore+, ahead of the Communist Party of China).
[65:3:7] - **Richest party** per National Election Watch (**Aug 2010**): **Congress**.
[65:3:8] - **BJP growth:** Lok Sabha vote share about **7.4% (1984) → 11.4% (1989) → 20-22% (1991)**; seats 2 → 85 → 120. First government in **Assam – 2016** (Sarbananda Sonowal). Impact of its rise (APPSC key): **polarisation of voters on communal lines**.
[65:3:9] > Asked as: partyless democracy (JP – asked twice, one key gave Gandhi); inner-party democracy; social base of communists; Kamaraj Plan; largest party; "Grand Old Party".
[65:3:10] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.352-353; PMF Polity Part 4 (src/polity/pmf-polity-04.txt) p.53-54; Britannica (Jayaprakash Narayan; M.N. Roy); app notes 2:65 sub 4-5
## SUB 4 | Recognition, Symbols and Legal Framework
[65:4:0] - **Registration:** by the **ECI** under **Sec. 29A, RPA 1951** – apply **within 30 days** of formation; pledge allegiance to the Constitution and to **socialism, secularism and democracy**, and India's sovereignty, unity and integrity.
[65:4:1] - **Recognition** (national/State) under the **Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968** – an ECI order, **not a constitutional provision**; based on poll performance, **not** on the number of States contested.
[65:4:2] - **National party** (any one): 6% votes in 4+ States + 4 Lok Sabha seats; or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from 3 States; or State party in 4 States.
[65:4:3] - **State party** routes include 6% votes + 2 Assembly seats; 6% + 1 Lok Sabha seat; 3% of Assembly seats or 3 seats; 1 Lok Sabha seat per 25; **8% of votes alone** (not 10%).
[65:4:4] - **National parties (2025): six** – **BJP, INC, BSP, CPI(M), AAP, NPP** (AAP got status in 2023; CPI, NCP, AITC lost it). **NPP** = first national party from the **North-East**.
[65:4:5] - **Symbols:** recognised parties → **reserved symbols**; RUPPs and independents → **free symbols**. **BSP – elephant** (the elephant is also the US **Republican** Party's symbol). **Bicycle**: TDP, SP, J&K Panthers Party; **RJD – hurricane lantern**.
[65:4:6] - **Split disputes** over name and symbol are decided by the **ECI** (para 15, Symbols Order) – **not the High Court**.
[65:4:7] - **Parties in the Constitution:** not in the original text; entered via the **Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985)**. Art. 19(1)(c) protects forming **associations** in general.
[65:4:8] - **INC v Institute of Social Welfare (2002):** the ECI **cannot ordinarily deregister** a party.
[65:4:9] - **Funding:** donors above **₹20,000** disclosed yearly; donations above **₹2,000** only by cheque/bank transfer; **ADR v UoI (15 Feb 2024)** struck down electoral bonds.
[65:4:10] > Asked as: number of national parties (6, as of 2025); "more than 10 national parties" (false); recognition provision in the Constitution (false); symbol not bicycle (RJD); BSP elephant.
[65:4:11] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.354-355; PMF Polity Part 4 (src/polity/pmf-polity-04.txt) p.53-54; NextGen Rocket Polity Part 2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt) p.22, 24; eci.gov.in (list of political parties and symbols); app notes 2:65 sub 6-7

## SUB 1 | Nature of the Indian Party System
[66:1:0] - **Party systems (Laxmikanth):** **one-party** (USSR; today China, **Cuba, North Korea, Eritrea** – not **Chile**, a multi-party democracy); **two-party** (USA, Britain); **multi-party** (France, Switzerland, Italy, **India**).
[66:1:1] - **India is multi-party** – continental size, diverse society (region, language, caste, religion, class), universal adult franchise; India has the **largest number of parties** in the world.
[66:1:2] - The **party system is a part (sub-system) of the political system**.
[66:1:3] - **Features:** one-dominant party (Congress) till 1967; lack of clear ideology (except BJP, CPI, CPM); **personality cult**; parties on traditional factors; rise of **regional parties**; factions and defections (after 1967); lack of effective opposition.
[66:1:4] - The **original Constitution had no provision on parties**; they entered via the **Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985)**.
[66:1:5] - **ECI classes:** national, State, **registered-unrecognised** parties (RUPPs – over 2,800, only ~750 contested in 2024).
[66:1:6] - **Ruling-party misuse:** government servants, vehicles and discretionary grants may be misused to woo voters – "political parties" are not such a government resource.
[66:1:7] TABLE head: Assertion – Reason (UP PSC) | Key
  [66:1:7.0] A: No fixed party system in India. R: There are too many parties. | Both true, R explains A
  [66:1:7.1] A: Parties are the life-blood of democracy. R: People blame parties for bad governance. | Printed key: both true, R explains A (strictly R does not explain A)
  [66:1:7.2] A: India has a written Constitution. R: Strong regional parties indicate regional aspirations. | Both true, R does not explain A
  [66:1:7.3] A: India has a multi-party system. R: Society is divided by region, language, caste, religion, class. | Both true, R explains A
[66:1:8] > Asked as: assertion-reason (3); which country is not one-party (Chile); party system part of which system (political).
[66:1:9] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.352-353; Ch86 p.394; app notes 2:66 sub 0
## SUB 2 | One-Party Dominance – the "Congress System"
[66:2:0] TABLE head: Term / work | Scholar
  [66:2:0.0] "Congress system" (Asian Survey, Dec 1964) / "one-party dominance system" | Rajni Kothari
  [66:2:0.1] "Dominance co-existing with competition, without a trace of alternative" | W.H. Morris-Jones
  [66:2:0.2] *Party Building in a New Nation* | Myron Weiner
[66:2:1] - **Congress system (1952-77):** Congress as an **umbrella** of many interests – **one-party dominance within a competitive multi-party democracy**. Kothari also wrote **Politics in India** and **Caste in Indian Politics**.
[66:2:2] TABLE head: Election | Significance
  [66:2:2.0] 1967 (4th) | Congress lost several States → Samyukta Vidhayak Dal coalitions; coalition era in the States begins
  [66:2:2.1] 1971 (5th) | Indira Gandhi's Congress (R) wins after the 1969 split (APPSC 2007 key: end of Congress dominance)
  [66:2:2.2] 1977 | First non-Congress government at the Centre (Janata)
  [66:2:2.3] 1980 | Congress returns
  [66:2:2.4] 1989 (9th) | End of the "Congress system"; Congress (197) still the single largest party; era of minority/coalition governments – the single-party government ended
  [66:2:2.5] 2014 | BJP majority on its own (282) – ended the 1989-2014 coalition era
[66:2:3] > Asked as: who called it one-party dominance (Rajni Kothari); election ending single-party government (1989); RPSC 2023 – 1989 ended the Congress system and INC was the largest party (both true).

## SUB 3 | First Non-Congress and Coalition Governments
[66:3:0] - **Centre, 1977:** the **Janata Party** (merger of Congress (O), Jana Sangh, BLD, Socialists; PM **Morarji Desai**, 1977-79) – the **first non-Congress government** and, in most books, the **first coalition government** at the Centre (Laxmikanth Table 85.1 lists it first).
[66:3:1] - Strictly, Janata was one merged party with its own majority (295); the first formal multi-party coalition was the **National Front (1989)**.
[66:3:2] - **States:** the usual answer for the first non-Congress government is the **CPI in Kerala (1957, E.M.S. Namboodiripad)** – the first elected communist government; strictly, **PEPSU's United Front** ministry (**Gian Singh Rarewala, April 1952**) came first.
[66:3:3] - **Coalition government** = an **arrangement of convenience** among parties (Latin *coalitio*, "to grow together") – **not mentioned in the Constitution**, not at the will of the President or Speaker.
[66:3:4] > Asked as: year of the first non-Congress / coalition government (1977 – four PYQs); Janata came to power (1977); first non-Congress State government (CPI, Kerala).
[66:3:5] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch85 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.387-388; Britannica (Patiala and East Punjab States Union; E.M.S. Namboodiripad); app notes 2:66 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Coalition and Minority Governments at the Centre
[66:4:0] TABLE head: Government | PM(s) | Period | Support
  [66:4:0.0] Janata Party | Morarji Desai | 1977-79 | First non-Congress
  [66:4:0.1] Janata (S) | Charan Singh | 1979-80 | Congress (I) outside – withdrew
  [66:4:0.2] National Front | V.P. Singh | Dec 1989-90 | Minority; outside support of BJP and the Left
  [66:4:0.3] Samajwadi Janata Party | Chandra Shekhar | Nov 1990-91 | Congress (I) outside – withdrew (resigned March 1991)
  [66:4:0.4] Congress | P.V. Narasimha Rao | 1991-96 | Minority, completed full term
  [66:4:0.5] BJP | A.B. Vajpayee | May 1996 | 13 days
  [66:4:0.6] United Front | H.D. Deve Gowda, I.K. Gujral | 1996-98 | Congress outside – withdrew from Deve Gowda (1997)
  [66:4:0.7] BJP-led / NDA | A.B. Vajpayee | 1998-99, 1999-2004 | "National Agenda for Governance"
  [66:4:0.8] UPA | Manmohan Singh | 2004-14 | "National Common Minimum Programme"; CPI and CPM outside (2004-08)
[66:4:1] - **Governments formed in 1990-99: seven** – Chandra Shekhar (1990), Rao (1991), Vajpayee (1996), Deve Gowda (1996), Gujral (1997), Vajpayee (1998), Vajpayee (1999); with V.P. Singh's (Dec 1989) eight; **six** different PMs.
[66:4:2] - **UPA-I partners (2004):** Congress 145, **RJD 24 (second largest)**, **DMK 16**, NCP 9, PMK, LJP, JMM.
[66:4:3] - **Coordination:** CMP + **coordination committee** (critics: a "super-cabinet"). The NDA's National Agenda gave **policy guidance, promises and a few guiding principles** without detailing everything.
[66:4:4] - **Why the coalition era:** growth of **regional parties**; inability of national parties to meet **regional aspirations**; coalitions **reflect popular opinion** more broadly – **not** greater stability (they are prone to instability).
[66:4:5] - **Consequences:** increased role of **regional and small parties**; consensus but slow decisions; no single party has absolute power; PM becomes "**primus inter pares**" (first among equals) who must consult partners; defections → **Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985)**; India did **not** become a two-party system.
[66:4:6] - Deve Gowda – 12th PM (counting Nanda); **Narendra Modi – 15th** PM.
[66:4:7] > Asked as: Congress (I) withdrew support from Charan Singh, Chandra Shekhar and Deve Gowda (all); second largest UPA party; reasons for coalition politics (A, B, D); primus inter pares; NDA national agenda (A-R); number of governments in the 1990s.
[66:4:8] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch85 Table 85.1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.388-390 and Table 81.1 p.366; app notes 2:66 sub 4-5, 7
## SUB 5 | Party Systems in the States (incl. Andhra Pradesh)
[66:5:0] - **After 1967:** almost every opposition-ruled State had a coalition – exception **Tamil Nadu (DMK alone)**; **Bihar** saw the **most coalition governments (nine) in 1967-71**.
[66:5:1] TABLE head: State | Pattern
  [66:5:1.0] Kerala | Bipolar: UDF (Congress-led) vs LDF (CPI(M)-led); A.K. Antony resigned as CM of the UDF government on 29 Aug 2004 after the Lok Sabha rout
  [66:5:1.1] Andhra Pradesh | Congress dominance until 1983; then Congress vs TDP; since 2014 TDP vs YSRCP; now a coalition led by a dominant regional party with the BJP as a supporting partner
[66:5:2] - **Congress's lowest AP Assembly tallies (undivided AP):** 1983 – 60, 1985 – 50, **1994 – 26 (lowest)**, 1999 – 91 – against **NTR's TDP**.
[66:5:3] - **AP roots:** Justice Party-era rise of **non-Brahmin agrarian castes** → base for regional parties.
[66:5:4] - **Aug 2026:** BJP rules alone in **11** States, Congress 3, regional parties alone 4, coalitions 10.
[66:5:5] > Asked as: Bihar 1967-71 record; Congress's lowest AP tally (1994); Antony's UDF government (2004).
[66:5:6] ~~ Sources: ECI Statistical Reports, AP Assembly 1983-1999 (eci.gov.in); NCERT XII Politics in India since Independence ch.6 (coalitions after 1967); app notes 2:66 sub 8
[66:5:7] - **TDP (N.T. Rama Rao, 1982):** came to power within **nine months** (Jan 1983) on '**Telugu atma gauravam**' (Telugu self-respect) – the textbook regional party.

## SUB 1 | Telugu Desam Party – Founding, Firsts and National Role
[67:1:0] # Founding and first victory
[67:1:1] - Founded by **NTR** on **29 March 1982** on **Telugu self-respect (Telugu atma gauravam)**; ideology: none specific beyond safeguarding the **political, economic, social and cultural foundations of Telugu-speaking people**.
[67:1:2] - Won power within **nine months** – **January 1983** Assembly election – ending the **Congress's unbroken rule since 1956**.
[67:1:3] - NTR was CM three times (1983-84, 1984-89, 1994-95) – **about seven years** in all.
[67:1:4] - **Pragathi Patham:** TDP's **15-point programme** (NTR era) – welfare thrust: drinking water, SC/ST/BC programmes, farm inputs.
[67:1:5] # National role
[67:1:6] - **8th Lok Sabha (1984):** TDP with **30 seats** = **main opposition party** – the **first regional party** to reach that position.
[67:1:7] - **1988:** NTR = **chairman of the National Front**, which formed the **V.P. Singh** government in **1989**.
[67:1:8] - **Gujarat censure motion (debated 30 April, voted 1 May 2002):** the **TDP** (backing the NDA from outside) **walked out before the vote** – it did not take part; the **AIADMK** and National Conference abstained, the **BSP voted against**; the motion was defeated (276-182).
[67:1:9] - **2018:** TDP **left the NDA** over **Special Category Status** for residuary AP; **2024:** back with the NDA – TDP leads AP's ruling coalition with **BJP** (and Jana Sena) support.
[67:1:10] - AP politics: **Congress vs TDP** (1983-2014); **TDP vs YSRCP** since 2014.
[67:1:11] > Asked as: largest opposition party in 1984 (TDP); incorrect statement on the TDP; party that did not vote on the 2002 Gujarat censure motion (2 PYQs); Pragathi Patham.
[67:1:12] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.807; Tribune 2 May 2002 "Censure motion defeated" (tribuneindia.com/2002/20020502/main1.htm); app notes 2:67 sub 3

## SUB 4 | Rise, Role and Impact of Regional Parties
[67:4:0] # Features and classification (Laxmikanth)
[67:4:1] - Operates within one State/region; articulates a cultural, linguistic, religious or ethnic identity; seeks power at State level and **greater State autonomy**.
[67:4:2] TABLE head: Type | Examples
  [67:4:2.0] Regional culture / ethnicity | Akali Dal, National Conference, DMK, Telugu Desam, Shiv Sena, AGP
  [67:4:2.1] All-India outlook, no national base | Samajwadi Party, NCP
  [67:4:2.2] Split from national parties | BJD, RJD, Trinamool, YSR Congress
  [67:4:2.3] Personalised (charismatic leader) | short-lived
[67:4:3] # Causes of rise
[67:4:4] - Cultural/ethnic pluralism; **economic disparities and regional imbalance (neglect)**; linguistic reorganisation of States; **failure of national parties** to meet regional aspirations; charismatic leaders; Congress centralisation; caste and religion.
[67:4:5] - Roots of regionalism: **historical, geographical, linguistic, religious, ethnic**. In Andhra, the **Justice Party** era awakened non-Brahmin agrarian castes – **Reddys, Kammas, Kapus, Velamas**.
[67:4:6] - After **1989** coalition arithmetic raised their weight.
[67:4:7] # Role and dysfunctions
[67:4:8] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [67:4:8.0] Coalitions | Kingmakers – supplied Speakers, Union Ministers, survival votes; PM became "first among equals"
  [67:4:8.1] Federalism | Challenged one-party dominance; made Centre-State bargaining real
  [67:4:8.2] Merits | Representation of backward regions, balanced development, wider voter choice
  [67:4:8.3] Demerits | Parochialism, instability, populism, inter-State disputes
[67:4:9] - **Special Category Status** for residuary AP – TDP left the NDA over it (**2018**).
[67:4:10] - BJP defeated regional parties: **BJD (Odisha, 2024)**, **AAP (Delhi, 2025)**, **Trinamool (West Bengal, 2026)**.
[67:4:11] # Autonomy demands
[67:4:12] TABLE head: Document / body | Party / State | Year
  [67:4:12.0] Rajamannar Committee | DMK government of Tamil Nadu (CM M. Karunanidhi) | set up 1969, report 1971
  [67:4:12.1] Anandpur Sahib Resolution | Shiromani Akali Dal (Punjab autonomy) | October 1973
  [67:4:12.2] Justice Kurian Joseph High-Level Committee | Tamil Nadu (CM M.K. Stalin) | 2025
[67:4:13] > Asked as: cause of rise (regional neglect); classification; autonomy documents (Rajamannar – see row 55).
[67:4:14] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch80 Role of Regional Parties (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.810-812; app notes 2:67 sub 0, 5-7

=== NOTES 2:68 | Recognition of National and State Parties – Criteria and the Symbols Order
## SUB 0 | National Party Criteria – Paragraph 6B of the Symbols Order
[68:0:0] - A party is a **national party** if it fulfils **any one** of three conditions (**Para 6B**, Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968):
[68:0:1] TABLE head: # | Condition
  [68:0:1.0] 1 | 6% of valid votes in four or more States at a Lok Sabha or Assembly general election AND at least 4 Lok Sabha seats from any State(s) – both mandatory
  [68:0:1.1] 2 | 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11 of 543) with members elected from at least three States
  [68:0:1.2] 3 | Recognised as a State party in four or more States
[68:0:2] - Memory hook: **6%-4 States + 4 seats / 2%-3 States / 4 States**.
[68:0:3] - Distractors (all wrong): "recognised in **2 or more** States", "**5%** of seats", "**3** States' recognition", "**5%** of votes in four States", "4% in one State", "10 Lok Sabha seats", "contests all constituencies", "power in four States", "10 Rajya Sabha seats".
[68:0:4] - APPSC G2: all three listed conditions valid → "**None of the above**" is the answer to "which is NOT a condition".
[68:0:5] > Asked as: which is a condition (5 PYQs); which is not (None of the above); State-party status in how many States (four); 6% in 4 States; statements with 2 States / 5% seats (neither).
[68:0:6] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.806; NextGen Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.63; NextGen Rocket Polity 2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt) p.24, p.26
## SUB 1 | National Parties – Number and List (dated)
[68:1:0] TABLE head: Date | National parties
  [68:1:0.0] 1952 (first Lok Sabha) | 14 national, 39 State parties
  [68:1:0.1] 1999 general election | 7 national (BJP, BSP, CPI, CPI(M), INC, JD(S), JD(U)), 40 State parties (ECI); some books print "6 and 48"
  [68:1:0.2] Eve of 2019 (March 2019) | 7 national (BJP, INC, CPI, CPI(M), BSP, NCP, AITC), 59 State parties (ECI data, 9 March 2019; Laxmikanth prints 52)
  [68:1:0.3] June 2019 | NPP (Meghalaya) recognised – first North-East national party → 8
  [68:1:0.4] May 2020 | Eight
  [68:1:0.5] 10 April 2023 review → now | Six: BJP, INC, CPI(M), BSP, NPP, AAP; AAP recognised; CPI, NCP, AITC derecognised
[68:1:1] - **18th general election (2024):** six national parties.
[68:1:2] - **AITC** got national status on **2 September 2016** – the latest after the 2014 Lok Sabha polls; lost it in **April 2023**.
[68:1:3] - **AAP:** **State party** (Delhi, Punjab) in 2019; **National party since April 2023**.
[68:1:4] - **Never national:** **DMK, Revolutionary Socialist Party, All India Forward Bloc, Peasants and Workers Party**, **Samajwadi Party**, **TDP**, YSRCP (TDP and YSRCP are **recognised State parties** in AP).
[68:1:5] - The ECI reviews status after each general election – the number of recognised parties keeps changing.
[68:1:6] > Asked as: number of national parties on a date (2019, May 2020); number of State parties (2019); AAP's status (2 PYQs – date-dependent); which is (not) a national party (5 PYQs); latest party to get national status (AITC 2016).
[68:1:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.807, 809; ECI notification 10-04-2023 (eci.gov.in); Business Standard / PIB 17-03-2019 "India now has 2,293 political parties"; Zee News "Story of 1999 Lok Sabha election"; app notes 2:68 sub 4
## SUB 2 | Registration and Recognition – Role of the ECI
[68:2:0] TABLE head: Step | Law | Authority
  [68:2:0.0] Registration | Sec. 29A, RPA 1951 | ECI
  [68:2:0.1] Recognition (national/State) and symbols | Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 | ECI
  [68:2:0.2] Split disputes | Para 15; Sadiq Ali (1971) majority test | ECI
  [68:2:0.3] Suspend/withdraw recognition | Para 16A – defying the Model Code of Conduct | ECI
[68:2:1] - Three statuses: **unregistered**; **registered but unrecognised (RUPP)**; **recognised** (national or State).
[68:2:2] - Apply for registration within **30 days** of formation; the party constitution must pledge allegiance to the **Constitution, socialism, secularism, democracy** and the unity and integrity of India.
[68:2:3] - The ECI **recognises** parties (not the President, Law Ministry or Speaker) on the basis of **poll performance**, and acts as a **court** in recognition and symbol disputes – it **does** settle disputes between splinter groups of recognised parties.
[68:2:4] - NCERT: the ECI requires parties to hold **organisational elections** and file income-tax returns.
[68:2:5] - **Nature of the 1968 Order:** a **statutory order of the ECI** under the RPA 1951 and **Art. 324** – not an Act of Parliament.
[68:2:6] - **Deregistration:** only for **fraud** in obtaining registration, ceasing allegiance to the Constitution, or being declared unlawful (**INC v. Institute of Social Welfare, 2002**); Law Commission **255th** Report seeks a limited power.
[68:2:7] - RUPPs: over **2,800**; about **750** contested in 2024.
[68:2:8] > Asked as: who recognises parties (ECI); wrong statement on the ECI and parties (splinter-group disputes); RPA 1951 registration statements.
[68:2:9] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.806; NextGen Rocket Polity 2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt) p.22; NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.2; NCERT Democratic Politics II ch.6 (src/polity/onlyias-ncert-polity-03.txt); app notes 2:68 sub 0-1
## SUB 3 | State Party Criteria
[68:3:0] - A party is a **State party** in a State if it fulfils **any one** of five conditions:
[68:3:1] TABLE head: Route | Condition
  [68:3:1.0] 1 | 6% valid votes in the Assembly election + 2 Assembly seats
  [68:3:1.1] 2 | 6% valid votes in the Lok Sabha election from the State + 1 Lok Sabha seat
  [68:3:1.2] 3 | 3% of Assembly seats or 3 seats, whichever is more
  [68:3:1.3] 4 | 1 Lok Sabha seat for every 25 allotted to the State
  [68:3:1.4] 5 | 8% of valid votes (Lok Sabha or Assembly) – no seat needed
[68:3:2] - The **8%** vote-only route is the one candidates forget (not 10%).
[68:3:3] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.806-807; app notes 2:68 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Symbols – Reserved and Free
[68:4:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [68:4:0.0] Reserved symbol | Only for recognised parties (Lotus – BJP, Hand – INC); national party: whole country; State party: its State(s); two recognised parties in different States may hold the same symbol
  [68:4:0.1] Free symbol | For RUPPs and independents from a notified list; latest May 2025 – 184 symbols
  [68:4:0.2] Common symbol for RUPPs | If they contest at least 2 Lok Sabha seats or 5% of Assembly seats
[68:4:1] - **CPI** – **ears of corn and sickle** since **1952**: the party that has contested **every** Lok Sabha election on the **same symbol** (Congress moved from bullocks → cow and calf → **hand**; the DMK first contested in 1957).
[68:4:2] - **Sadiq Ali (1971):** split disputes over name/symbol decided by **majority support** of the factions (Para 15). 2026: Trinamool rebel MPs chose a merger over a Para 15 claim.
[68:4:3] > Asked as: party with the same symbol in all 17 Lok Sabha elections (CPI).
[68:4:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.806; Business Standard 25-03-2019 "CPI writes to poll panel on its corn and sickle symbol"; app notes 2:68 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Recognition Benefits and RUPP Obligations
[68:5:0] TABLE head: Benefit | Recognised party | RUPP
  [68:5:0.0] Symbol | Reserved | Free / common on conditions
  [68:5:0.1] Proposers for nomination | One | Ten
  [68:5:0.2] Star campaigners (travel outside the candidate's limit) | Up to 40 | 20
  [68:5:0.3] Electoral rolls | Two free sets | –
  [68:5:0.4] Broadcast time | Akashvani and Doordarshan | –
[68:5:1] - RUPP obligations: tax exemption under **Sec. 12, Income Tax Act 2025**; disclose donors above **₹20,000**; donations above **₹2,000** only by cheque/bank transfer; must **contest at least once in six years** or be **delisted**.
[68:5:2] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch79 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.806; app notes 2:68 sub 6

=== NOTES 2:69 | Union Public Service Commission and State Public Service Commissions – Composition, Functions, Removal
## SUB 0 | Appointment, Composition and Term – UPSC, SPSC, JSPSC
[69:0:0] TABLE head: Point | UPSC | SPSC | JSPSC
  [69:0:0.0] Appointed by | President | Governor (Art. 316(1)) | President
  [69:0:0.1] Strength and service conditions fixed by | President (usually 9-11 incl. Chairman) | Governor | President
  [69:0:0.2] Term | 6 years or age 65 | 6 years or age 62 | 6 years or age 62
  [69:0:0.3] Resigns to | President | Governor | President
  [69:0:0.4] Removed by | President | President (not Governor) | President
  [69:0:0.5] Suspended during SC inquiry by | President | Governor | President
  [69:0:0.6] Annual report to | President | Governor | each concerned Governor
[69:0:1] - The Constitution does **not fix** the number of members; **at least half** must have held office under the GoI or a State Government for **10 years**.
[69:0:2] - **Acting Chairman** (Art. 316(1A), 15th Amendment 1963): a member appointed by the **President** (Governor for an SPSC) when the Chairman's office is vacant – **not** automatically the senior-most member.
[69:0:3] - **Conditions of service** of UPSC members are determined by the **President** (Art. 318) – not by Parliament or the CJI.
[69:0:4] - SPSC age limit was **60**, raised to **62** by the **41st Amendment (1976)**.
[69:0:5] - **MPPSC:** maximum **five** members (MPPSC 2021 key); the 1973 Regulations as amended read "not more than seven".
[69:0:6] - Compare: **CJI and SC judges retire at 65**; **High Court judges at 62**.
[69:0:7] > Asked as: who appoints SPSC members / Chairman (8 PYQs); who appoints UPSC / JSPSC members (3); term 6 years and age (65 UPSC, 62 SPSC/JSPSC – 4 PYQs); acting chairman (wrong statement); who fixes service conditions.

## SUB 1 | Constitutional Status – Part XIV, Articles 315-323
[69:1:0] - UPSC is an **independent constitutional body**, directly created by the **Constitution** (Art. 315) – not by an Act, ordinance or Presidential order; the **central recruiting agency** of India.
[69:1:1] - SPSCs are equally constitutional; the **UPSC has nothing to do with the SPSCs** (no supervision, no guidelines).
[69:1:2] - **Election Commission, Finance Commission and UPSC** all have **constitutional status**.
[69:1:3] - Provisions: **Part XIV, Articles 315-323** (not Part XIII, XVI or Arts 324-329).
[69:1:4] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [69:1:4.0] 315 | PSCs for the Union and the States (incl. JSPSC)
  [69:1:4.1] 316 | Appointment and term of members
  [69:1:4.2] 317 | Removal and suspension
  [69:1:4.3] 318 | Regulations on conditions of service
  [69:1:4.4] 319 | Bar on holding office after ceasing to be a member
  [69:1:4.5] 320 | Functions
  [69:1:4.6] 321 | Power to extend functions (by law)
  [69:1:4.7] 322 | Expenses – charged on the Consolidated Fund
  [69:1:4.8] 323 | Reports – UPSC to President, SPSC to Governor
[69:1:5] - **Sources of UPSC functions:** the **Constitution** (Art. 320), **Parliamentary laws** (Art. 321), **executive rules and orders** (e.g. Exemption from Consultation Regulations, 1958) and **conventions**.
[69:1:6] > Asked as: UPSC created by (Constitution – 3 PYQs); which Article / Part (4); constitutional bodies; A-R on central recruiting agency (G2 2025); UPSC and SPSC relation.
[69:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.4, p.6; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch44 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.604, 607-608; app notes 2:69 sub 0, 5
## SUB 2 | Removal and Suspension – Article 317
[69:2:0] # Grounds (President removes)
[69:2:1] - 1. Adjudged **insolvent**.
[69:2:2] - 2. **Paid employment** outside the duties of office during the term.
[69:2:3] - 3. **Infirmity of mind or body** – in the **President's opinion**.
[69:2:4] - 4. **Misbehaviour** – only after the President refers the matter to the **Supreme Court**, and the Court upholds it after an enquiry; its **advice is binding**.
[69:2:5] - **Misbehaviour (Art. 317(4))** includes being **interested in a government contract** or sharing in its profit.
[69:2:6] - **Parliament has no role** (unlike SC/HC judges and the CAG, who are removed on an address of both Houses).
[69:2:7] - **SPSC:** appointed by the Governor, **removed only by the President** after the **Supreme Court** enquiry (not the Governor, not a HC enquiry, not impeachment in the Vidhan Sabha); the **Governor** may suspend during the enquiry.
[69:2:8] - Being found guilty in a **civil case** is **not** a ground; "inquiry committee headed by the CJI" and "misconduct in the President's opinion" are loose versions of the real grounds.
[69:2:9] > Asked as: who removes a UPSC / SPSC member (7 PYQs); Article of removal (317); role of Parliament (none – UPSC 2020); grounds statements.
[69:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.4, p.7; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch44-45 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.604-605, 609-610; app notes 2:69 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Joint State PSC and UPSC Serving a State
[69:3:0] - **JSPSC (Art. 315(2)):** two or more States **agree**, their **Legislatures pass resolutions**, and **Parliament creates it by law** – a **statutory**, not constitutional, body. Example: **Punjab and Haryana** (once).
[69:3:1] - Chairman and members **appointed, suspended and removed by the President** (not the Governors, not a committee of Governors); resign to the **President**; term 6 years or **62**.
[69:3:2] - **Art. 315(4):** the **UPSC** may serve all or any needs of a State **on the request of the Governor** with the **approval of the President**.
[69:3:3] - On the request of two or more States the UPSC assists in **joint recruitment** schemes.
[69:3:4] > Asked as: who provides a JSPSC (Parliament – 3 PYQs); who appoints its Chairman (President – 3); UPSC serving a State (Governor's request + President's approval – 2).
[69:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.5, p.9; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch45 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.612; app notes 2:69 sub 8
## SUB 4 | Annual Report and Nature of Advice – Article 323
[69:4:0] TABLE head: Body | Report to | Laid before
  [69:4:0.0] UPSC | President (annually) | both Houses, with a memorandum on advice not accepted
  [69:4:0.1] SPSC (e.g. Rajasthan PSC) | Governor | State Legislature, with a similar memorandum
  [69:4:0.2] JSPSC | each concerned Governor | his State Legislature
[69:4:1] - **Non-acceptance** of UPSC advice: every case needs approval of the **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet**.
[69:4:2] - Advice is **advisory, not binding**; consultation is **directory, not mandatory** – action without consulting is **not invalid**; **selection confers no right to the post** (Supreme Court).
[69:4:3] - **Art. 321:** functions extended only by an **Act of Parliament** (State Legislature for an SPSC) – may cover **local bodies, corporate bodies, public institutions**.
[69:4:4] - **CVC** (1964; statutory 2003) is also consulted on disciplinary matters; the UPSC has the edge. SPSC = "**watchdog of the merit system**" in the State.
[69:4:5] > Asked as: UPSC annual report to (President – 4 PYQs); how often (annually); SPSC report to (Governor).
[69:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.5-6, p.8; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch44-45 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.606-607, 611; app notes 2:69 sub 6-7
## SUB 5 | Functions and Limitations – Article 320
[69:5:0] # Consulted on
[69:5:1] - Conducts **examinations** for **All-India, Central and Group-A services** and services of Union territories (SPSC: State services).
[69:5:2] - **Methods of recruitment**, framing and amendment of **recruitment rules**.
[69:5:3] - Principles of **appointment, promotion and transfer from one service to another**; suitability of candidates.
[69:5:4] - **Disciplinary matters** affecting civil servants; claims for **legal expenses**; **pension** for injuries on duty; any matter **referred by the President**.
[69:5:5] - **Temporary appointments of more than one year**; extension of service / re-employment.
[69:5:6] # NOT consulted
[69:5:7] - **Reservations** of posts for backward classes (**manner of reservation**); claims of SCs/STs.
[69:5:8] - **Temporary posts of less than one year**; **Group C/D** posts; chairpersons of boards/tribunals; **heads of diplomatic missions**.
[69:5:9] - **Classification, pay and training** of services (DoPT).
[69:5:10] - Actual **transfers** of civil servants (only the *principles* of transfer are referred).
[69:5:11] - **Departmental examinations** are not an Art. 320 function.
[69:5:12] - President (Governor for an SPSC) may exclude posts by **regulations**, laid before Parliament/Legislature for **14 days**.
[69:5:13] > Asked as: which is NOT a function (manner of reservation; departmental exams; transfers – 3 PYQs).
[69:5:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.5-6, p.8; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch44-45 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.605-607, 611; upsc.gov.in "Functions"; app notes 2:69 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Independence Safeguards and Post-Retirement Bar – Article 319
[69:6:0] - Removal only in the manner and on the grounds in the Constitution (**security of tenure**).
[69:6:1] - **Conditions of service** cannot be varied to the member's disadvantage after appointment.
[69:6:2] - **Expenses** charged on the **Consolidated Fund** (Art. 322) – not voted.
[69:6:3] - **No reappointment** to the same office (no second term).
[69:6:4] TABLE head: Office (on ceasing to hold it) | May later hold
  [69:6:4.0] UPSC Chairman | No further employment under GoI or any State (a Governor's post is not "employment" – A.R. Kidwai, 1979)
  [69:6:4.1] UPSC member | Chairman of the UPSC or of an SPSC only
  [69:6:4.2] SPSC Chairman | UPSC Chairman/member, or Chairman of another SPSC
  [69:6:4.3] SPSC member | UPSC Chairman/member, or Chairman of the same or another SPSC
[69:6:5] - A former SPSC member can get **no other government employment** (e.g. under the Government of India).
[69:6:6] > Asked as: employment open to a retired UPSC member (UPSC Chairman).
[69:6:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity APPSC Part 26 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-26.txt) p.4, p.7; Laxmikanth 8th ed. Ch44 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt) p.605, 608; app notes 2:69 sub 4

## SUB 8 | Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission
[69:8:0] - **APPSC** came into existence on **1 November 1956** with the formation of Andhra Pradesh, merging the **Andhra PSC (1953)** and the **Hyderabad PSC**.
[69:8:1] - **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 (s.83):** the existing PSC becomes the **PSC of AP**; a separate PSC to be constituted for **Telangana** under Art. 315; until then the **UPSC**, with the President's approval, may serve Telangana; the sitting Chairman and members continue with **AP** – they were **not divided on population basis**.
[69:8:2] - HQ moved to **Vijayawada**; strength **Chairman + 9 Members** (enhanced 1994); appointed by the **Governor of AP**, removed by the **President**; term 6 years / **62**.
[69:8:3] - Also conducts **lower judicial service** exams (SPSC consulted under **Art. 234**).
[69:8:4] - **Chairperson:** retired IPS officer **A.R. Anuradha** (**October 2024**), after **Gautam Sawang** resigned.
[69:8:5] > Asked as: year APPSC established (1956 – 2 PYQs); APRA 2014 wrong statement.
